# OpenMVIS: open-source multi-visual-inertial sensor calibration

URL: https://openmvis.com/

## The whole rig in one solve

OpenMVIS is developed by the OpenMVIS Contributors. The method is in our paper Multi-visual-inertial system: analysis, calibration, and estimation (Yang, Geneva and Huang, IJRR 2024). We test it on our own VI-Rig, shown here, and on recordings shared by device makers.
MVIS is the calibration toolbox behind the OpenMVIS benchmark. It solves camera intrinsics and distortion, extrinsics, time offsets, rolling-shutter readout, board poses and (optionally) the board shape, camera–IMU transforms, IMU intrinsics and biases in a single GTSAM factor graph.
It reads ROS1 and ROS2 bags through rosbags, so ROS does not need to be installed. It also reads EuRoC/ASL folders, image folders and timestamped images.

VI-Rig, our own rig: up to 5 IMUs and 4 cameras across its recordings. They are in Datasets.

## What Kalibr and Basalt do not cover

Kalibr and Basalt are the open-source camera–IMU toolboxes most people use. Neither covers these six cases. See the full comparison.

-

### Rolling shutter + IMU

A rolling-shutter camera reads its rows one after another. MVIS solves that readout time together with the IMU. Kalibr's rolling-shutter tool is camera-only; Basalt has none.
Guide Why calibrate rolling shutter

-

### Global + rolling shutter + IMU

Global-shutter and rolling-shutter cameras on one rig, solved with all its IMUs in one run. Our VI-Rig recording has 2 global-shutter cameras, 2 rolling-shutter cameras and 4 IMUs.
Example Config

-

### Board shape and pose

MVIS solves the board pose and, optionally, one height per corner (estimate.board_points). Kalibr and Basalt assume a flat board. On our VI-Rig mount, a flat solve biases the focal length by up to 1 % and the gyro scale by about 1 %.
Why calibrate the board shape

-

### Gyro-to-accel time offset

t_ga is the time offset between an IMU's gyroscope and its accelerometer. MVIS fits it by default in camera–IMU runs. Kalibr and Basalt use one IMU clock, so the offset leaks into the camera time offset.
Why calibrate t_ga

-

### Digital-twin simulation

A digital twin is a simulated copy of your recording where the truth is known. MVIS re-solves it and reports the error of each parameter, so you can test the solver on your own rig.
Guide

-

### Round-trip verification

mvis roundtrip applies the calibration to its own data and calibrates again. It reports PASS or FAIL without ground truth, and exits non-zero on FAIL so it can run in CI.
Guide

## What the graph estimates

Quantity | Symbol | Per | Unit | Notes |
Intrinsics + distortion | f, c, k | camera | px | Eight models, mixable within one rig |
Camera–IMU extrinsics | T_CtoI | camera | m · log(R) rad | Every camera to the base IMU, the reference IMU of the rig |
Camera time offset | t_d | camera | ms | About −123 ms of USB lag on the VI-Rig ELP stereo, against the Xsens IMU |
Rolling-shutter readout | t_r | camera | ms | Each corner projected at its own row time |
IMU–IMU extrinsics | T_IstoI | aux IMU | m · log(R) rad | Plus a per-IMU time offset |
IMU intrinsics | D_w, D_a | IMU | — | kalibr, rpng or calyx convention |
Gyro–accel offset | t_ga | IMU | ms | About −6.7 ms on the T265 IMU over 15 recordings; why calibrate t_ga |
Biases | b_g, b_a | IMU | rad/s · m/s² | Along the whole trajectory |
Board pose + trajectory | T_BinW, T_ItoW(t) | recording | m · log(R) rad | Chessboard, AprilGrid or ArUco targets |
Board shape | z_k | corner | mm | Optional, off by default; on for our VI-Rig runs; why calibrate the board shape |

## Camera models

- radtanPinhole, radial–tangential
- kb4Kannala–Brandt, the fisheye default (fisheye means kb4); why
- equidistantKB polynomial, under 90°
- fovField-of-view model
- double_sphereWide-angle fisheye
- eucmExtended unified camera
- ucmUnified camera
- omni_radtanOmnidirectional

## Checked against Kalibr on TUM-VI

0.2pxlargest median focal-length (fx, fy) difference from Kalibr; principal point within 0.35 px. Camera-only stereo, 8 raw recordings, view angles cut to 85° or less for every tool

<0.1mmmedian stereo-baseline difference, inside the 0.1 mm run-to-run spread; same 8 recordings

1.8mmlargest median lever-arm difference (camera position in the IMU frame), 4 raw and 4 512×512 recordings. Kalibr was given MVIS's intrinsics and baseline here

0.9msmedian camera time offset above Kalibr's; Basalt is within 0.1 ms of Kalibr. MVIS also fits t_ga (−1.5 to −1.6 ms here), which Kalibr does not have

Benchmark batch 2026-11-10a. See the Leaderboard and each device's calibration.

# install (Python 3.11 or 3.12)
$ pip install "pymvis[apriltag,ros1]"

# cameras only
$ mvis cam -c camera.yaml

# cameras + IMUs, jointly
$ mvis cam-imu -c cam_imu.yaml

# check the result: PASS / FAIL
$ mvis roundtrip -c cam_imu.yaml
One self-contained HTML report per run.
Package pymvis 0.1.0 on PyPI · command mvis · GPL-3.0-only or commercial · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24239182

## Checking a calibration

A low reprojection error says a calibration fits its own data, not that it is right. In a round trip, PASS needs the IMU intrinsics and biases to collapse to identity and zero, and the geometry to hold. See Round-trip validation.

Inputs: ROS1 and ROS2 bags, EuRoC/ASL folders, image folders, timestamped images

Targets: AprilGrid, chessboard, ArUco

Interop: Reads and writes Kalibr camchain and camchain-imucam

Export: mvis apply-calib writes a copy of a raw ROS1 bag with the calibration applied

}

journal = {The International Journal of Robotics Research},

pages = {1995--2026},

## MVIS toolbox

MVIS is dual-licensed. The copyright holder is named in the header of each
source file.

- GPL-3.0-only (LICENSE):
free for everyone, companies included, for research, teaching and internal
use. If you distribute software that includes or is derived from MVIS, you
must release it under GPL-3.0.

- Commercial licence
(COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md):
for closed-source products, or whenever you cannot meet the GPL-3.0 terms.
Write to licensing@openmvis.com.

### Calibration results

The GPL covers the MVIS code, not what it computes.

- Your recordings: results you compute on your own recordings
(intrinsics, extrinsics, time offsets, residuals, plots, reports) are yours.
You may publish them anywhere, including on commercial product pages, without
a commercial licence.

- Our datasets: results computed on the recordings we host (parameters,
metrics, plots, reports) are CC BY 4.0, commercial use included, also where
the recording itself is CC BY-NC 4.0. Our published results are in
calibench-vi/results.

- Third-party datasets: results you compute are yours; results that the
owner publishes, such as UZH-FPV’s own Kalibr files, keep the owner’s licence.

### Contributing code

Pull requests come with a contributor licence agreement, stated in
CONTRIBUTING.md.
It lets the maintainer also offer your contribution under the commercial
licence.

title = { {OpenMVIS}: open-source multi-visual-inertial sensor calibration } ,

author = { {OpenMVIS Contributors} } ,

year = { 2026 } ,

doi = { 10.5281/zenodo.24239182 } ,

url = { https://openmvis.com }

}

Results come in dated batches. If you compare against them, name the batch you
used, so the comparison stays citable after later batches land:

https://openmvis.com/benchmark/results/

The batch shown on the Leaderboard is the current one.
Methodology explains what the numbers mean.

Cite the MVIS paper, the preferred citation in

@article {yang2024mvis,

title = { Multi-visual-inertial system: Analysis, calibration, and estimation } ,

author = { Yang, Yulin and Geneva, Patrick and Huang, Guoquan } ,

journal = { The International Journal of Robotics Research } ,

year = { 2024 } ,

volume = { 43 } ,

number = { 13 } ,

pages = { 1995--2026 } ,

doi = { 10.1177/02783649241245726 }

}

If you use analytic combined IMU integration, ACI2, or ACI3 (ACI2 with IMU
intrinsics, from the MVIS paper above), also cite the ACI2 paper. Every MVIS
camera–IMU solve uses ACI3 in its IMU factors.

@inproceedings {yang2020aci2,

title = { Analytic Combined {IMU} Integration ({ACI}$^2$) For Visual Inertial Navigation } ,

author = { Yang, Yulin and Wisely Babu, Benzun Pious and Chen, Chuchu and Huang, Guoquan and Ren, Liu } ,

booktitle = { 2020 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) } ,

year = { 2020 } ,

pages = { 4680--4686 } ,

doi = { 10.1109/ICRA40945.2020.9197280 }

}

# Overview | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/getting-started/overview/

MVIS is open-source multi-visual-inertial sensor calibration: a Python toolbox
for camera and camera–IMU calibration, from a single camera to multi-camera,
multi-IMU rigs. An IMU (inertial measurement unit) is the sensor with a
gyroscope and an accelerometer.

- Package: pymvis. You import it as mvis and run it as the mvis command.

- Runs on: Linux and macOS (Windows tentative), Python 3.11 and 3.12, with no ROS install.
See Requirements.

- Code: github.com/openmvis/openmvis.

OpenMVIS, the project around MVIS, also publishes calibration
datasets, a benchmark against Kalibr and
Basalt, and a device wiki of calibrated sensors.

## What it solves

MVIS solves the quantities below from one recording, in a camera solve and
then a camera–IMU solve.

Quantity | Scope | Notes |
Camera intrinsics + distortion | per camera | Focal length, image centre and lens model. Eight models, mixable in one rig (Camera model) |
Camera extrinsics | per camera | Where each camera sits relative to the reference camera |
Camera–camera time offset | per camera | For cameras that are not hardware-synced |
Rolling-shutter readout | per rolling-shutter camera | The time the camera takes to read its rows, top to bottom (why) |
Board poses and board shape | per frame / per corner | The shape is one height per corner, off by default (why) |
Camera–IMU extrinsics T_CtoI and time offset td | per camera | |
IMU–IMU extrinsics and time offset | per auxiliary IMU | Each extra IMU relative to the base IMU, the first IMU in the config |
IMU intrinsics Dw, Da, optional Tg | per IMU | Gyro and accel scale and misalignment, in one of three conventions (IMU model) |
IMU biases | per IMU | |
Gyro–accel time offset t_ga | per IMU (not gyro-only IMUs) | The delay between the gyro and accel channels of one IMU, on by default (why) |

Several of these have no counterpart in Kalibr or Basalt. The
comparison lists them.

## How a run works

A calibration has two solves and a check.

- Cameras: mvis cam solves each camera’s lens and the camera–camera
extrinsics from a board recording. It writes a camera YAML and an HTML
report.

- Cameras + IMUs: mvis cam-imu reads that camera YAML as its starting
point and solves the camera–IMU extrinsics, time offsets and IMU
intrinsics. It writes a JSON result, a calibration YAML, a Kalibr
camchain where the camera model allows, and an HTML report.

- Check: mvis verdict grades a result GREEN, YELLOW or RED.
mvis roundtrip applies a camera–IMU calibration to its own recording and
calibrates again: the IMU intrinsics must come back as identity and the
geometry must not move. A digital twin of your rig
tells you what the recording can pin down before you trust it.

mvis run starts either solve from the config’s mode: field. Every command
is in the CLI reference.

Inside the camera solve, the steps are:

- Detection: find the board corners in every image.

- Quality gating: drop frames with too few tags and corners seen too
rarely.

- Init: a first guess of each lens and each board pose.

- Per-camera solve: refine each camera on its own, with its
rolling-shutter readout if it has one.

- Alignment: find where the cameras sit relative to each other, and
their time offsets.

- Joint solve: refine all cameras together.

- Outlier rerun: drop corners with large error and solve again.

The camera–IMU solve starts from the camera YAML, picks the part of the
recording with the most motion and runs one joint solve with the IMU data.

You can also start from an existing calibration, such as Kalibr output, and
pin what you trust. See Configuration.

## Where to go next

- First run: Requirements, then
Installation, then
Quickstart.

- Coming from Kalibr or Basalt: Comparison.

- Your own rig: the guides, from the board to the
round-trip check.

- Results on public data: Leaderboard and
Examples.

- The maths: Concepts.

# Comparison vs Kalibr / Basalt | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/getting-started/comparison/

Use this page to see where MVIS sits next to Kalibr and Basalt, the two
open-source camera–IMU toolboxes most people use. Kalibr is mature and widely
validated, and MVIS does not aim to replace it where it works well.

- Checked against: MVIS 0.1.0 and our benchmark runs of 10 November 2026
(Methodology).

- The numbers: per-dataset results of all three tools are on the
Leaderboard.

## Feature matrix

Capability | MVIS | Kalibr | Basalt |
Camera intrinsics + distortion | Yes | Yes | Yes |
Distortion models | radtan, kb4, equidistant, FOV, DS, EUCM, UCM, omni_radtan (experimental) | radtan, equidistant, FOV, omni, omni-radtan, DS, EUCM | radtan, KB4, DS, EUCM, UCM |
Different models in one rig | Yes | Yes | Yes |
Camera–IMU extrinsics + time offset | Yes | Yes | Yes |
Multiple IMUs in one solve | Yes | Yes | No, one IMU per run |
Gyro-only mode per auxiliary IMU | Yes | No | No |
IMU intrinsics (scale, misalignment) | Yes, 3 conventions (kalibr, rpng, calyx) | Yes | Yes, scale + misalignment |
G-sensitivity Tg | Yes | Yes | No |
Gyro–accel offset t_ga | Yes, on by default | No | No |
Board shape (one height per corner) | Yes, estimate.board_points | No, flat board | No, flat board |
KB4-type polynomial past 90° | Yes, kb4, what fisheye means | No, pinhole-equi needs rays in front of the camera | Yes, KB4 |
Rolling-shutter readout | Yes, in camera and camera–IMU solves | camera-only, separate tool | No |
Global + rolling shutter + IMUs in one solve | Yes, readout per camera | No | No |
Corrected-dataset export | Yes, apply-calib | No | No |
Digital-twin simulation | Yes, mvis.simulation | No | No |
Round-trip PASS/FAIL validation | Yes, roundtrip | No | No |
Batch sweep over a dataset family | Yes, input.bags | No | No |
Dataset download + check | Yes, mvis datasets | No | No |
Trajectory model | discrete factor graph | continuous-time B-spline | continuous-time B-spline |
Boards | AprilGrid, chessboard, ArUco | AprilGrid, chessboard, circles | AprilGrid |
Input | ROS1/ROS2 bag, EuRoC, image folders | ROS bag | ROS bag, EuRoC |
Runs without ROS | Yes, pure Python | No | Yes, C++ build, no ROS |
Platforms | Linux, macOS, Windows (tentative) (Python 3.11–3.12) | Linux (ROS 1, or Docker) | Linux, macOS |
Kalibr interop | Yes, read + write camchain, read AprilGrid targets | native | No |

## What is different

- No ROS, no C++ build. MVIS installs with pip and reads ROS1 and ROS2
bags itself. Kalibr needs a ROS workspace; Basalt needs a C++ build.
Requirements.

- More than one IMU, each with its own mode. MVIS puts every IMU in one
graph, and each auxiliary IMU (every IMU but the base) can run gyro-only
when its accelerometer is unreliable.
Kalibr also solves several IMUs in one run. Basalt takes one IMU per run, so
a four-IMU rig is calibrated IMU by IMU and composed.

- It fits the gyro–accel offset. t_ga is the time offset between the
gyroscope and accelerometer channels of one IMU. It is on by default in
camera–IMU runs. Kalibr and Basalt give an IMU one clock.

- On two real IMUs (the Looper Insight 9 and the T265) MVIS measures a
t_ga of about −5 to −6 ms.

- There, Kalibr’s and Basalt’s camera time offset td differs from MVIS
by about 1.6–3.2 ms. A sweep in which we delay only the accel predicts most of
that gap from t_ga alone.

- Not yet tested: which td is closer to the truth. Details.

- It can solve the board shape. With estimate.board_points: true MVIS
solves one height per corner. Kalibr and Basalt take the board as flat. On
our VI-Rig mount a flat solve shifts the focal length, gyro scale and lever.
Details.

- Rolling shutter in the camera–IMU solve. MVIS solves the readout time
together with the IMU. Kalibr’s rolling-shutter tool is camera-only.

- Validation is a command. mvis roundtrip applies the calibration to
its own recording, calibrates again and prints PASS or FAIL. A PASS needs
the IMU intrinsics to come back as identity and the geometry to stay put.
Neither Kalibr nor Basalt ships a check like it.
Round-trip validation.

- Discrete-time. MVIS places pose, velocity and bias states at a fixed
rate (state_hz, 30 Hz by default). Kalibr and Basalt fit a B-spline, a
smooth curve in continuous time.

## Next

- Try it: check the Requirements, then
follow Installation.

- Results on public data: the Leaderboard shows
MVIS, Kalibr and Basalt side by side.


---

# Requirements | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/getting-started/requirements/

Use this page to check that your machine and your recording fit MVIS before you
install it. The install itself is on Installation.

## System

- Operating system: Linux or macOS, on x86-64 or arm64.

- Windows: tentative. MVIS has run there, but GTSAM publishes no Windows
wheels on PyPI, so the install steps aren’t written up yet.

- Python: 3.11 or 3.12.

- Not supported, Python 3.13: NumPy 1.x, which GTSAM needs, has no Python
3.13 wheel.

- Not supported, Python 3.10 or older: GTSAM publishes no wheels below
Python 3.11.

- Nothing to compile: every dependency installs from a pip wheel.

## Python dependencies

pip installs these with MVIS. The bounds are the ones in pyproject.toml.

Package | Version | Used for |
GTSAM | ≥ 4.2, < 4.3 | Factor-graph solver, with SO(3)/SE(3) rotations and poses as native types |
NumPy | ≥ 1.20, < 2 | Arrays. GTSAM 4.2 is built for NumPy 1.x; NumPy 2 crashes it |
OpenCV (opencv-python) | ≥ 4.5, < 4.12 | Board detection and initial poses. OpenCV 4.12 and later need NumPy 2 |
SciPy | ≥ 1.7 | Numerics |
PyYAML | ≥ 6.0 | Config and result files |
Matplotlib, Plotly | ≥ 3.5, ≥ 5.0 | Figures in the HTML reports |
tqdm | ≥ 4.60 | Progress bars |

Board detectors and bag readers are optional extras. They are listed on
Installation.

## Input formats

Detection reads one image at a time, so memory does not grow with the size of
the recording. Set source_type per camera:

source_type | Input | Extra needed |
images | A folder of images, sorted by filename (.jpg .jpeg .png .bmp .tiff .tif) | — |
timestamped_images | A folder of images plus a CSV of filename,timestamp | — |
euroc | EuRoC / ASL folder, as in TUM-VI, EuRoC MAV and Monado SLAM | — |
rosbag_topic | ROS1 bag, several cameras from one file. sensor_msgs/Image, or CompressedImage in PNG or JPEG | ros1 |
ros2bag | ROS2 bag: the folder with its metadata.yaml, or one .db3 or .mcap file. Same image types as ROS1 | ros1 |

- No ROS install: the ros1 extra installs rosbags, a pure-Python
reader for ROS1 and ROS2 bags.

- Camera–IMU runs read a ROS1 bag, a ROS2 bag or a EuRoC mav0 folder
(input.format: ros1 | ros2 | euroc).

- mvis apply-calib and mvis roundtrip read and write ROS1 bags only.

- JPEG images are lossy and can shift corners. MVIS warns once per topic.

- Video files are not read. Extract the frames to a folder first.

## Calibration boards

Set board_type and the fields for your board:

Board | board_type | Required fields | Extra needed |
AprilGrid | apriltag | rows, cols, tag_size (m), tag_spacing (ratio), tag_family | apriltag |
Chessboard | chessboard | rows, cols (inner corners), square_size (m) | — |
ArUco | aruco | rows, cols, marker_size, marker_separation, aruco_dict | aruco |

A Kalibr AprilGrid target YAML loads in Python with
mvis.detection.apriltag_board.AprilTagBoard.from_kalibr_yaml; in a config,
copy its values into board:.
Set up the board covers printing and measuring it.

## What the recording needs

- The board in view: in every camera, filling the image from centre to
corners, near and far, at many tilts.

- Overlap between cameras: for camera extrinsics, cameras must see the
board at the same time in part of the recording.

- Motion for the IMU: rotation about all three axes and acceleration
along all three. Without it, the IMU intrinsics, lever arm and time offset
stay weakly pinned (Degeneracy).

- Timestamps: every image and IMU sample needs a timestamp. MVIS solves
the offsets between clocks; it cannot recover missing stamps.

Record the dataset gives the motion pattern step
by step. The mvis inspect command reports what a recording holds before you
solve.

## Next

Install MVIS: Installation.


---

# Installation | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/getting-started/installation/

Use this page to install MVIS and check that it works. Check
Requirements first: Linux or macOS (Windows
tentative), Python 3.11 or 3.12.

## 1. Install from PyPI

MVIS 0.1.0 is on PyPI as pymvis. Install it into
a fresh Python 3.11 or 3.12 virtual environment, then check the install:

python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # or python3.11

pip install " pymvis[apriltag,ros1] " # AprilGrid boards + ROS1/ROS2 bags

mvis check --env --smoke

- Package name: the package is pymvis; the import and the command are
mvis.

- Python 3.11 or 3.12: with Python 3.13 the install stops, because MVIS
requires a version below 3.13.

- ArUco boards: add the optional aruco extra:
pip install "pymvis[apriltag,aruco,ros1]".

- Core only: pip install pymvis installs no board detector or bag reader.

### From source (to edit MVIS or run the Quickstart configs)

Clone the code repository and install it in editable mode:

git clone https://github.com/openmvis/openmvis && cd openmvis

python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # or python3.11

pip install -e " .[apriltag,ros1,dev] "

- -e: an editable install. Edits to the checkout take effect without a
reinstall.

- Keep the checkout: the Quickstart runs
example configs from it.

### With conda

The repository also ships a setup script. It creates a conda environment
named mvis with Python 3.11, installs MVIS with the apriltag, aruco,
ros1, viz and dev extras, adds ffmpeg for the simulator videos, runs
mvis check --env --smoke and then the unit tests:

bash scripts/setup_env.sh

conda activate mvis

## 2. Pick the extras

The core install solves camera and camera–IMU calibrations and writes the
reports. Extras add board detectors, bag readers and tools:

Extra | Installs | Needed for |
apriltag | aprilgrid | AprilGrid boards |
aruco | opencv-contrib-python (< 4.12) | ArUco boards |
ros1 | rosbags (≥ 0.11.6) | ROS1 and ROS2 bags, read in pure Python with no ROS install |
mcap | mcap, mcap-protobuf-support, PyAV | Converting MCAP recordings |
viz | rerun-sdk | The Rerun 3D viewer (rerun_visualization: true) |
dev | pytest, pytest-cov, pytest-timeout | Running the test suite |

- aruco and OpenCV: opencv-contrib-python and opencv-python both
provide cv2, and the one installed last wins. If cv2 misbehaves, install
into a clean environment or uninstall opencv-python first.

Keep NumPy below 2
GTSAM 4.2 from pip is built against NumPy 1.x. With NumPy 2 it crashes with a
segmentation fault, which Python cannot catch. MVIS pins numpy<2 and
opencv-python<4.12 for this reason. Do not upgrade NumPy in the same
environment.

## 3. Check the install

mvis check --env --smoke

- --env: checks Python, NumPy, GTSAM, OpenCV, each installed extra, and
the mvis command. Each line reads PASS, WARN or FAIL.

- --smoke: also runs a short synthetic camera solve.

- With a config: mvis check --env -c config.yaml also checks the extras
that config needs.

mvis --help lists every subcommand. The CLI reference
documents each one.

## Next

Run your first calibration in the Quickstart.


---

# Quickstart | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/getting-started/quickstart/

Use this page to run a first calibration end to end on one of our recordings.
You download one bag, solve one camera, then solve three cameras with four
IMUs, and read the reports.

You need:

- MVIS installed from source, with the apriltag and ros1 extras. Run
every command below from the root of the openmvis checkout. See
Installation.

- About 7 GB of free disk for the recording.

- A Hugging Face account. The VI-Rig data is gated: you accept its terms
once on the Hub.

## 1. Get the recording

We use the first recording of VI-Rig — 4 IMUs + 3 cameras,
a rig we built for calibration research. It has a FLIR Blackfly camera, an
Intel RealSense T265 fisheye pair and four IMUs, all recorded in front of a 6 × 6
AprilGrid.

-
Accept the terms on
calibench-vi/datasets.

-
Give MVIS your token: set HF_TOKEN to a read token from your
Hugging Face settings. Or pip install huggingface_hub and run
hf auth login; MVIS reads the token file it writes.

-
Download recording april_01:

mvis datasets list --dataset mvis_4imus_3cams

mvis datasets download --select mvis_4imus_3cams/april_01

- Where it goes: $MVIS_DATASETS/mvis_4imus_3cams/virig_4imus_3cams_april_01.bag.
MVIS_DATASETS defaults to ~/Datasets. Configs refer to it as
${MVIS_DATASETS}.

- Checked: the download is verified against the checksum in the catalog.

- Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included.
If you publish with it, cite Calibench-VI and the MVIS paper; see
Citing the datasets
and Citing the paper.

mvis inspect <bag> prints the topics, rates and duration of a recording.

## 2. Calibrate one camera

Save this as quickstart/blackfly_cam.yaml inside the checkout:

quickstart/blackfly_cam.yaml
mode : cam

input :

cameras :

- camera_id : 0

name : Blackfly

source_type : rosbag_topic

source_path : ${MVIS_DATASETS}/mvis_4imus_3cams/virig_4imus_3cams_april_01.bag

topic : /blackfly/image_raw

distortion_model : radtan

shutter_type : global

board :

board_type : apriltag

rows : 6

cols : 6

tag_size : 0.088 # metres, measured on the printed board

tag_spacing : 0.3 # gap between tags, as a fraction of tag_size

tag_family : t36h11

solve :

max_iterations : 15

pixel_sigma : 1.0

huber_threshold : 1.345

estimate :

board_points : true # solve the board shape too

output :

path : results/quickstart/blackfly.yaml

format : yaml

- distortion_model: radtan: the Blackfly has a standard lens. For a
fisheye lens, use kb4. Camera model helps you
choose.

- tag_size: sets the scale of every distance MVIS reports. On your own
board, measure a printed tag; see Set up the board.

- estimate.board_points: our board is not flat, so we solve its shape.
Why.

Check the config, then solve:

mvis check -c quickstart/blackfly_cam.yaml

mvis cam -c quickstart/blackfly_cam.yaml -o results/quickstart/blackfly

On our Linux test machine this took about 7 minutes, mostly board detection.
The run folder results/quickstart/blackfly then holds:

File | Use |
quickstart_blackfly_cam.html | The report, one self-contained file |
quickstart_blackfly_cam_calib.yaml | The calibration. Deploy this, or feed it to mvis cam-imu |
quickstart_blackfly_cam_full.yaml | The calibration plus board poses, to replay the run |

The file names are <config folder>_<config name>. MVIS also copies the
result to output.path.

## 3. Calibrate cameras and IMUs

The repository ships a camera–IMU config for this recording. Run it as it is:

mvis cam-imu -c examples/configs/tga_mvis/tga_mti_01.yaml

- Sensors: all three cameras and all four IMUs. The Xsens MTi-100
(/imu/data) is the base IMU; the others are solved relative to it.

- Camera starting point: camera_input.path reads
examples/configs/tga_mvis/mvis_4imus_3cams_calib.yaml, the median of ten
camera-only solves per camera on this dataset. The lenses are held fixed
(estimate.camera.intrinsics: false). To use your own camera result,
point camera_input.path at its _calib.yaml.

- Solved: camera–IMU extrinsics and time offsets, IMU-to-IMU extrinsics
and time offsets, the IMU intrinsics Dw and Da in the calyx
convention, the biases, and each IMU’s gyro–accel offset t_ga.

- Window: window_mode: motion picks the 80 s with the most motion.

- Gravity: for your own data, set the local gravity where you recorded as the first
line of the config, for example gravity: 9.8013 # m/s², Newark, Delaware; the
Local gravity page has a calculator.

- Time: about 13 minutes on our Linux test machine.

It writes next to output.path (results/tga_mvis/mti_01/):

File | Use |
cam_imu.json | The full result |
cam_imu_calib.yaml | The calibration to deploy, or to pass to mvis apply-calib |
cam_imu_camchain-imucam.yaml | The same result as a Kalibr camchain |
cam_imu_report.html | The report |

## 4. Read the reports

Open the HTML files in a browser.

- Camera report: expand Calibration Data Quality and read the
motion-excitation assessment first, not the reprojection error. A fit can be tight while the recording never pinned a
parameter down. Then check the error per frame and the corner heatmaps for a
pattern.

- Camera–IMU report: start with the summary grades, then the 3D rig view:
each camera and IMU should sit where it sits on the real rig. Then read each
camera’s lever arm and td, and each IMU’s intrinsics.

- A grade for both: mvis verdict reads a result and prints GREEN, YELLOW
or RED with the reasons:

mvis verdict results/quickstart/blackfly.yaml

mvis verdict results/tga_mvis/mti_01/cam_imu.json

GREEN means every check passed; it does not mean the recording pinned every
parameter. Round-trip validation is the stronger test.

The Examples page shows our run of
this dataset, and its results page
compares it with Kalibr and Basalt.

## Next

- Your own rig: follow the guides from
Set up the board to
Round-trip validation.

- With an agent: the MVIS repository ships a Claude Code skill,
mvis-calibrate, that checks the installation (Stage 0) and then walks a
recording through seven gated stages (data qualification, sensor suite,
parameters, configs, solve, verification, release) on top of mvis inspect, mvis check,
mvis run, mvis verdict and mvis roundtrip. Start Claude Code in a
checkout, or copy its .claude/ folder next to your data, and run
/mvis-calibrate. See
doc/agent.md.

- Second reference dataset: TUM-VI, on Examples.

- Every config key: Configuration.

# Set up the calibration board | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/board-setup/

Step 1 of the walkthrough. Here you pick a board, measure it and describe it to MVIS.

- You need: a printed board, or a monitor to show one on.

- You get: a board: block for your config. Step 2 records with this board,
and step 3 puts the block in its config.

- Check: the tag or square size in the block matches what you measured on the board.

Running example
Every guide step uses the same rig: the VI-Rig recording set
virig-4imus-4cams. It has 4 IMUs, a RealSense T265 fisheye pair and an
ELP stereo pair. You can download it from the Hub,
calibench-vi/datasets. Access is gated.

## 1. Pick a board type

AprilGrid 6 × 6

Chessboard 10 × 7 squares

We recorded the calibration motion with these two boards. You can download
both as images with configs in section 5. Each board type needs these
fields:

Board | board_type | Required fields |
AprilGrid | apriltag | rows, cols, tag_size (m), tag_spacing (gap ÷ tag size), tag_family |
Chessboard | chessboard | rows, cols (inner corners), square_size (m) |

- Which to pick: an AprilGrid still gives corners when part of it is out of view. A chessboard has to be
fully in view.

- AprilGrid tags: tag_family: t36h11 is the Kalibr AprilGrid, which has a 2-bit black border round each
tag. Use t36h11b1 for standard AprilTag 3 tags, which have a 1-bit border.

- ArUco boards also work (board_type: aruco). See Configuration.

- A Kalibr target file: no config key reads one. Copy its values into the board: block, as in section 2.

## 2. The board in the running example

The VI-Rig recordings use a printed AprilGrid:

- Grid: 6 × 6 tags, family t36h11.

- Tag: 0.088 m, edge to edge.

- Spacing: 0.3, the gap between tags divided by the tag size.

Its Kalibr target file, april.yaml, sits next to the bags on the Hub. It reads target_type: 'aprilgrid',
tagCols: 6, tagRows: 6, tagSize: 0.088, tagSpacing: 0.3.

The same board in MVIS:

config.yaml
board :

board_type : apriltag

rows : 6

cols : 6

tag_size : 0.088

tag_spacing : 0.3

tag_family : t36h11

## 3. Measure what you printed

Measure the printed board
Print at 100 % and measure one tag with calipers. If it differs from tag_size, every translation in the
rig scales by the same factor. No residual shows this error.

## 4. A board is never flat

A printed board bends and twists a little. A solve that takes it as flat pushes that error into the
calibration.

We estimated the shape of the VI-Rig board from the camera residuals:

- Size of the bend: 10–11 mm peak to peak, 2.3–2.4 mm rms, on the mount we used. A different mount gives
a different shape.

- One run: the 4 IMUs + 4 cameras example estimates it at
2.21 mm rms and 8.94 mm peak to peak.

- Effect: the camera-only residual drops and the focal length moves. The numbers are in
Why calibrate the board shape.

Turn it on with one key. MVIS then solves one height per board corner, in camera-only and camera–IMU runs:

config.yaml
board :

# ... the fields above ...

heights_file : board_shape_4imus_4cams.yaml # optional start values (camera–IMU runs only)

estimate :

board_points : true

- estimate.board_points: true: solves the board shape together with everything else. It is off by
default. We turn it on for every VI-Rig solve.

- board.heights_file: optional start values for the heights. Only camera–IMU runs read it. Without it
the heights start flat.

- Where a heights file comes from: a camera–IMU run with board_points: true writes
<output>_board_shape.yaml next to its output. The example’s board_shape_4imus_4cams.yaml is such a file.

- Prior: each height has a weak prior of 3 mm, so a corner the cameras never saw stays near its start. In
camera–IMU runs you can change it with solve.board_height_sigma (in m). Camera-only runs keep 3 mm.

- One board only: a camera–IMU run with several boards cannot estimate the shape.

## 5. No printer? Use a screen board

You can show the board on a monitor. We made two full-screen images for a 2560 × 1440 monitor, with configs
for MVIS and Kalibr:

Board | Size | Downloads |
AprilGrid 6 × 6 | tag36h11, tag 43.47 mm, spacing 0.3 | image (PNG, 75 KB) · MVIS config · Kalibr config |
Chessboard 10 × 7 squares | 9 × 6 inner corners, square 43.47 mm | image (PNG, 30 KB) · MVIS config · Kalibr config |

How to show them:

- Open the image full screen at 100 % on a 2560 × 1440 monitor.

- Turn off display scaling and zoom, so one image pixel is one screen pixel.

- Measure one tag or square with a ruler. On our monitor, 160 px (one tag or one square) is 43.47 mm, the
size in the configs.

- If yours differs, put your size in the config:

- MVIS: tag_size or square_size.

- Kalibr: tagSize, or rowSpacingMeters and colSpacingMeters.

Setup:

- Keep the screen upright and still.

- Use enough light for a short exposure (about 2 ms), so the corners do not blur.

## Next

- Step 2: Record the dataset. It shows how to move the rig in front of the
board.

- Why it matters: Why calibrate the board shape.


---

# Record the dataset | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/calibration-motion/

Step 2 of the walkthrough. Here you record takes the solver can use.

- You need: the board from step 1,
set up and measured.

- You get: one bag (recording file) per take. Step 3 calibrates the cameras
from it.

- Check: each take passes the rules in section 1, and the solve in steps 3 and 4 converges.

A calibration can only find what the motion shows it. The 60 s motion below turns the rig about every axis
and sweeps the board across the whole image.

We built it from a real hand-held recording with our
Looper Insight 9. Then we checked it on a digital twin: a simulated copy of
that rig, with realistic noise, which we record, solve and compare with the known truth. A motion is good if
the twin still converges on every calibration parameter, that is, the solve settles on the true value within
its uncertainty.

## 1. What a good take has

- About 60 s long. 50 s also works.

- Fill the frame. Cover the image out to its corners. The lens distortion is only pinned down where the
board was seen.

- Vary distance and angle. Move in and out, and turn the rig about every axis.

- No motion blur. Use enough light for a short exposure (about 2 ms).

- Rest at both ends. Hold still for about 3 s at the start and at the end.

## 2. Watch and practise the motion

More detail

1 Watch it once 2 Practise each move 3 Follow along with your rig

Done. Did your board reach every corner?

Read the steps

0.0 s

Space play · ←/→ move · R repeat · F full screen · Esc exit practice

Sensor traces (gyro, accelerometer)
IMU x y z
The fine wobble is natural hand shake; do not add it on purpose.

Pick the chip for your board, then follow the Now panel. It names the move, says what to do, counts down
and shows what comes next. The camera card on the right shows what the camera sees, and which parts of the
image are still empty.

Chessboard motion: the same four moves, built from our chessboard example. It swings less, comes in only
to 0.28 m and turns only a little in the loop, so the whole board stays in view. It also passes the twin.

## 3. Step by step

Do the moves in order and blend each into the next. Keep a comfortable hand pace: at most about 0.4 m/s and
1.9 rad/s.

# | Move | Time | What to do |
0 | Rest | 0–3 s | Hold still in front of the board and count to 3. |
1 | Left–right + turn | 3–20 s | Swing left and right round the board, 2 times. At each end, turn the camera a little past facing the board, so the board slides to the left or right edge of the picture. Turn round sharply. |
2 | Up–down + tilt | 20–32 s | Move up and down, 2 times. Tilt the camera a little past the board, so the board reaches the top or bottom edge of the picture. |
3 | In–out + twist | 32–47 s | Move in to 0.22 m and out to 0.52 m, 3 times. Twist the camera about its view axis like a steering wheel: one way coming in, the other way going out. Hold the board off-centre, so the twist carries it into the corners. |
4 | Loop + twist | 47–57 s | Move round a loop parallel to the board, about 43 cm across, 2 times. Turn the camera a little against the loop and twist it a little, once per loop, so the board runs into every corner. |
5 | Rest | 57–60 s | Hold still and count to 3. |

- Vary the speed on every sweep: push through the middle, brake into the ends.

- Keep most of the board in view. An AprilGrid may run partly off the edge; a chessboard may not.

- Do not add shake. The natural wobble of a hand is all the motion needs.

## 4. The running example’s recordings

The VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cameras set has 15 takes, 4imus_4cams_01.bag to 4imus_4cams_15.bag. The
dataset page lists every sensor with its topic, rate and shutter.

- Download: calibench-vi/datasets → virig-4imus-4cams
on the Hub. Access is gated.

- Which file: use 4imus_4cams_NN.bag. In it, the ELP image stamps sit on the camera’s own clock. The
4imus_4cams_NN_raw.bag next to it is the recording as captured, with the ELP driver’s stamps. Moving
the stamps drops the ELP frames that cannot be matched to the camera clock, so the ELP rate in
4imus_4cams_NN.bag is about 20–22 Hz.

- Board config: the AprilGrid target file april.yaml sits next to the bags.

Recording 09 starts one frame early
In 4imus_4cams_09.bag the right T265 fisheye starts one frame before the left one. MVIS and Basalt pair
frames by the nearest stamp, so they handle it. Kalibr reads each camera on its own, so its pairs come out
one frame off. Give Kalibr a trimmed copy of the bag.

## 5. Record and check

- Record the 60 s motion with your rig. For 50 s, drop one in–out and one loop.
Note where you record (the city, or latitude and altitude): step 4 sets the local gravity from it,
with the Local gravity calculator.

- Calibrate the cameras with the board block from step 1:
step 3: camera-only calibration.

- Calibrate cameras and IMUs together and read the result:
step 4: camera–IMU calibration.

## Real examples

Two hand-held recordings of our Looper Insight 9, solved with MVIS. Both pass the twin. The cards show the
corners MVIS detected in each of the three cameras, drawn without the camera images.

More detail

Watch the path and the corners each camera detected

Done. Did your board reach every corner?

Read the steps

0.0 s

Space play · ←/→ move · R repeat · F full screen

Sensor traces (gyro, accelerometer)
IMU x y z

Both move faster than the guide motion. At a comfortable pace, follow the 60 s guide.

## Motions that fail

Each of these leaves some parameters loose: the solve cannot pin them down.

- Fast shaking from one spot, face-on: the lens distortion stays loose.

- One slow axis at a time, never tilted: the lever arm (where the camera sits relative to the IMU), the
time offsets and the IMU scales stay loose.

- A missing rotation (no tilt, no twist, or only turning left–right): the matching gyroscope and
accelerometer scales, or the whole camera–IMU rotation, cannot be found.

- The board always in the centre: the image edges are never seen, so the distortion stays loose.

## How we judged it

The twin is a simulated Looper Insight 9 in front of the board, with realistic corner and IMU noise, motion
blur and dropped detections.

We solved each motion on 3 noise draws and once without noise. Each solve estimated t_ga (the time offset
between the gyroscope and the accelerometer) and left the camera intrinsics (focal length, image centre and
lens distortion) free.

A motion is good if, on all 22 parameters:

- every solve converges;

- every error stays within its uncertainty;

- every uncertainty is at most 3 × that of a well-excited 80 s reference motion.

The 22 parameters are the camera–IMU rotation and lever arm, td (the camera–IMU time offset), t_ga, the
gyroscope and accelerometer scales, and the camera intrinsics.

To run the same kind of check on your own calibration, see step 7: digital-twin check.

## Replay it yourself

Run our motions through your own simulator and calibration tool with the
replay pack (zip, 3.2 MB). It holds:

- the four motions at 200 Hz: IMU pose, ideal gyroscope and accelerometer;

- the two twin rigs: camera, IMU, truth, noise and detection rules;

- our twin results, with the pass rule.

Its README gives the frames, units and replay steps. The files are plain CSV, YAML and JSON, so you do not
need MVIS to use them. We ran the twin with the MVIS simulator (mvis.simulation).

Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included, for every motion, rig and result in the pack. That includes the two
real-example trajectories since 2026-11-25; a README that still lists them as CC BY-NC 4.0 is from before that date.

## Next

- Step 3: calibrate the cameras from your bags: Camera-only calibration.

- Why it matters: a weak motion leaves parameters loose. See Degeneracy.


---

# Camera-only calibration | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/camera-calibration/

Step 3 of the walkthrough. Here you solve each camera’s lens and the camera-to-camera extrinsics.

- You need: a recording from step 2 and the board: block from
step 1.

- You get: a camera YAML that step 4 reads as its starting point.

- Check: the reprojection error and the motion-excitation grades in the report
(section 7).

The solve estimates:

- Intrinsics: focal length and image centre of each camera.

- Distortion: how the lens bends straight lines.

- Extrinsics: where each camera sits relative to the others.

- Our example: recording 01 of the
VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cameras dataset. It has a
T265 fisheye pair (global shutter, 848 × 800) and an ELP pair (rolling
shutter, 640 × 480).

## 1. Solve the cameras in pairs

The rig has two kinds of camera on two clocks. Solve each pair on its own.

- T265 pair: both fisheyes are global shutter and share one clock. Solve
them together.

- ELP pair: both cameras are rolling shutter and share one clock. Solve
them together.

- Do not put the T265 and the ELP in one camera-only solve. Their shutters
differ and their clocks are far apart.

- Between the pairs: the joint camera–IMU solve in
step 4 finds the extrinsics and time
offsets (td).

The evidence is on Why calibrate cameras together.

## 2. Write the T265 config

Save this as t265_cam.yaml, next to the bag:

t265_cam.yaml
input :

cameras :

- camera_id : 2

name : T265-1

source_type : rosbag_topic

source_path : 4imus_4cams_01.bag

topic : /t265/fisheye1/image_raw

distortion_model : kb4

shutter_type : global

- camera_id : 3

name : T265-2

source_type : rosbag_topic

source_path : 4imus_4cams_01.bag

topic : /t265/fisheye2/image_raw

distortion_model : kb4

shutter_type : global

board :

board_type : apriltag

rows : 6

cols : 6

tag_size : 0.088

tag_spacing : 0.3

tag_family : t36h11

solve :

max_iterations : 15

max_init_frames : 100

pixel_sigma : 1.0

huber_threshold : 1.345

output :

path : t265_calib.yaml

format : yaml

reference_camera : 2

estimate :

board_points : true

corner_subsample : all

- board:: the block from step 1.

- estimate.board_points: true: solve the board shape too. Each corner gets
a height off the flat board. See
A board is never flat · why.

- corner_subsample: all: every corner of every tag, so the board shape gets all 144 corners. The
camera-only default is two_anti, about half the solve time. See Speed.

- reference_camera: 2: the other camera’s pose is given relative to the T265 left camera (T265-1).

- shutter_type: global: no readout time to solve.

Run it:

shell
mvis cam -c t265_cam.yaml

- -o / --output: the run folder for the report, log and detection
cache. The default is an ablation folder next to output.path.

### Other input formats

source_type takes five formats:

- ROS1 bag
- ROS2 bag
- EuRoC
- Images
- Timestamped images

source_type : rosbag_topic # ROS1; several cameras from one bag

source_path : data.bag

topic : /cam0/image_raw

source_type : ros2bag

source_path : data_ros2

topic : /cam0/image_raw

source_type : euroc # EuRoC / ASL folder, e.g. TUM-VI

source_path : cam0

source_type : images # a folder, sorted by filename

source_path : cam0_images

source_type : timestamped_images # a folder plus a CSV of timestamps

source_path : cam0_images,timestamps.csv # folder, then CSV, comma-separated

## 3. Choose a fisheye model for the T265

Set distortion_model per camera. MVIS has eight models:

- radtan, equidistant, kb4, fov, double_sphere, eucm, ucm,
omni_radtan (experimental)

- Fisheye default: kb4. The names fisheye and kannala_brandt also
mean kb4.

- Removed: kb8. MVIS refuses it.

- Normal lenses: radtan.

- Mixed rigs: each camera can use its own model.

kb4 and equidistant give the same result on the T265.

- Why: they share one polynomial. They differ only for rays more than 90°
off axis.

- T265 coverage: on recording 01 the board corners stay under 75° off axis
(the report’s Corner Accounting table).

- Checked: in the model study below, every reprojection number of the two
models agreed to about 2e-6 px.

- So: the benchmark rows that use equidistant stand for kb4 too.

- Past 90°: equidistant cannot project those rays; kb4 can. See
Why kb4.

- Fold warning in the T265 report: the kb4 model of the T265 left camera folds
back at 96.3° off axis. That angle lies inside the image corners, so the report
says “NO (fold inside image)” and the fold level “warn”. The right camera’s model
does not fold (“none (monotonic)”). No board corner gets near the fold (at most
74.8°, 0 corners past it), so the result is not affected.

How the models compare on the T265. We ran this study on the 5-IMU rig
(virig-5imus-4cams, 7 recordings,
same T265 model):

Model | Verdict | What we saw |
kb4 / equidistant | Use this | Lowest error at the image edge, most repeatable between recordings |
eucm | Usable | 9–12 % higher edge error (p95 of the outer image ring); 1.57× the smallest spread |
double_sphere | Avoid | 3.10× the smallest spread; needs bounds in cam-IMU |
omni_radtan | Avoid | 2.93× the smallest spread; needs bounds in cam-IMU |
fov | Avoid | 3.39× the smallest spread |
radtan | Fails | Cannot follow the lens |

- Spread: how far each recording’s fit moves the projected pixels,
compared with the most central fit. The ratio is for the worst camera,
against the model with the smallest spread on that camera.

- Bounds: with free intrinsics in cam-IMU, the double-sphere focal length
went negative on 4 of 7 recordings, omni-radtan on 3 of 7. Set
solve.bound_intrinsics: true in the step 4 config if you use them.

To try another model, change only the distortion_model line on both cameras:

- kb4 (default)
- double_sphere
- eucm

t265_cam.yaml
distortion_model : kb4

t265_cam.yaml
distortion_model : double_sphere

t265_cam.yaml
distortion_model : eucm

The models in equations are on Camera model.

## 4. Result on the running example

Recording 01, the two configs on this page (mvis cam, MVIS 0.4.0, run
2026-11-24):

| T265 left | T265 right | ELP left | ELP right |
Model | kb4 | kb4 | equidistant | equidistant |
fx / fy (px) | 285.00 / 284.57 | 285.03 / 284.40 | 427.83 / 426.94 | 424.66 / 423.73 |
cx / cy (px) | 415.20 / 403.55 | 414.81 / 397.89 | 350.11 / 267.37 | 336.31 / 258.58 |
Rolling-shutter readout | — | — | 14.62 ms | 14.61 ms |
Median / P95 reprojection (px) | 0.18 / 0.65 | 0.17 / 0.64 | 0.28 / 0.95 | 0.30 / 0.97 |

Pair | Baseline | Translation (mm) | Rotation, log(R) (rad) |
T265 right in T265 left | 63.71 mm | 63.70, −0.59, −0.52 | 0.0025, 0.0063, 0.0010 |
ELP right in ELP left | 59.44 mm | 59.44, 0.70, −0.09 | −0.0217, −0.0136, −0.0027 |

- Reprojection error: the pixel gap between the detected corners and where
the solved model puts them.

- Board shape: both runs find a similar board, all 144 corners: 8.7 mm (T265)
and 9.5 mm (ELP) peak to peak, 2.1 mm RMS in both.

- Run time: 30 min (T265) and 28 min (ELP) in our run. Each run had 4 CPU
cores and one thread for the linear-algebra libraries; four guide jobs ran side
by side on one machine. AprilTag detection took 14 min of the T265 run and the
solve 16 min; the ELP solve took 24 min. With the default two_anti the
solve takes about half as long (Speed).

- The reports of both runs are in Read the report.

All 15 recordings (results page,
T265 fisheye stereo, camera only, median and standard deviation). These runs
use equidistant, which gives the same numbers as kb4 here:

| MVIS | Kalibr | Basalt |
Stereo baseline (mm) | 63.667 (sd 0.036) | 63.468 (sd 0.099) | 63.555 (sd 0.135) |
T265 left fx (px) | 286.53 (sd 0.65) | 285.09 (sd 2.40) | 284.14 (sd 0.65) |

- Baseline: the distance between the two T265 cameras.

- Board shape: MVIS estimates it. Kalibr assumes a flat board. On this
board the flat assumption shifts the focal length (why).

- Repeatable: the MVIS baseline moves by about 0.04 mm between recordings.

- Recording 01 is low: in these benchmark runs its fisheye 1 fx (284.74 px) is the lowest of the 15 MVIS
runs, about 1.8 px below the median; the run on this page gives 285.00 px. Basalt also gives its lowest fx on recording 01 (282.85 px), and Kalibr its second lowest. The low
value comes from the recording, not the settings.

## 5. Write the ELP config

The ELP pair uses the same layout. Only the camera block and the reference
camera change:

elp_cam.yaml
input :

cameras :

- camera_id : 0

name : ELP-L

source_type : rosbag_topic

source_path : 4imus_4cams_01.bag

topic : /elp/split_sync_image_node/left/image_raw

distortion_model : equidistant

shutter_type : rolling

- camera_id : 1

name : ELP-R

source_type : rosbag_topic

source_path : 4imus_4cams_01.bag

topic : /elp/split_sync_image_node/right/image_raw

distortion_model : equidistant

shutter_type : rolling

# board:, solve:, estimate: and corner_subsample: as in t265_cam.yaml

output :

path : elp_calib.yaml

format : yaml

reference_camera : 0

shell
mvis cam -c elp_cam.yaml

- distortion_model: equidistant: what our ELP runs use. The ELP lens
stays under 57° off axis, where equidistant and kb4 agree.

- shutter_type: rolling: mvis cam then solves each ELP camera’s
readout time, the time the sensor takes to read the image from the first row
to the last. Details are in step 5.

## 6. Speed

corner_subsample sets how many corners of each tag enter the solve. The
camera-only default is two_anti.

t265_cam.yaml
corner_subsample : two_anti # two_anti | two_diag | all | top_left

- two_anti (default): 2 corners per tag, top-left and bottom-right. About half the solve
time of all (all takes about 1.8×: 12 against 22 min on an ELP stereo recording with board_points on); cx and cy stay within about 0.1 px. This page uses all for the full board shape. With two or more
cameras, the joint solve (stage 4) adds the other diagonal on frames that see at
least 35 of the 36 tags, so every corner gets a board height (“144 of 144” in the
report), but those corners have few views (22 frames on the ELP pair here). A
one-camera solve sees 72 of 144; use corner_subsample: all for the full shape.

- two_diag: 2 corners per tag, the other diagonal.

- all: 4 corners per tag. Most data, no speed-up.

- top_left: 1 corner per tag, fastest. The fit is unchanged, but cx and
cy can shift by up to about 0.8 px.

- factor_hz: how many frames per second of each camera enter the solve.
The default is 5 Hz (solve.factor_hz, or per camera). Set it lower to use
fewer frames from a long recording.

## 7. Read the report

MVIS writes:

- output.path: the result to deploy. Step 4 reads this file.

- *_calib.yaml: the same result, in the run folder.

- *_full.yaml: the result plus the board poses, to replay the run.

- .log: the run log, in the run folder.

- HTML report: one self-contained file, in the run folder.

The report has these sections:

- Summary: median and P95 reprojection error, cameras, frames and corner
count, a per-camera error table, and Calibration parameters by sensor: one
folded block per camera with its model, intrinsics, readout, pose in the
reference camera (log(R) in rad), error, and a YAML snippet to copy.

- Camera Intrinsics: focal length, image centre and distortion per camera.
For kb4 it also shows the valid domain: the angle where the lens model
folds back, and whether that fold lies inside the image. Its Corner
Accounting table gives, per camera, how many corners were used, how many
fell past the fold or out of the model’s domain, and how many were dropped as
outliers; the full table is folded below it. Only used corners count in the
error figures.

- Board Shape: shown when estimate.board_points is on. Each corner’s
height off the flat board, as a table and a map. The tilt of the board
belongs to its pose, so a truly flat board shows only noise here.

- Camera Extrinsics: each camera’s pose relative to the reference camera,
with the rotation as log(R) in rad, and a 3D view of the rig.

- Temporal Calibration: the readout time of each rolling-shutter camera
(ELP report only).

- Calibration Process: the solved camera path around the board, as a
player.

- Reprojection Error Analysis: per camera, by frame, by tag and over the image.

- Calibration Data Quality (folded): the motion-excitation table and grade,
and the feature coverage of each image.

- Detection Statistics: sample frames with the detected corners.

- Appendix A–C: where the time went (stage timings folded), the files the
run wrote, and the config it read.

- Appendix D (folded): per-frame, per-tag error heatmaps, one tab per camera.

Check the motion-excitation grade before the reprojection error. It says
how well your motion constrained each parameter: depth range for focal length,
image coverage for distortion, tilt in all directions for rotation, and
angular speed for time offset and readout. On recording 01 every ELP grade is
good. The T265 distortion grade is marginal: the area the corners cover (their
convex hull) is under 60 % of the image, and 30–60 % counts as marginal. See
Evaluation & metrics.

Below are the reports of the two recording 01 runs. They are as MVIS wrote
them, except that local folder names are cut down to file names:

- T265 pair
- ELP pair

Open full screen (HTML, 10.5 MB)

Open full screen (HTML, 11.9 MB)

## What the pipeline does

Error messages name these stages:

Stage | What happens |
Detection | AprilTag detection at scale 1.0, then up to 3 extra scales picked from the tag sizes seen; small, far boards get an upscaled crop |
Quality gating | Corner subsampling; a frame’s pose is kept when it sees at least 20 % of the tags (at least 4), counted over all cameras at that time; each corner needs at least 5 views, and at least 3 in each camera; each frame needs at least 6 tags |
1 | Per-camera start: focal length from vanishing points, board poses by RANSAC PnP, then a sanity check |
2 | Per-camera refinement, with the rolling-shutter readout if the camera has one |
3 | Camera-to-camera extrinsics from the board poses by RANSAC; time offsets too when estimate.camera.td: true (older configs: optimize_time_offset) |
4 | One joint optimisation of all cameras and all parameters |
5 | Drop outliers and run stage 4 again, with a guard against a run that gets worse |

## Next

- Step 4: point camera_input.path at the camera YAML from this page. It
takes one file, so join the T265 and ELP results into one YAML first. See
Camera–IMU calibration.
The cam-IMU solve refines the intrinsics further.

- Renumber when you join: MVIS sorts the joined file’s cameras by id and
matches them to cam_topics in order. Step 4 lists the T265 first, so give
the T265 cameras id 0 and 1 and the ELP cameras 2 and 3. The configs on
this page use other ids (ELP 0 and 1, T265 2 and 3).

- Our example’s starting point: the camera_prior.yaml of the
example run joins two earlier
camera-only results. The ELP pair is the median of the 15 ELP camera-only
solves. The T265 pair comes from an earlier camera-only solve of the T265,
not from the config on this page. That solve used equidistant, so the
cam-IMU report lists the T265 cameras as equidistant; on this lens it gives
the same result as kb4 (section 3).
The file is camera_prior.yaml.

- Step 5: Rolling-shutter calibration for the ELP.

- Why it matters: Why calibrate cameras together and
Why kb4 for fisheye.


---

# Camera–IMU calibration | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/camera-imu-calibration/

Step 4 of the walkthrough. Here you solve the cameras and IMUs in one graph.

- You need: the recording from step 2 and the camera YAML from
step 3.

- You get: cam_imu.json, the calibration YAML cam_imu_calib.yaml and an HTML report.

- Check: read the report’s summary and the t_ga of each IMU (section 5), then run the
round trip of step 8.

The running example is recording 01 of our VI-Rig with 4 IMUs and 4 cameras
(dataset page):

- Cameras: a T265 fisheye pair (global shutter) and an ELP stereo pair (rolling shutter).

- IMUs: Xsens MTi-100, MicroStrain GX3-25 and GX3-35, and the T265 IMU.

The solve estimates, all at once:

- Extrinsics: where each camera and IMU sits relative to the base IMU (lever arm and rotation).

- Time offset td: the clock delay of each camera and each aux IMU to the base IMU.

- IMU intrinsics: scale and misalignment of each gyroscope (Dw) and accelerometer (Da).

- t_ga: the delay between an IMU’s own gyroscope and accelerometer samples.

- Camera intrinsics: refined from the step 3 result, not held fixed.

- Biases of every gyroscope and accelerometer.

## 1. Point at the camera prior

Step 3 (Camera-only calibration) writes a camera
YAML. Name it in the cam-IMU config:

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
camera_input :

path : camera_prior.yaml

- What it gives: the starting intrinsics of each camera (the prior).

- One file, in cam_topics order: join the T265 and ELP results of step 3.
MVIS sorts the cameras by id and matches them to cam_topics by order. So
here the T265 fisheyes are id 0 and 1, the ELP left and right 2 and 3.

- Our example’s prior: camera_prior.yaml.
It joins earlier camera-only results and uses equidistant for the T265,
which gives the same result as kb4 on this lens
(step 3).
So the report lists the T265 cameras as equidistant.

- What happens next: the cam-IMU solve refines the intrinsics (estimate.camera.intrinsics: true). It solves the extrinsics and time offsets itself; the prior’s extrinsics are not used.

## 2. Write the config

This is the config of the VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cameras example,
recording 01, with two changes: gravity: 9.8013 in place of the example’s gravity: 9.81 and its site: block,
and every corner enters the solve in place of two_anti. The highlighted lines matter for this step.

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
gravity : 9.8013 # m/s², Newark, Delaware

input :

format : ros1

path : 4imus_4cams_01.bag

cam_topics :

- /t265/fisheye1/image_raw

- /t265/fisheye2/image_raw

- /elp/split_sync_image_node/left/image_raw

- /elp/split_sync_image_node/right/image_raw

imu_topics :

- /imu/data

- /gx3_25/data

- /gx3_35/imu/data

- /t265/imu

window_mode : motion

segment_length : 80.0

board :

board_type : apriltag

rows : 6

cols : 6

tag_size : 0.088

tag_spacing : 0.3

tag_family : t36h11

heights_file : board_shape_4imus_4cams.yaml

camera_input :

path : camera_prior.yaml

cameras :

- {}

- factor_hz : 4.0

- estimate_readout : true

factor_hz : 4.0

- estimate_readout : true

factor_hz : 4.0

solve :

max_iterations : 40

estimate_t_ga : true

sigma_t_ga : 0.01

vision_pose : imu

sigma_g : 0.00065

sigma_a : 0.0026

sigma_bg : 0.001

sigma_ba : 0.002

estimate :

board_points : true

camera :

intrinsics : true

tr : false

td : true

extrinsics : true

imu :

intrinsics : dw_da

model : calyx

extrinsics : true

td : true

output :

path : cam_imu.json

What the highlighted lines do:

-
gravity: the local gravity, in m/s². MVIS holds the gravity magnitude fixed in the solve, so the
accelerometer scale Da takes up any error in it. Set the value where you recorded: the
Local gravity page has a calculator and a table of cities from Singapore to London.
The report then says the value was set in the config; from MVIS 0.4.1 it also names the place in the comment.

Or give the place with site:, for example
site: {latitude_deg: 39.68, altitude_m: 40, name: "Newark, Delaware"}. MVIS computes the WGS84 normal gravity
from latitude_deg (negative south of the equator) and altitude_m, and the report names the site. You can give
both keys if they agree within 0.01 m/s².

With neither, MVIS uses 9.81 m/s² and warns in the run log; near the equator Da then reads up to 0.3 % high.
At Newark the difference is only −0.09 %.

-
input: a ROS1 bag. The first imu_topics entry (/imu/data, the Xsens) is the base IMU. Every other sensor is solved relative to it.

-
window_mode: motion: MVIS uses the segment_length seconds (here 80 s) with the most IMU motion.

-
board.heights_file + estimate.board_points: true: solve the board shape too, starting from a measured shape. board_shape_4imus_4cams.yaml ships with MVIS in examples/regression/mvis_elp/. Our board is not flat; a flat solve shifts the gyro scale and the lever arm (why).

-
solve.corner_subsample: not set, so every corner of every tag enters the solve (the cam-IMU default, all). two_anti (two opposite corners per tag) is faster, but the board shape then gets only 72 of the 144 corners.

-
solve.estimate_t_ga: true, sigma_t_ga: 0.01: solve t_ga for each IMU. Keep this on (why).

-
solve.vision_pose: imu: moves the pose to each corner’s capture time with the raw base-IMU samples. It is the default.

-
sigma_g, sigma_a, sigma_bg, sigma_ba: gyro and accel noise, and their bias random walk.

-
estimate.camera: intrinsics free, td and extrinsics solved.

-
estimate.imu: IMU intrinsics dw_da with the calyx model (see section 3), plus extrinsics and td of the aux IMUs.

The other lines belong to later steps:

- camera_input.cameras: one entry per camera, in cam_topics order. The three cameras after the first enter the graph at 4 frames per second (factor_hz), which keeps the solve small. The first camera keeps the cam-IMU default of 10 Hz.

- ELP readout lines (estimate_readout, tr): estimate.camera.tr: false is the rig-wide default and holds the readout fixed. The per-camera estimate_readout: true on the two ELP entries overrides it, so the run solves the ELP readout and keeps the T265 (global shutter) at zero. Details in step 5, Rolling-shutter calibration.

- The three aux IMUs: step 6, Multi-IMU spatial-temporal calibration.

For your own rig, change the topics, the board and the prior path. Keep the
rest as a starting point.

## 3. Turn on IMU intrinsics

estimate.imu.intrinsics sets how much of each IMU model we solve:

Value | What is solved |
pinned | nothing: Dw and Da stay at their start values |
dw_da | scale and misalignment of gyro (Dw) and accel (Da). Our setting, and the default |
dw_da_r | as dw_da, plus the gyro–accel rotation. Same as dw_da for calyx, which keeps that rotation inside Dw |
full | as dw_da_r, plus Tg (how linear acceleration leaks into the gyro) |

- A bool also works: true means full, false means pinned.

- estimate.imu.model picks the model family: calyx (default), kalibr or rpng.

- Priors: freed terms get a weak prior. solve.sigma_dw_da defaults to 0.1, solve.sigma_tg to 0.05.

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
estimate :

imu :

intrinsics : dw_da # pinned | dw_da | dw_da_r | full

model : calyx # calyx | kalibr | rpng

What the terms mean: IMU model. Why it pays off:
Why calibrate the IMU.

## 4. Run

shell
mvis cam-imu -c virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml

- Other bag: --bag <file> replaces the config’s source with that ROS1 bag.

- Time: 31 min in our run (MVIS 0.4.1, 2026-11-25), on 16 CPU cores with
one thread for the linear-algebra libraries, with other jobs on the machine.
About 12 min of that is AprilTag detection on the four cameras; the solve
stages take about 19 min, of which the 6 iterations take about 16 min
(solve_s in the report’s Appendix, Timing).

- Output: in the folder of output.path:

- cam_imu.json: a summary of the solve.

- cam_imu_calib.yaml: the full calibration, the file to deploy.

- cam_imu_camchain-imucam.yaml: the same rig in Kalibr’s camchain format.

- cam_imu_board_shape.yaml: the solved board shape (when estimate.board_points is on).

- cam_imu_report.html: the report.

- cam_imu_views.json: the data of the report’s 3D views.

## 5. Read the result

Recording 01 gives the values below. The full table and a 3D view of the rig
are on the example page.

The report. Every run writes cam_imu_report.html next to cam_imu.json.
It has these sections:

- Summary: status, the gravity used and where it came from (the config value, or the site and its city), reprojection median and P95, χ²/dof of the camera and
IMU terms with a grade each, and the base IMU’s t_ga. χ²/dof near 1 means
the residuals match the noise you set; well below 1 (0.13 here) means the
noise settings are conservative.

- 3D Geometry: the solved rig path around the board as a player, and the
rig to scale.

- Cameras: per camera, intrinsics, distortion, lever arm and rotation
(log(R), rad) with their σ, td, readout time, and the corner accounting
(corners used, past the lens fold, dropped as outliers).

- Board Shape: the solved corner heights as a table and a map, with the
median σ of a height. Shown because estimate.board_points is on.

- Reprojection Analysis: error by frame, by tag and over the board, per
camera.

- Motion & Excitation: the angular velocity of the solved path, which shows
how well the motion constrains the lever arms and td.

- Base IMU, Aux IMUs, IMU Residuals: biases and their drift, Dw, Da,
Tg and t_ga of each IMU; each aux IMU’s pose and td relative to the
base IMU. The block is titled “IMU intrinsics (full)” whatever level you
solve; with dw_da, as here, Tg stays at zero. With the calyx model the
report also splits Dw as R · U: a misalignment rotation R (as log(R)) times
U, the per-axis scale and cross-coupling. IMU Residuals gives the residuals per
state block (rotation, position, velocity, bias steps).

- Appendix (folded): Timing, the files the run wrote, and the config it read.

This is the report of the recording 01 run, unchanged except that local folder
names are cut down to file names:

Open the report full screen (HTML, 13.4 MB).

Fit and geometry:

Value | Recording 01 |
Reprojection median, all cameras | 0.24 px (rms 0.51, p95 0.68) |
cam0–cam1 baseline (T265 pair) | 63.7 mm |
cam0 td | −5.39 ms |
cam0 lever arm | 131.0 mm |
Board shape | 9.2 mm peak to peak, 2.2 mm RMS (144 of 144 corners seen) |

- cam0: T265 left. cam1 is T265 right, cam2 and cam3 are ELP left and right.

- 144 of 144 corners: every corner enters the solve, so every height is
solved. With two_anti, the other 72 would stay at the measured shape from
heights_file.

- Reprojection shows how well the model fits the corners. It does not show
how accurate the model is.

Base IMU (Xsens) intrinsics, the diagonal of the full Dw and Da matrices
(the report’s “IMU intrinsics (full)”; Dw_diag and Da_diag in cam_imu.json):

| x | y | z |
Dw (gyro) | 0.99849 | 0.99786 | 1.00076 |
Da (accel) | 0.99917 | 0.99609 | 1.00053 |

t_ga per IMU:

IMU | t_ga ms |
Xsens (base) | −0.82 ± 0.02 |
GX3-25 | +0.10 ± 0.02 |
GX3-35 | +0.01 ± 0.02 |
T265 IMU | −6.74 ± 0.02 |

- Rotations are in cam_imu.json as log(R) rotation vectors in rad.

- The T265 IMU has by far the largest t_ga. The other three stay under 1 ms.

Over 15 recordings (results page,
the “ELP RS stereo + two IMUs (IMUs only)” rows). These runs use a different
setup: the ELP pair only, the T265 IMU as base IMU, the Xsens as aux IMU, and
the Kalibr IMU model. So they are not the same quantities as the tables above;
the Xsens t_ga, for example, is −0.47 ms there against −0.82 ms here. sd is
the standard deviation over the 15 recordings.

IMU | Da diagonal x / y / z, median | t_ga ms, median |
T265 IMU | 1.01989 / 1.01905 / 1.01668 | −6.697 (sd 0.135) |
Xsens | 0.99997 / 0.99932 / 1.00093 | −0.466 (sd 0.237) |

- T265: the Da diagonal sits 1.7 to 2.0 % above 1 on every axis.

- Xsens: stays within 0.1 % of 1.

- Why this table: one run says little; the spread over many recordings
shows how repeatable a value is.

## 6. Leave state_hz alone

solve.state_hz sets how many pose, velocity and bias states per second the
solve keeps. It defaults to 30 Hz; our config does not set it. In our tests
on several rigs:

- Fast motion: at low rates the states undersample the motion. The
reprojection error, lever arm and td drift, and settle around 30 Hz.

- Slow, smooth motion: the rate does not matter.

- Not affected either way: stereo baseline, IMU intrinsics and biases.

So:

- Leave it at 30 unless your motion is slow and you want the speed.

- Check it first if td or the lever arm look wrong on a fast-moving rig.

## Batch: many recordings from one config

To calibrate many recordings at once, list them under input.bags instead of a
single path:

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
input :

format : ros1

bags :

- 4imus_4cams_01.bag

- 4imus_4cams_02.bag

- 4imus_4cams_03.bag

- Output: each bag gets its own bag<NN>/ folder in the folder of output.path (results/sweep when it has none). <NN> is the bag’s trailing number (4imus_4cams_01.bag gives bag01).

- Formats: ROS1 bags, ROS2 bags and EuRoC mav0 folders all work. Each inherits the config’s format (input.format: ros1, ros2 or euroc).

- Use: a repeatability sweep over many recordings.

The spread of extrinsics and intrinsics across recordings tells you far more
about accuracy than any single run’s residual.

## t_ga: gyro–accel offset (on by default)

t_ga is each IMU’s internal delay between its gyroscope and its
accelerometer. MVIS solves it by default, and our config sets it:

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
solve :

estimate_t_ga : true

A driver that resamples the accelerometer to the gyro rate adds a timing
offset. Without t_ga, that offset leaks into td.

The T265 is the clearest case:

- IMU: Bosch BMI055, 62.5 Hz accel interpolated to 200 Hz.

- Measured: t_ga −6.74 ms on recording 01 with the Xsens as base, and −6.697 ms median over 15 recordings with the T265 IMU as base and the Kalibr IMU model (section 5).

- Not a pure shift: the delay changes with the motion, so one t_ga is a compromise.

Details in IMU model. Why it matters, with real numbers:
Why calibrate t_ga.

## Awkward IMUs

For an accelerometer you cannot trust, there are two options: t_ga (above),
or calibrate the IMU from its gyro alone.

Gyro-only: calibrate an aux IMU from its gyro alone.

- Solved: extrinsic rotation, td, Dw, gyro bias.

- Pinned: lever arm, Da, Tg.

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
input :

imus :

- {} # base IMU: needs the accel

- { gyro_only : true } # aux IMU

- Order: entries match imu_topics by order.

- Not on the base IMU: the base needs its accelerometer for gravity and metric scale.

- Gyro-only or t_ga: both target the same failure. When to prefer which:
IMU model.

-
Step 5: Rolling-shutter calibration explains the ELP readout lines.

-
Step 6: Multi-IMU spatial-temporal calibration explains the three aux IMUs.

-
Step 7: Digital-twin check tests the solver on a copy of the rig with known truth.

-
Step 8: Round-trip validation checks the result. Do not stop at the residual:

shell
mvis roundtrip -c virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml

-
Why it matters: Why calibrate the IMU and Why calibrate t_ga.

# Rolling-shutter calibration | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/rolling-shutter/

Step 5 of the walkthrough. Here you solve the readout time of the two rolling-shutter ELP cameras.

- You need: the camera-only config from step 3 and the camera–IMU config
from step 4.

- You get: a readout time for each ELP camera.

- Check: the readout repeats across recordings (section 3).

Two terms:

- Rolling shutter: the camera exposes its rows one after another, so one image spans a range of times.

- Readout: the time from the first row to the last row of one image.

In the running example the two T265 fisheyes are global shutter (all rows at
once) and the two ELP cameras are rolling shutter. One rig can mix both.

## 1. Camera-only: mark the ELP as rolling shutter

The camera-only ELP config of step 3 already sets
shutter_type: rolling on each ELP camera. That one key turns on the readout estimate:

elp_cam.yaml (excerpt)
input :

cameras :

- camera_id : 0

name : ELP-L

# ... other keys as in step 3

shutter_type : rolling # global | rolling | auto (auto = global)

- camera_id : 1

name : ELP-R

# ... other keys as in step 3

shutter_type : rolling

shell
mvis cam -c elp_cam.yaml

- What it does: mvis cam solves the readout of every camera marked rolling.

- Global cameras: leave the T265 fisheyes at shutter_type: global.

- auto: the default. It counts as global, so no readout is solved.

Result over the 15 recordings (results page, “ELP RS stereo +
readout”, camera only), median and standard deviation (sd):

Readout (ms) | ELP left | ELP right |
MVIS | 14.604 (sd 0.404) | 14.601 (sd 0.404) |
Kalibr, rolling-shutter model | 16.354 (sd 2.00) | 17.369 (sd 1.42, n = 13) |

- Kalibr: its rolling-shutter model calibrates one camera per run. Two ELP right recordings failed, so it has
13 of 15.

- Lens models differ: MVIS uses equidistant, Kalibr radtan. So only the readout is compared.

- Kalibr inputs: Kalibr was not re-run after the ELP stamp correction, so its rows come from the bags as
captured. It also assumes a flat board; MVIS estimates the board shape. Do not read the whole 2–3 ms gap
as a tool difference.

## 2. Camera–IMU: turn readout on per camera

In the step 4 config, the camera_input.cameras list holds one entry per
camera:

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
camera_input :

cameras :

- {}

- factor_hz : 4.0

- estimate_readout : true

factor_hz : 4.0

- estimate_readout : true

factor_hz : 4.0

estimate :

camera :

tr : false

- Order: the list follows the camera order in input.cam_topics. cam0 and cam1 are the T265 fisheyes,
cam2 and cam3 the ELP left and right. (In the camera-only elp_cam.yaml above, the ELP cameras are
camera_id 0 and 1.)

- estimate_readout: true: solves the readout of that camera.

- factor_hz: 4.0: adds that camera’s frames to the solve at 4 Hz, which keeps the solve small.

- estimate.camera.tr: false: the rig-wide default, which keeps readout off for the global-shutter
T265. The per-camera estimate_readout: true wins for the ELP.

- Readout on every camera: set estimate.camera.tr: true and leave out the per-camera key.

shell
mvis cam-imu -c virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml

The full config is on the example page.

## 3. Read the result

Recording 01 (example run):

| ELP left (cam2) | ELP right (cam3) |
Readout (ms) | 16.684 | 16.732 |
td (ms) | −123.25 | −123.30 |

- td: the camera’s time offset to the base IMU. The ELP td is large; the T265 cameras sit at −5.41 and
−7.47 ms.

All 15 recordings (results page, the “MVIS” column, not “MVIS (K-IMU)”, median
and sd):

Run on the results page | ELP left readout (ms) | ELP right readout (ms) |
ELP RS stereo + two IMUs | 16.618 (sd 0.122) | 16.594 (sd 0.111) |
Mixed t265-f1 + ELP-L, aux Xsens | 16.680 (sd 0.089, n = 14) | — |

- Repeatable: the camera–IMU readout moves by about 0.1 ms between recordings. A readout that moves much
more was not observed by the motion.

- Check it on your rig: calibrate several recordings from one config with
batch mode and compare.

## 4. Camera-only and camera–IMU readouts differ

- The gap: on these recordings camera-only gives 14.6 ms, camera–IMU 16.6 ms. We have not found the
cause yet.

- Which to use: the camera–IMU value when you have an IMU. It repeats about 4 × more tightly (sd about
0.1 ms against 0.4 ms).

## Why it is solved jointly

The readout is fitted by the same residuals as everything else, not applied as a fix afterwards.

- Per-row time: each corner is projected with the rig pose at the time of its row, not of the frame.

- One error term: projection, td, readout and pose interpolation sit in one factor.

The math: Camera model.

## What to expect

The readout is one of the weakest parameters in the solve.

- It needs fast motion: the rows must see clearly different geometry.

- A slow, smooth recording will not pin it. The estimate then stays near where it started.

Readout and td trade against each other
Both shift when a corner is taken to have been seen. With too little motion the solver cannot separate
them: the pair can slide along a ridge of equally good solutions while the residual stays flat. If a
rolling-shutter camera’s td is off from its global-shutter neighbours by about one readout, suspect this
before the hardware. On recording 01 the ELP td differs from the T265 td by about 118 ms, far more than one
readout (about 17 ms), so this is not the cause there.

## Checks

- Repeatability: see section 3.

- The round trip cannot test it: mvis roundtrip corrects the bag with
mvis apply-calib, which re-stamps each frame but does not unwarp its rows. So a readout error stays
hidden.

- The digital twin can: it simulates the rows. See step 7.

## Next

- Step 6: Multi-IMU calibration.

- Why it matters: Why calibrate rolling shutter.
