# Multi-IMU spatial-temporal calibration | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/multi-sensor-rigs/

Step 6 of the walkthrough. Here you add more IMUs to the camera–IMU solve.

- You need: the config from step 4.

- You get: for every aux IMU, its lever arm and rotation to the base IMU, its time offset td and its
t_ga.

- Check: compare the numbers across recordings (section 3), and name the base IMU when you quote them.

Two terms:

- Base IMU: the IMU every other sensor is measured against. It sets the clock and carries the
trajectory.

- Aux IMU (auxiliary IMU): any other IMU on the rig. MVIS solves where it sits and how its clock runs
against the base.

All IMUs enter one factor graph with the cameras. There is no pairwise step.

The running example is VI-Rig: 4 IMUs + 4 cameras, recording 01
(4imus_4cams_01.bag).

## 1. Pick the base

The first entry in input.imu_topics is the base IMU. It is the reference clock for the whole rig and
the only IMU that carries the trajectory. Every other entry is an aux IMU, in the order you list it.

In the running example the base is the Xsens (/imu/data):

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
input :

imu_topics :

- /imu/data # base: Xsens MTi-100

- /gx3_25/data # aux: GX3-25

- /gx3_35/imu/data # aux: GX3-35

- /t265/imu # aux: T265 IMU

- Pick a good IMU as the base: its errors spread to the whole rig.

- Say which base you used when you quote a number. A td or a lever means “against this base”.

Two bases on this dataset
The recording 01 run on this page uses the Xsens as base. The 15-recording runs on the
results page that include IMUs use the T265 IMU as base, with
the Xsens as the only aux IMU.

## 2. Turn on the aux spatial and temporal terms

These keys in the step-4 config control the aux IMUs:

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
estimate :

imu :

extrinsics : true # lever + rotation of each aux IMU to the base

td : true # time offset of each aux IMU to the base

solve :

estimate_t_ga : true # base and aux IMUs

- estimate.imu.extrinsics: solves each aux IMU’s lever and rotation. Default true.

- estimate.imu.td: solves each aux IMU’s time offset to the base. Default true.

- false on either holds that value at its start value instead.

- solve.estimate_t_ga: t_ga is the delay between an IMU’s accelerometer and its gyroscope. One flag
covers the base and the aux IMUs. Default true.

- IMU intrinsics (scale and misalignment) follow estimate.imu.intrinsics for every IMU, base and aux.
Step 4 sets it to dw_da.

### An aux IMU with a bad accelerometer

Set gyro_only: true on that IMU. The entries in input.imus match input.imu_topics by order:

virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml
input :

imu_topics : [ /imu/data , /gx3_25/data , /gx3_35/imu/data , /t265/imu ]

imus :

- {} # base: needs its accelerometer

- {}

- {}

- { gyro_only : true } # aux calibrated from its gyroscope alone

- What it solves: rotation, td, Dw (gyroscope scale and misalignment) and gyroscope bias.

- What it holds fixed: the lever and the accelerometer terms. There is no t_ga.

- Not on the base: the base always needs its accelerometer. MVIS stops with an error if you set it there.

The running example does not need it: all four IMUs run in full mode. When to prefer it over t_ga:
t_ga in step 4 and
IMU model.

### Speed

Each aux IMU adds factors to the graph. Two keys thin them out:

Key | Default | What it does |
solve.aux_imu_stride | 3 | One aux factor per this many base intervals. Overrides aux_imu_factor_hz. |
solve.aux_imu_factor_hz | 0 | Aux factor rate in Hz. 0 = one per base interval. |

Not accuracy-neutral
The levers change with aux_imu_stride. Keep it the same across runs you compare.

Run it as in step 4:

shell
mvis cam-imu -c virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml

## 3. Read the result

Recording 01, Xsens base. The values are from the example run
(“Solved rig”):

IMU | td to base (ms) | t_ga (ms) | lever (mm) | rotation log(R) (rad) |
Xsens (base) | 0 | −0.82 ± 0.02 | 0 | 0 |
GX3-25 | −0.69 | +0.10 ± 0.02 | [−122.8, −45.3, −3.1] | [+2.2502, +2.1849, −0.0279] |
GX3-35 | −2.07 | +0.01 ± 0.02 | [−82.3, −46.2, −3.5] | [+2.2304, +2.2070, −0.0192] |
T265 IMU | −7.17 | −6.74 ± 0.02 | [+54.7, −107.4, −30.3] | [+1.5724, −0.0054, −0.0113] |

- Frame: lever and rotation place each IMU in the base IMU frame. The rotation is the log(R) rotation
vector.

- td sign: t_imu = t_sensor + td, with t_imu on the base clock.

- t_ga: the T265 IMU has by far the largest offset (−6.74 ms), the Xsens −0.82 ms. The two MicroStrain
IMUs sit near 0.

Repeatability over 15 recordings (“Mixed t265-f1 + ELP-L, aux Xsens” on the results page, T265 IMU base,
Xsens aux), median and sd:

Xsens to base | MVIS | Kalibr |
td (ms) | 7.240 (sd 0.146) | 7.260 (sd 0.122) |
distance ‖p‖ (mm) | 124.09 (sd 0.32) | 114.10 (sd 2.96) |

- td agrees with Kalibr to 0.02 ms.

- Kalibr inputs: Kalibr got its camera intrinsics and baselines from an MVIS export, and ELP left’s stamps
were shifted by the MVIS td of the same recording before each run. It treats ELP left as global shutter. So its td
and lever are solved given these MVIS inputs, not independently.

- The lever does not: the two tools are 10 mm apart, and Kalibr spreads about 9 × wider.

- MVIS column: MVIS with Kalibr’s IMU model, 15 recordings. Kalibr has 14 (recording 8 failed).

- Base swap: this +7.24 ms and recording 01’s −7.17 ms both link the Xsens and the T265 IMU. The sign flips
because the base flips.

Full tables: VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cameras results.

## 4. Sensor numbering when comparing with Kalibr

Both tools number sensors in input order, but they name the IMUs differently. Getting this wrong silently
compares the wrong pair.

- MVIS: cameras are cam0, cam1, … in input.cam_topics order. The base IMU, the first
input.imu_topics entry, is imu0. Each aux IMU is named after the first part of its topic:
/gx3_25/data becomes gx3_25, /t265/imu becomes t265, /imu/data becomes imu. These names appear
in cam_imu.json, the calibration YAML and the HTML report.

- Kalibr: cameras are cam0, cam1, …; imu0 is its reference IMU, the first IMU it is given, and the
others are imu1, imu2, … in input order.

- Same input order, same base: in the runs below both tools get the same topic lists, so imu0 is the
same IMU in both. Match the aux IMUs by topic, not by number.

4 IMUs + 3 cameras (virig-4imus-3cams, Xsens base)

Sensor | Blackfly | T265 left | T265 right | Xsens MTi-100 | GX3-25 | GX3-35 | T265 IMU |
Kalibr | cam0 | cam1 | cam2 | imu0 | imu1 | imu2 | imu3 |
MVIS | cam0 | cam1 | cam2 | imu0 | gx3_25 | gx3_35 | t265 |

4 IMUs + 4 cameras (the recording 01 run above, Xsens base, MVIS only)

Sensor | T265 left | T265 right | ELP left | ELP right | Xsens | GX3-25 | GX3-35 | T265 IMU |
MVIS | cam0 | cam1 | cam2 | cam3 | imu0 | gx3_25 | gx3_35 | t265 |

Mixed t265-f1 + ELP-L, aux Xsens (T265 IMU base)

Sensor | T265 left | ELP left | T265 IMU | Xsens |
Kalibr | cam0 | cam1 | imu0 | imu1 |
MVIS | cam0 | cam1 | imu0 | imu |

MVIS reads Kalibr camchain and camchain-imucam files and writes camchain-imucam. See
Result formats.

## 5. Several cameras

Cameras join the same graph. You set them up in step 3:

- reference_camera: the camera the other cameras’ extrinsics are expressed against.

- estimate.camera.td: true (camera-only): solves a time offset between cameras that are not
synchronised.

- Per-camera td: in the camera–IMU solve every camera gets its own td to the base IMU. In recording 01 the T265
cameras sit at −5.41 and −7.47 ms, the ELP cameras at −123.25 and −123.30 ms.

Why one joint solve beats separate ones: Why calibrate cameras together.
Why aux IMUs pay off: Why calibrate IMUs together.

## Worked runs

- 4 IMUs + 3 cameras

- 4 IMUs + 4 cameras

- 4 IMUs + 3 cameras, ArUco board

- 5 IMUs + 4 cameras

- Step 7: check that the solve recovers a known answer: Digital-twin check.

- The math behind the aux terms: Auxiliary IMU factor.

- Why it matters: Why calibrate IMUs together.

# Digital-twin check | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/simulation/

Step 7 of the walkthrough. Here you test the solver on a simulated copy of your recording, where the truth is
known.

- You need: the camera–IMU config and bag from step 4, and MVIS
installed from source or from the package.

- You get: the error of each calibration parameter against the truth.

- Check: the noise-free errors are near zero (section 2).

A digital twin is a simulated copy of your recording:

- The truth is your real solve: calibration, board pose and shape, biases and trajectory. A small
seeded perturbation then moves the camera intrinsics, the camera and aux-IMU extrinsics, each td and
each t_ga, by up to 1 % focal, 4 px principal point, 5 % of each distortion coefficient, 10 mrad per
rotation axis, 5 mm per lever axis, 1 ms td and 0.5 ms t_ga. Readout, IMU intrinsics, biases,
gravity, board and trajectory stay as solved. The perturbation makes the solve recover values it was not
given, and keeps your real calibration out of a twin you save or share. perturb_seed=None in capture keeps the real
solve as it is.

- The timing is real: MVIS keeps the real frame times, the corner ids seen in each frame and the IMU
stamps.

- The data is new: MVIS regenerates the corners and the IMU readings from the truth, with rolling shutter
and t_ga (the time offset between the gyroscope and the accelerometer).

- The solve is the real pipeline, run again on the new data.

So any gap between the result and the truth comes from the solver, not from the recording.

## 1. Build and solve a twin

The twin is the Python module mvis.simulation.twin.

twin.py
from mvis.simulation import twin

# Runs the real solve once (it needs the bag) and takes it as the truth.

# noise_from_residuals sets the noise to match the real residuals.

tw = twin. capture ( " virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml " , " virig4 " ,

noise_from_residuals = True )

report = twin. solve ( tw , seed = 0 ) # with noise

clean = twin. solve ( tw , noise = False ) # without noise

tw. save ( " virig4_twin.npz " ) # keep it; it holds no images

tw = twin.Twin. load ( " virig4_twin.npz " )

- capture runs your camera–IMU config once on the real bag. Its outputs go to results/twin_capture
(set another folder with work_dir=).

- noise_from_residuals=True measures the corner noise from the real solve. It runs one extra solve of
the twin to scale the IMU noise, so the twin’s IMU fit matches the real one.

- solve simulates, solves and returns the errors (estimate minus truth).

- seed picks the noise draw. Run a few seeds, not one.

- A saved twin needs no bag. Solve it again after any change to MVIS or to the solve settings.

What the twin does not test
The simulated noise is Gaussian, and the twin has no lens or timing model errors. So it checks the
estimator, not the recording.

## 2. Read the errors

Each solve returns, per sensor:

- Cameras: lever arm (mm), rotation as a log(R) vector (mrad), td (the camera–IMU time offset, ms),
readout (ms), focal length (px).

- Base IMU: t_ga (ms), gyroscope and accelerometer scale (%).

- Each aux IMU: lever, rotation, td, t_ga and scales.

- Board: rms height error (mm), when the board shape is estimated.

Read the two kinds of run side by side:

- The noise-free error should be near zero. If it is not, the solver does not recover the truth even
from perfect data. That is a model or observability problem.

- The error with noise shows what your data can support. Large errors with noise and small noise-free
errors mean the data limits the result, not the solver.

## 3. Watch the twin of the full rig

We ran the step-4 config (all 4 cameras, all 4 IMUs, recording 01) and simulated the same 80 s from its result.
Each video shows:

- Left: the IMU trajectory and the board, with each camera’s pose.

- Right: each camera’s corners, observed (circles) and reprojected (dots), with the RMS for that frame.

- Bottom: position (m) and orientation as log(R) from the start (rad), with a cursor at the current
time.

The real solve. Corners as the cameras saw them. Reprojection RMS over the run: 0.52 px.

The digital twin. Every corner simulated from the solved calibration and trajectory, at 30 Hz, with 0.5 px noise.

This video twin is simpler than the twin module of section 1:

- Truth: the real solve as it is, with no perturbation: trajectory, board, every camera and IMU.

- Cameras: all four at 30 Hz, each seeing every tag in its view, with 0.5 px corner noise.

- IMUs: 200 Hz, with a fixed noise model (gyroscope 1.7e-4 rad/s/√Hz, accelerometer 3e-3 m/s²/√Hz).

So its corners are cleaner than the real ones. On real data the per-frame RMS jumps when the board is
blurred or far away.

Solved against its truth (one noise draw, all 4 cameras and all 4 IMUs, reprojection RMS 0.71 px):

Sensor | Lever error | Rotation error | Readout error |
T265 left | 0.13 mm | 0.17 mrad | — |
T265 right | 0.14 mm | 0.14 mrad | — |
ELP left | 0.16 mm | 0.12 mrad | 0.05 ms |
ELP right | 0.14 mm | 0.16 mrad | 0.04 ms |
GX3-25 (to the base IMU) | 0.18 mm | 0.54 mrad | — |
GX3-35 (to the base IMU) | 0.24 mm | 0.23 mrad | — |
T265 IMU (to the base IMU) | 0.18 mm | 0.45 mrad | — |

Every lever lands within 0.25 mm and every rotation within 0.6 mrad of the truth. The solve converges on the
full rig.

## 4. Twin of the ELP pair

We built a twin module twin of the ELP-pair camera–IMU run on
virig-4imus-4cams recording 01:

- Cameras: ELP left and right, rolling shutter.

- IMUs: the T265 IMU as base, the Xsens as aux IMU.

- Settings: as in the “ELP RS stereo + two IMUs” run on the
results page: camera intrinsics free, t_ga on, board shape on.

Errors against the truth (estimate minus truth). For lever and rotation the table gives the length of the 3D
error; for a scale, the largest of its three axis errors.

Parameter | Noise-free | With noise, RMS over seeds 0–2 |
Camera lever | 0.094 mm | 0.44 mm |
Camera rotation | 0.177 mrad | 0.32 mrad |
Camera td | 0.007 ms | 0.024 ms |
Camera readout | 0.003 ms | 0.017 ms |
Camera focal length | 0.009 px | 0.096 px |
Base t_ga | 0.015 ms | 0.053 ms |
Base gyroscope scale | 0.011 % | 0.108 % |
Base accelerometer scale | 0.013 % | 0.033 % |
Board height rms | 0.23 mm | 0.23 mm |
Aux lever | 0.164 mm | 0.20 mm |
Aux rotation | 0.245 mrad | 0.58 mrad |
Aux td | 0.007 ms | 0.036 ms |

The camera rows are ELP left; ELP right is close. What it shows:

- The solver converges to the truth. Without noise every error is a fraction of a mm, mrad or ms, and the
scales land within 0.02 %. This is the check that matters.

- Noise sets the limit, and it matches real data. With noise, the gyroscope scale lands within 0.11 %,
t_ga within 0.05 ms and the ELP readout within 0.02 ms. That is no larger than the real spread over the 15
recordings, which also vary the motion: T265 gyroscope scale sd 0.03–0.13 % per axis, t_ga sd 0.13 ms, ELP
readout sd 0.12 ms (results page, “ELP RS stereo + two IMUs”).

- The board height keeps about 0.2 mm of error even without noise.

A check for every MVIS change. We keep these errors as a reference and re-run the twin for new MVIS
versions. A version fails if a solve fails, takes no step, or an error grows past the reference by more than:

Quantity | Allowed growth (noise-free) |
Lever | 0.2 mm |
Rotation | 0.2 mrad |
td, readout | 0.05 ms |
t_ga | 0.1 ms |
Gyroscope scale | 0.01 % |
Accelerometer scale | 0.02 % |
Focal length | 0.2 px |
Board height rms | 0.1 mm |

Errors with noise may grow by twice these amounts, as three seeds are a rough sample. Smaller errors never
fail.

## 5. Twin of the motion

We also used twins to choose the recording motion of step 2. A simulated Looper Insight 9 ran each motion on
3 noise seeds and once without noise. See how we judged it.

## Without ground truth

On real data there is no truth. Two checks stand in for it, strongest first:

- Round trip: mvis roundtrip applies the calibration to its own bag and
calibrates again. PASS needs the IMU intrinsics to collapse and the geometry to hold.

- Repeatability: calibrate several recordings of the same rig with
batch mode. A parameter
that moves between recordings was not pinned down by their motion.

## Simulate without a recording

To try a rig or a motion you have not recorded, start from a simulator example. Each one holds a real motion
and a full rig setup (cameras, IMUs, board), with a perturbed truth like a twin:

sim.py
from mvis.simulation.examples import load_example, simulate

from mvis.calibration.pipeline_cam_imu import run_cam_imu_calibration_multi

ex = load_example ( " twin_gs " ) # ships with the package

data = simulate ( ex , seed = 0 ) # cams, t_imu, w_m, a_m, aux_imus

result = run_cam_imu_calibration_multi (

data [ " cams " ] , ex.board_points_flat , data [ " t_imu " ] , data [ " w_m " ] , data [ " a_m " ] ,

aux_imus = data [ " aux_imus " ] or None )

- In the package: twin_gs, a global-shutter stereo twin with one IMU.

- In a source checkout (data/sim_examples/): more examples, among them virig_4imus_3cams (our VI-Rig),
elp_t265, tum_vi_raw, twin_rs (a rolling-shutter twin), guide06c_60 (the AprilGrid guide motion
of step 2) and guide60b (an earlier chessboard motion). mvis.simulation.examples.available() lists
what your install has.

- Licences: each example’s
setup.yaml names its licence; check it before you reuse a guide motion.

- Lower level: mvis.simulation.scenario builds a dataset from a trajectory, a true calibration and a
board placed in the world.

For the theory of weak motions, see Degeneracy.

## Next

- Step 8: Round-trip validation checks the calibration on real data.

- Why it matters: a twin showed that slow IMUs bias the lever on short windows:
Why calibrate IMUs together.


---

# Round-trip validation | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/guides/roundtrip/

Step 8 of the walkthrough. Here you check the calibration on real data, where there is no ground truth.

- You need: the camera–IMU config from step 4. It must read a ROS1
bag.

- You get: PASS or FAIL, with a check list.

- Check: read the check list (section 2). A FAIL is a finding, not a flaky test.

Why a round trip:

- Reprojection error (how far the detected corners land from where the calibration predicts them) tells
you a calibration fits its own data. It does not tell you the calibration is right.

- A round trip does. We apply the calibration to the data it came from, then calibrate again. If the
first answer was right, there is nothing left to find.

Why both checks: a solver that hides an IMU error inside the geometry can still collapse the IMU
terms, but then a lever arm or the baseline moves. A solver that measured nothing keeps the geometry,
but nothing collapses. Only a right calibration passes both, with no ground truth needed.

## 1. Run it

shell
mvis roundtrip -c virig_4imus_4cams_cam_imu.yaml

One command runs four steps:

- Calibrate (calibration A).

- Correct the bag with mvis apply-calib.

- Calibrate the corrected bag (calibration B).

- Compare A and B and report PASS or FAIL.

It exits non-zero on FAIL, so it can run in CI.

Flag | Effect |
-c, --config | The camera–IMU config to check (ROS1 bag) |
--out | Output folder (default results/roundtrip/<config name>) |
--bag | Use this ROS1 bag instead of the config’s source |
--keep-corrected | Keep the corrected bag (deleted by default) |
--keep-bias | Do not remove the IMU biases in step 2 |

- Disk space: the corrected bag is written next to the raw bag and is about as large. After
calibration A, MVIS checks the disk has room for it and stops if not.

- Detection cache: the corrected bag gets its own name, so its corners are detected afresh.

- Output: report.txt and report.json in the output folder, with the results of both calibrations in
forward/ and recal/.

- EuRoC input: convert the folder to a ROS1 bag first, then pass it with --bag. For a catalog dataset
use mvis datasets convert --dataset <key>; for any mav0 folder call
mvis.datasets.converters.euroc_folder_to_rosbag.convert_euroc_folder_to_rosbag(src, "out.bag").

## 2. What PASS means

PASS needs two things. They pull in opposite directions, which is what makes the test useful.

- Collapse. On the corrected bag, every IMU’s Dw and Da (the gyroscope and accelerometer scale and
misalignment matrices) must go to identity, and the biases b_g and b_a to zero. Calibration A claimed
to measure them; if it was right, the correction used them up.

- Preserve. Each camera’s lever arm (its position in the base IMU frame) must not move, nor must the
stereo baseline between the first two cameras. The correction changes timing and IMU scaling, not
geometry. A lever that moves means calibration A traded geometry against something else.

The limits:

- Dw and Da: every diagonal entry within 1 % of 1.

- Biases: below 0.02 (rad/s for the gyroscope, m/s² for the accelerometer).

- Lever arms and the stereo baseline: at most 2 mm of drift.

The timing terms are warnings, not failures: each camera’s td (time offset to the base IMU) and each
IMU’s t_ga (gyroscope-to-accelerometer offset). How much of them survives depends on how well the data
observes them. The aux IMUs’ td is not checked.

- In report.txt: every timing row is marked warn, whatever its value. It only means the row is a
warning-only check. The value should be near 0; above 2 ms it is worth a look.

## 3. Limits on this rig

- Rolling shutter is not tested. apply-calib re-stamps each frame but does not unwarp its rows. So a
round trip on the ELP pair does not check its readout.

- Use other checks for the readout: Rolling-shutter calibration and the
digital-twin check.

## 4. Results on the running example

The full rig: VI-Rig recording 01, all 4 cameras and all 4 IMUs, the step-4 config, run on 2026-11-25 with MVIS 0.4.1, local gravity at Newark (gravity: 9.8013 # m/s², Newark, Delaware).
Result: PASS. All 16 IMU checks (4 per IMU) and all 5 geometry checks (4 levers, 1 baseline) pass.

IMUs: what calibration A measured collapses. A ran on the raw bag, B on the corrected bag. A right
calibration leaves nothing for B to find.

Check | Calibration | Xsens (base) | GX3-25 | GX3-35 | T265 IMU | Pass if |
Gyroscope scale Dw: worst axis off 1 | A | 0.21 % | 0.26 % | 0.10 % | 0.35 % | |
| B | 0.00 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % | < 1 % |
Accelerometer scale Da: worst axis off 1 | A | 0.39 % | 0.50 % | 0.55 % | 1.97 % | |
| B | 0.01 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % | < 1 % |
Largest bias (m/s²) | A | 0.029 | 0.086 | 0.064 | 0.168 | |
| B | 0.002 | 0.0003 | 0.0004 | 0.002 | < 0.02 |
t_ga (ms) | A | −0.82 | +0.10 | +0.01 | −6.74 | |
| B | +0.30 | 0.00 | 0.01 | 0.00 | warn-only, near 0 |
td to base (ms) | A | — | −0.69 | −2.07 | −7.17 | |
| B | — | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | shown only |

The largest corrections A made, the T265 IMU’s 2 % accelerometer scale and its −6.74 ms t_ga, are fully
gone in B. The base Xsens keeps +0.30 ms of t_ga, well under 2 ms.

Full scale diagonals (x, y, z)

Cameras: the geometry stays. apply-calib does not touch the lever arms, rotations and intrinsics that A
found, so B should find them again. Only the lever rows and the T265 baseline are graded; the other rows are
shown for reference.

Check | Calibration | T265 left | T265 right | ELP left | ELP right | Pass if |
Lever arm to base (mm) | A | 130.95 | 112.26 | 145.04 | 185.84 | |
| B | 131.03 | 112.33 | 145.08 | 185.86 | |

T265 pair (cam0–cam1, graded) | 63.69 mm | 63.69 mm | moves ≤ 2 mm |

- Geometry: every camera moves by under 0.1 mm and turns by under 0.12 mrad; fx and fy move by under
0.01 px. The reprojection error stays at 0.51 px RMS.

- Camera td: it collapses with the IMU terms. It is a timing term that A measured and apply-calib
removed.

- Not tested: the ELP readout, as apply-calib does not unwarp rolling-shutter rows (section 3).

The check list as mvis roundtrip prints it: report.txt.
The report of calibration B, as MVIS wrote it except for local folder names:

Open full screen (HTML, 16.4 MB). The report
of calibration A is the one in step 4.

## Export a corrected dataset

mvis apply-calib is the correction step inside the round trip. You can also run it on its own. It takes a
camera–IMU calibration and a raw ROS1 bag, and writes a new bag with the calibration applied:

- IMU intrinsics removed: scale, misalignment and g-sensitivity.

- Biases removed.

- One timeline for every stream.

Downstream tools then get corrected data and need to know nothing about the calibration.

### Run apply-calib

With flags:

shell
mvis apply-calib --calib cam_imu_calib.yaml --in raw.bag --out corrected.bag

Or from a config file:

shell
mvis apply-calib -c recalib.yaml

- Calibration: mvis cam-imu writes cam_imu_calib.yaml next to cam_imu.json. Pass that YAML to
--calib.

- Output: defaults to <input>.corrected.bag. An existing bag is not overwritten.

- Topics: the calibration records each sensor’s source topic, so MVIS finds which topic belongs to which
sensor. Use --map only to override that.

- Example config: examples/configs/recalib_example.yaml
in the MVIS repo. It lists every config key.

### What gets corrected

Correction | Detail | Turn off with |
IMU intrinsics | Dw, Da and Tg removed through the inverse IMU model | --no-imu-intrinsics |
Static bias | The calibrated biases subtracted | --keep-bias |
Time alignment | Every camera and aux IMU re-stamped onto the base IMU clock by its td | --no-td |
Gyroscope-to-accelerometer offset | The accelerometer re-sampled at t + t_ga, when t_ga was calibrated | --no-t-ga |
Undistortion | Images undistorted (mono8 images only) | on only with --undistort |

The terms:

- Dw / Da: the scale and misalignment of the gyroscope and the accelerometer.

- Tg: the g-sensitivity, how linear acceleration leaks into the gyroscope.

- td: the time offset of a sensor to the base IMU.

- t_ga: the time offset between the gyroscope and the accelerometer.

More flags:

- --strict: stop on missing or empty topics, wrong message types, duplicate IMU stamps and non-finite
values, instead of passing them through.

Re-stamping uses the header clock
The correction works on each message’s header stamp, the time the sensor reported. Working on the bag’s
record time instead would bake each topic’s receive latency into the corrected bag, and turn a driver
artefact into permanent data.

### Many recordings

One calibration usually serves many recordings of a rig. To correct a whole folder of bags, run
scripts/recalib_batch.py --calib cam_imu_calib.yaml --in-dir raw/ --out-dir corrected/ from the
MVIS repo. It runs the same correction as apply-calib on every
*.bag in the folder.

The t_ga study starts from such a corrected bag: Why calibrate t_ga.

## When it fails

A FAIL is a real finding. The usual causes:

- Wrong camera model. The intrinsics absorbed an error that comes back once the timing is corrected. Try
another camera model.

- Wrong IMU convention. See IMU model.

- An interpolated accelerometer that corrupts td, as on the T265. The fix is gyro_only on that IMU,
or estimating t_ga. With t_ga off the round trip still passes, but td does not return to 0: in our
T265 test (older MVIS code) the second calibration finds td = −1.47 ms on both T265 cameras. That is the
unmodelled gyro–accel offset, showing up as a camera time error. Turn t_ga on and read it. See
Why calibrate t_ga, section 5.

- Not enough motion. The parameter was never observed, so correcting by it does nothing consistent.

## Next

- Done: you have finished the walkthrough.

- Why it matters: the corrected bag from apply-calib is also what the Why calibrate pages test. Start with
Why calibrate the IMU.


---

# Why calibrate the IMU | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/why/imu/

This page shows what an IMU calibration gains a tracker downstream.
Data: 24 headset recordings from the Monado SLAM Datasets,
plus VI-Rig in the last section.

The answer first:

- Mono gains most: correcting the IMU and timing with MVIS cuts the median OpenVINS mono SE3 ATE from 28.80 to
9.56 mm, by two thirds.

- Stereo gains less: the median stereo SE3 ATE drops from 8.94 to 7.04 mm, and the 1 s drift improves on 24/24
recordings.

- Online calibration does not replace it: on the as-published recordings, only stereo with online td ties
the corrected recording.

- Online calibration on top adds nothing: on the corrected recordings, leave it off.

- VI-Rig shows the same kind of error: the T265 accel scale is off by 1.7–2.0 % on every axis.

How to turn it on: estimate the IMU intrinsics in Camera–IMU calibration,
then write a corrected recording with mvis apply-calib.

## The setup

We ran the OpenVINS visual-inertial tracker twice on each recording: once as published, once corrected by MVIS.

Recordings: 24 imucalib recordings from the Monado SLAM Datasets:

Headset | Recordings |
Valve Index | 8 |
HP Reverb G2 | 12 |
Samsung Odyssey+ | 4 |

Two arms: the two runs of a recording differ only in the input.

- As published: the recording as the dataset ships it.

- Corrected: the same recording after mvis apply-calib with the MVIS calibration. It applies:

- the IMU intrinsics Dw and Da, the gyro and accel scale and misalignment;

- removal of the static bias;

- each camera’s camera–IMU time offset td, by shifting the image stamps;

- the gyro–accel time offset t_ga, by re-interpolating the accelerometer.

- Images: unchanged.

Shared by both arms:

- the same MVIS camera intrinsics (kb4) and camera–IMU extrinsics;

- identical OpenVINS configs, byte for byte.

So the test measures one thing: the MVIS IMU and time correction, given the MVIS geometry.

Ground truth: the lighthouse poses that come with the dataset.

Metrics:

- SE3 ATE (mm): position error after a rigid alignment to the ground truth. This is the primary metric.

- RPE 1 s (mm): position drift over 1 s windows.

- Scale error (%): $\lvert s - 1 \rvert$, where $s$ is the scale of a similarity (Sim3) alignment. It shows
how far the trajectory size is off.

- Medians and wins: each number is a median over recordings. “Better” counts the recordings where the
corrected recording wins.

- p: Wilcoxon signed-rank p, paired by recording, not corrected for multiple tests.

## 1. Correcting the IMU cuts mono position error by two thirds

OpenVINS estimates no calibration online here. Lower is better.

Metric | As published | Corrected | Corrected better | p |
Stereo SE3 ATE (mm) | 8.94 | 7.04 | 20/24 | $9.1\times10^{-5}$ |
Stereo RPE 1 s (mm) | 5.51 | 4.23 | 24/24 | $1.2\times10^{-7}$ |
Mono SE3 ATE (mm) | 28.80 | 9.56 | 21/23 | $2.1\times10^{-4}$ |
Mono RPE 1 s (mm) | 9.95 | 6.79 | 21/23 | $2.1\times10^{-4}$ |
Mono scale error (%) | 5.81 | 1.90 | 19/23 | $3.3\times10^{-5}$ |
Stereo scale error (%) | 1.40 | 1.15 | 11/24 | 0.88 (not significant) |

- Mono has 23 pairs: one Valve recording never starts in mono in either arm.

- Mono gains most: one camera cannot see metric scale, so the tracker leans on the IMU, and a wrong IMU
likely shows up directly.

- Stereo gains less: the stereo baseline gives scale, which likely hides part of the IMU error.

Per headset, SE3 ATE in mm:

Headset | Stereo | Mono |
Valve Index (8 stereo, 7 mono) | 4.13 → 2.73 | 12.15 → 7.55 |
HP Reverb G2 (12) | 9.91 → 7.39 | 29.08 → 9.49 |
Samsung Odyssey+ (4) | 21.29 → 9.96 | 47.51 → 13.67 |

- Mono failures as published: five mono runs lost scale or diverged.

- Mono failures corrected: one, MIC10, a Valve recording that fails in both arms.

## 2. Online calibration on the published recordings does not catch up

OpenVINS can estimate some calibration online: one td for all cameras, the IMU intrinsics and the camera–IMU
extrinsics. Here the corrected recording with nothing online meets the as-published recording with online
estimation on. SE3 ATE in mm, medians:

Cameras | Online on the as-published recording | Corrected, nothing online | As published + online |
Stereo | td | 7.04 | 6.80 |
Stereo | IMU intrinsics | 7.04 | 10.74 |
Stereo | IMU intrinsics + td | 7.04 | 8.19 |
Stereo | IMU intrinsics + td + extrinsics | 7.04 | 11.62 |
Mono | td | 9.56 | 18.06 |
Mono | IMU intrinsics | 9.56 | 25.50 |
Mono | IMU intrinsics + td | 9.56 | 14.57 |

- Stereo + online td is a tie: corrected better in 14/24, p = 0.2.

- Every other stereo setting stays behind the corrected recording.

- Mono stays behind at every setting, each in 21/23 recordings.

- t_ga: OpenVINS has no t_ga parameter, so it cannot model this offset. See
Why calibrate t_ga.

## 3. Online calibration on corrected recordings adds nothing

- Stereo + td: 7.04 → 7.33 mm; online is better in only 7/24.

- No setting lowers SE3 ATE significantly.

The online values still check MVIS:

- Independent start: online td starts at 0, so the agreement does not lean on MVIS.

- Agreement: camera td in ms, as-published recording, stereo + online td:

Headset | MVIS td (cam0) | OpenVINS online td |
Valve Index | −0.19 | −0.22 |
HP Reverb G2 | −1.33 | −1.12 |
Samsung Odyssey+ | −1.44 | −1.21 |

- Corrected recording: online td stays near 0, as it should once the offset is removed.

## 4. On VI-Rig, the T265 accel scale is off on every axis

The same kind of error shows on our own rig, virig-4imus-4cams. We take the
ELP stereo + two IMUs run (T8 in the results), 15 recordings:

- Rig: ELP stereo, the T265 IMU as base IMU, the Xsens as aux IMU.

- IMU model: MVIS with Kalibr’s IMU convention (kalibr), the “MVIS (K-IMU)” column.

Accel scales, the diagonal of Da, medians:

IMU | Da x | Da y | Da z |
T265 IMU | 1.01989 | 1.01905 | 1.01668 |
Xsens MTi | 0.99997 | 0.99932 | 1.00093 |

- T265 IMU: accel scale off by 1.7–2.0 % on every axis.

- Xsens: within 0.1 % of 1, a check on the T265 result.

- Same fix: the corrected Monado recordings apply Da and Dw the same way.

Conclusion:

- Correct the IMU before the tracker: it cuts mono SE3 ATE by two thirds and helps stereo too.

- Online calibration is no substitute: it does not catch up on the as-published recordings. On the corrected
ones it adds nothing, so leave it off.

## Limits

- In-sample: MVIS was solved on the same recordings. No held-out check yet.
- Shared geometry: both arms use the MVIS camera intrinsics and extrinsics. This is not MVIS against
the best calibration for the as-published data.
- ”As published” is not raw: the dataset already carries its own Basalt IMU correction.
- Valve corrected twice: on Valve that correction was applied twice, which leaves an accel scale
error of about 6 %. Part of the Valve mono gain likely undoes that.
- One combined gain: the correction fixes IMU intrinsics, bias, td and t_ga together. Their effects
were not separated.
- Too-large trajectories: Reverb G2 and Odyssey+ trajectories come out about 1–2 % too large in
both arms. The cause is not known.
- One recording gets worse: Odyssey+ MOC11 stereo goes from 11.4 to 16.6 mm with the correction,
though its RPE and mono improve.
- Small group: Odyssey+ has only 4 pairs.
- Priors not tuned: the OpenVINS online priors were left at fixed values.
- Who ran it: we ran every solve.

## Data

- Monado: the imucalib recordings of the
Monado SLAM Datasets, CC BY 4.0, with their
lighthouse ground truth. The MVIS configs are in the Monado example.

- VI-Rig: virig-4imus-4cams, run T8 of the
results. Licence and
citation are on the dataset page.

- Runs: the OpenVINS runs date from October 2026. They use MVIS calibrations made with older code (August 2026), before the results batch.

- Citation: please cite the Monado SLAM Datasets, the VI-Rig dataset and MVIS.

## Related

- Camera–IMU calibration

- Why calibrate t_ga

- Monado example

- Round-trip validation

# Why calibrate t_ga | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/why/tga/

This page shows what happens to a camera–IMU calibration when the gyroscope and the accelerometer inside one IMU
are not in step. Data: the Looper Insight 9 and the Intel T265 IMU on VI-Rig,
with the swept recordings on the Hub, calibench-vi/datasets.

The answer first:

- Real IMUs have a t_ga: MVIS measures a few ms on the Looper and on the T265 IMU.

- Tools without it move td: Kalibr and Basalt treat the IMU as one clock, so their td takes a steady
share of t_ga.

- No warning: every run of every tool converged.

- MVIS keeps td flat: it reports the delay as t_ga, and its IMU scales barely change.

- A corrected dataset needs it: without t_ga, a round trip leaves a camera time error.

How to turn it on: t_ga in step 4. MVIS fits t_ga by default
(solve.estimate_t_ga: true, with a weak 10 ms prior, sigma_t_ga: 0.010), as in these runs.

## The setup

- t_ga: the time offset between the gyroscope and the accelerometer inside one IMU.

- td: the time offset between a camera and the IMU.

- Who fits what: MVIS fits both. Kalibr and Basalt fit only td.

- The question: what happens to td and the IMU scales when the IMU has a t_ga?

## 1. With t_ga = 0, the three tools agree

- Two datasets: Looper Insight 9 (looper_1) and Intel T265 (VI-Rig april_01).

- Prepared so t_ga is 0: MVIS calibrated each raw recording, and we resampled the camera and IMU streams
with that result. On the new recording, by MVIS’s estimate, td = 0, t_ga = 0 and the IMU scales are 1.

- Settings: each tool’s usual settings. T265: camera intrinsics pinned. Looper: intrinsics free.

- Result: all three tools read td within 0.3 ms of 0, and the IMU scales within 0.4 % of 1, except Basalt
on the T265.

Tool | Looper Insight 9 | Intel T265 |
td (ms) | scale error (%) | td (ms) | scale error (%) |
MVIS | −0.01 | 0.01 | +0.07 | 0.30 |
Kalibr | −0.04 | 0.13 | −0.19 | 0.34 |
Basalt | −0.04 | 0.21 | −0.28 | 1.50 |

Corrected bag, no injected delay. Scale error is the largest |scale − 1| over the six IMU axes.

- Basalt on the T265: gyro x and accel z read about 1.2 % and 1.5 % from 1.

- Not caused by t_ga: that offset is there with no delay.

## 2. Without a t_ga, td takes a steady share of the delay

- Sweep: we delayed only the accel by $\tau$ = −50, −20, −10, −5, −2, 0, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 ms, and left
everything else unchanged. That is 11 recordings per device; the true t_ga of each is $\tau$.

- Run: all three tools on every recording, with the settings above.

- Gravity: the T265 sweep was solved at 9.81 m/s², before 2026-11-25. The example config now sets
9.8013 (Newark); with it the accel scale moves by about −0.09 %.

Accel delayed by τ. MVIS puts it in t_ga (solid blue) and keeps td flat (dashed); Kalibr and Basalt have
no t_ga, so their td takes a steady share of τ.

- MVIS: it reports the delay as t_ga, with slope 1.00 on both devices. Its td
stays flat, and its IMU scales change by under 0.01 %.

- Kalibr and Basalt: with no t_ga, their td takes a steady share of $\tau$. A share of
0.64 means td moves 0.64 ms per 1 ms of t_ga.

- The shares: 0.64 for Kalibr and 0.59 for Basalt on the Looper;
0.30 and 0.28 on the T265.

- Their IMU scales drift too: mostly under 0.2 % within ±10 ms, up to about 1.8 % at ±50 ms. Basalt on the
T265 reaches 0.3 % in accel at ±2 ms.

- No warning: every run of every tool converged.

- Not a bug: with one IMU clock, the best fit puts td somewhere between the gyro and the accel.

- Where it lands: it depends on the recording, likely on how much the gyro and the accel each drive the fit.
We have not tested this.

## 3. Real devices have a t_ga

- Measured: on the raw recordings MVIS reads t_ga = −5.03 ms on the Looper and
−5.69 ms on the T265.

- The effect: a tool without t_ga moves td by its share of that.

Device | t_ga on the raw bag (MVIS) | Kalibr: share → td moved | Basalt: share → td moved |
Looper Insight 9 | −5.03 ± 0.02 ms | 0.64 → −3.21 ms | 0.59 → −2.97 ms |
Intel T265 | −5.69 ± 0.43 ms | 0.30 → −1.72 ms | 0.28 → −1.60 ms |

On the raw bags, Kalibr's td really differs from MVIS's by about this much
(−3.16 ms on Looper, −1.91 ms on the T265).

## 4. On the running example, only the T265 IMU has a large t_ga

The guides use the VI-Rig recording virig-4imus-4cams. Its four IMUs on one rig
show t_ga on four devices at once.

- One run, recording 01: MVIS solved all four cameras and all four IMUs together, with t_ga on, as in
step 4. The Xsens is the base IMU.

- t_ga per IMU: ± 0.02 ms on each, from the run’s result table.

IMU | t_ga (ms) |
Xsens MTi-100 (base) | −0.82 |
MicroStrain GX3-25 | +0.10 |
MicroStrain GX3-35 | +0.01 |
T265 IMU | −6.74 |

- Only the T265 IMU has a large offset. The other three read within 1 ms of 0.

- It repeats over 15 recordings: in the results, the T265 IMU reads
−6.692 ms, sd 0.112, in the mixed T265 + ELP run
(T7) and −6.698 ms,
sd 0.135, in the ELP stereo run (T8). In
those two runs the T265 IMU is the base IMU.

## 5. Without t_ga, a round trip leaves a td error

This test ran on older MVIS code; the date is in Data.

- Setup: recording 01, T265 cameras and the T265 IMU, camera intrinsics pinned. We ran a
round trip twice: calibrate, correct the recording, calibrate again. The only change was
t_ga on or off.

- Both runs pass: the IMU scales and biases go back to 1 and 0.

- With t_ga: the second calibration finds td of −0.03 and −0.04 ms on the two cameras, and t_ga
goes from −6.97 to +0.17 ms.

- Without t_ga: the second calibration finds td = −1.47 ms on both cameras, not 0. This is the
unmodelled gyro–accel offset, showing up as a camera time error.

Conclusion:

- t_ga matters for camera–IMU calibration: on these two devices, a tool without it moves td by about
1.6–3.2 ms.

- It keeps a corrected dataset consistent in time: to use a tool without t_ga, remove the offset first
with corrected-dataset export.

## Limits

- The test favours MVIS: the zero point is MVIS’s own calibration, and the sweep injects exactly the
shift MVIS models, a pure accel delay.
- Raw data: which tool’s td is right on raw data is not tested.
- Not a pure shift: on the T265 the real offset shrinks with frequency, from −6.8 ms at 2–4 Hz to
−3.6 ms at 16–22 Hz, less certain above 22 Hz. One t_ga is a
compromise.
- One recording per device: each sweep starts from a single recording.
- Who ran it: we ran all three tools.

## Data

- Sweep recordings: on the Hub, each with a README, the MVIS calibration used for the correction and a
provenance.json (sign, $\tau$, crop, sha256 per recording):

- calibench-vi/datasets → looper-insight9/tga-sweep

- calibench-vi/datasets → virig-4imus-3cams/tga-sweep

- Running example: the T7 and T8 rows are in the VI-Rig results.

- Round trip: older MVIS code, July 2026.

- Citation: please cite the VI-Rig dataset and MVIS.

## Related

- IMU model: t_ga

- Step 4: Camera–IMU calibration

- Round-trip validation

- Comparison vs Kalibr / Basalt

# Why calibrate the board shape | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/why/board-shape/

This page shows why MVIS can solve the shape of the calibration board, and what a flat solve does on our board.
Data: our VI-Rig recordings on the Hub, calibench-vi/datasets.

The answer first:

- Our board is not flat: our AprilGrid on a panel is a saddle 10–11 mm peak to peak on this VI-Rig mount.

- A flat solve hides it: camera-only fx comes out 0.4–1.0 % low on average. Camera–IMU puts the gyro
scale Dw about 1.1 % high and a lever about 9 mm off. No check fails; only the camera-only
board_point_bias diagnostic hints at it.

- What MVIS solves: estimate.board_points: true adds one height per corner, in camera-only and camera–IMU
runs. Kalibr and Basalt treat the board as flat.

- The cost: 144 more unknowns. On these runs the solve took no longer, and fx repeated no worse.

- Off by default: we turn it on for VI-Rig.

How to turn it on: A board is never flat.

## The setup

- Board: an AprilGrid with 6 × 6 tags of 88 mm, 144 corners.

- Recordings: the VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cameras set, recordings 1–15, all on one
mount of the board.

- Code: every solve in sections 1–4 ran on MVIS main f902d39 (2026-11-11), unless a line says otherwise.

- Lever: the translation between a camera and the IMU.

## 1. The board is a saddle

We estimated the height of every corner four ways, all on recordings 3–5:

- ELP left camera, rolling shutter, camera-only.

- T265 left, global shutter, camera-only.

- ELP stereo pair, camera-only, two corners per tag (10.4–10.8 mm, 2.1–2.3 mm rms).

- Camera–IMU: the ELP stereo pair with the T265 and Xsens IMUs. This one also ran on recordings 1–15 with
two corners per tag, for the recording-to-recording row.

Measure | Value |
Out of plane, peak to peak (all-corner estimates) | 10.5–11.0 mm |
Out of plane, rms (all-corner estimates) | 2.3–2.4 mm |
Shape | A ridge across the middle (+3 to +4.5 mm); two opposite corners sag to −5 to −6 mm |
Agreement between the four estimates | 0.04–0.32 mm rms, correlation 0.991–0.9999 |
Recording to recording | 0.05–0.16 mm rms; recordings 1–2 sit about 0.4 mm from the 15-recording mean |

Height of each corner off the flat board: peak to peak 10.9 mm, rms 2.4 mm. Numbers are the tag column and row (row 0 at the bottom). Hover or tap a corner for its value.

VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cameras, recording 3: camera–IMU solve with all 144 corners (ELP stereo pair, T265 and Xsens IMUs), MVIS main f902d39. Red corners stand out of the best-fit plane, blue ones sink below it.

- Two corners per tag: over the 72 corners they observe, these solves read 2.2–2.7 mm rms and 9.1–11.7 mm
peak to peak (camera–IMU, recordings 1–15; recording 1 is the 9.1 mm low end). The other 72 heights have no
data (section 4), so the first two rows leave them out. Since
2026-11-12 MVIS main writes the rms and peak to peak over the observed corners only, with a per-corner count
n_obs, in the camera-only board shape output.

- Agreement: the three estimates that use the ELP left camera agree within 0.04–0.13 mm. The T265 estimate,
from another camera and lens, is 0.23–0.32 mm from them. Each comparison removes the best-fit plane first.

- Not low-order: a biquadratic surface still leaves 0.9–1.0 mm rms, a biquartic 0.5 mm. A few bending terms
cannot replace one height per corner.

- Per mount: the shape depends on the mount. On another mount, the 5 IMUs + 4 cameras recordings, an older
run estimated 7.3 mm peak to peak. That shape correlates only 0.60 with the stored 15-recording shape of this
mount.

## 2. Camera-only: a flat board pulls the focal length down

Recordings 3–5, equidistant model, all 144 corners. We solved each once with the shape and once with a rigid flat
board:

Camera | Board | Reprojection rms (px) | fx (px), mean ± std over 3 recordings | cy (px) |
ELP left (rolling shutter) | shape | 0.445 | 428.12 ± 0.88 | 267.32 ± 0.28 |
| flat | 0.614 | 426.58 ± 1.17 | 270.57 ± 0.75 |
T265 left (global shutter) | shape | 0.427 | 286.72 ± 0.44 | 404.63 ± 0.47 |
| flat | 0.573 | 284.29 ± 0.63 | 406.63 ± 0.90 |

- Residual: the shape cuts it by 27.5 % on the ELP and 25.5 % on the T265. Across all camera-only arms,
including two corners per tag and stereo, the cut is 25–29 %.

- Focal length: flat reads fx 0.36 % low on the ELP and 0.85 % low on the T265. It is low on every
recording, by 0.25–0.48 % and 0.77–0.93 %.

- Two corners per tag: the fx gaps are 0.42 % and 0.99 %, up to 1.09 % on one recording.

- Principal point: flat also moves cy, by +3.3 px on the ELP and +2.0 px on the T265.

- Stereo: with two corners per tag, the ELP stereo pair reads fx 0.48 % low flat. Flat also moves its
baseline by 0.3 %, from 59.23 to 59.04 mm, the stereo rotation by 1.2–1.8 mrad as log(R), mostly about y, and
the rolling-shutter readout by 0.16 ms.

- With the IMU: in the camera–IMU solves of section 3, on recordings 3–5, ELP left fx with the shape is
427.9 px with two corners per tag and 428.2 px with all corners. Camera-only gives 428.1 px, so all are within
0.2 px.

- Smaller flat bias with the IMU: there the flat-board fx bias is 0.1–0.2 %: +0.4 ± 0.6 px over 15
recordings, with the opposite sign on 3 of them, and +0.8 px with all corners on recordings 3–5.

## 3. Camera–IMU: a flat board shows up as gyro scale and lever

15 recordings of the ELP stereo pair with the T265 and Xsens IMUs, two corners per tag. We solved each once with
the shape, starting from an earlier 7.7 mm estimate of the same board, and once with a rigid flat board. A good
gyroscope reads a scale Dw close to 1.

Mean ± std over the 15 recordings, range in brackets:

Quantity | Flat board | With the shape |
T265 gyro scale x | 1.0117 ± 0.0029 [1.0061–1.0161] | 1.0000 ± 0.0011 [0.9986–1.0021] |
T265 gyro scale y | 1.0148 ± 0.0029 [1.0084–1.0188] | 1.0034 ± 0.0012 [1.0016–1.0058] |
T265 gyro scale z | 1.0046 ± 0.0007 [1.0035–1.0066] | 1.0039 ± 0.0003 [1.0034–1.0044] |
Xsens gyro scale x | 1.0115 ± 0.0032 [1.0050–1.0163] | 1.0008 ± 0.0012 [0.9991–1.0033] |
ELP left lever z | −4.6 ± 3.3 mm [−8.5 to 0.9] | 4.6 ± 1.3 mm [1.9 to 6.7] |
Reprojection rms | 0.61 ± 0.03 px [0.57–0.65] | 0.33 ± 0.02 px [0.30–0.39] |

- Gyro scale: with the shape, every axis of both IMUs is within 0.6 % of 1. The largest is T265 y, 1.0058,
on recording 11; the Xsens stays within 0.33 %.

- Per recording: the shape lowers T265 x and y by 1.17 ± 0.28 % and 1.13 ± 0.23 %, and Xsens x by
1.07 ± 0.30 %, with the same sign on all 15.

- T265 z: about 0.4 % high either way.

- Accelerometer: the T265 accel scale Da moves by −0.31 ± 0.20 % in z; x and y barely move.

- Lever: the shape moves ELP left lever z by +9.3 ± 2.7 mm per recording. The lever also repeats better,
std 1.3 mm against 3.3 mm flat.

- Time offsets: t_ga moves by −0.18 ms and td by under 0.1 ms.

- Start value and corner set: on recordings 3–5 we also solved all 144 corners from a flat start, instead of
two per tag from the 7.7 mm estimate. The answer is nearly the same: gyro scale within about 0.1 % and lever z
within 1 mm (on average 0.08 % and 0.9 mm), at about 1.5× the solve time. Both changed at once, so this run
does not separate them.

- No alarm: the flat solves converged, and their 0.61 px residual failed no check. In the camera-only runs of
section 2, the per-corner board_point_bias shows the twist: median 0.15–0.27 px flat against 0.06–0.13 px
with the shape. Camera–IMU output has no such diagnostic.

- Other mount: an older run used 7 recordings of the 5 IMUs + 4 cameras rig, 4 cameras each, with the EUCM
and kb4 lens models. Turning the shape off rotated the camera extrinsics by a median 6.8 mrad (log(R), after
aligning the two solutions as a whole; 7.4–8.0 mrad as solved). It moved the lever by 1.3–2.2 mm and cy by
1.8 px. That run compared extrinsics only, not gyro scale or fx.

## 4. The cost, and when to turn it on

- More unknowns: 144 heights, each with a weak 3 mm prior (board_height_sigma: 0.003, in m).

- Solve time: not longer on these runs. Camera-only with all corners, means of 3 on 2 threads, shape against
flat: ELP 21.7 against 22.7 min, T265 12.1 against 13.9 min, ELP stereo 34.0 against 33.9 min. Camera–IMU:
+3 ± 35 s on 10–14 min solves.

- fx repeatability: no worse with the shape. Camera-only with all corners, the scatter with the shape is
0.55–0.93× the flat scatter: ELP 0.88 against 1.17 px, T265 0.44 against 0.63 px. Three recordings are too few
to rank. Camera–IMU over 15 recordings: 0.62 against 0.91 px.

- Earlier study: a study on development code found fx repeating 2–4× worse with the shape. Its flat runs
let each corner move under a 1 mm prior. These runs do not show that.

- Two corners per tag see half the heights: with corner_subsample: two_anti a camera–IMU solve or a one-camera solve
observes 72 of the 144 corners. The other 72 heights have no data and stay near their start values. A
camera-only solve with two or more cameras adds the other diagonal on frames that see at least 35 of the 36
tags, so it sees all 144, but half of them only from a few frames.

- Where two corners per tag is set: it is the camera-only default, and our camera–IMU configs set it too. The
camera–IMU default is all.

- Default: MVIS keeps estimate.board_points off. We turn it on for every VI-Rig solve, camera-only and
camera–IMU; our other rigs keep it off.

- When to turn it on: when your board is measurably not flat. Signs: a smooth camera-only board_point_bias
pattern across the board, or a gap under a straightedge. With the shape on, the MVIS report (main since
2026-11-12) adds a Board Shape section with a map of the heights.

- Start value: a camera–IMU run can start from an earlier estimate with board.heights_file, for example the
<output>_board_shape.yaml a previous run wrote. Camera-only runs do not read it.

Conclusion:

- A flat solve is biased and silent: on this mount it is off by 0.4–1.0 % in camera-only fx, about 1.1 %
in gyro scale and about 9 mm in lever, and no check fails.

- The shape fits better: the residual drops by about a quarter and the gyro scales sit within 0.6 % of 1, so
we read the flat numbers as biased.

- It is free here: on these runs the shape cost no repeatability and no solve time.

## Limits

- No measured reference shape: the four estimates agree with each other, but none was checked
against a metrology scan of the board.
- Who ran it: we ran every solve.
- Gyro near 1 is a prior, not a measurement: the same T265 reads its accel scale about 2 % high
with or without the shape.
- One board, one mount: sections 1–4 use one mount on one rig. The other mount appears only in the
shape comparison of section 1 and the extrinsic shifts at the end of section 3, both from one older run.
We did not test other mounts.
- Small camera-only sets: section 2 has 3 recordings per camera, with the equidistant model only.
- Stereo settings: the stereo runs used the regression settings (two corners per tag, 5 Hz with the
reference camera at 10 Hz, 15 iterations), not the mono ones (10 Hz, 30 iterations).
- Not re-run with the shape on and off: the camera–IMU setup that also puts the T265 camera in the
solve.
- Untested cause: why the flat-board fx bias is smaller in camera–IMU than in camera-only runs.
- Solve times: from 2-thread runs on a shared, loaded machine.

## Data

- Recordings: the VI-Rig datasets on the Hub,
calibench-vi/datasets. Please cite the VI-Rig dataset and MVIS.

- Board config: with the shape on, in the 4 IMUs + 4 cameras example.

- Main runs: MVIS main f902d39 (2026-11-11), unless a line says otherwise.

- Other mount: the 7.3 mm shape of section 1 and the extrinsic shifts of section 3 come from MVIS main
644f7a2 (2026-11-06), not repeated on f902d39. Its 0.60 correlation uses the stored 15-recording shape from
earlier regression rows, not recomputed against the f902d39 shape.

- Earlier study: the development-code study in section 4 dates from 2026-10-31.

## Related

- Board setup

- Camera calibration

- Camera–IMU calibration

- Why calibrate t_ga

- Fisheye model (kb4)

# Why kb4 for fisheye | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/why/kb4/

This page shows why kb4 is the MVIS fisheye model and equidistant is not. You need nothing to run here; the
numbers come from our runs on the Intel T265 (VI-Rig 5 IMUs + 4 cams),
TUM-VI and TUM-Fisheye.

The answer first:

- One polynomial: below 90° off axis the two formulas are identical. Fitted separately on the T265, they agree
to about $2\times10^{-6}$ px.

- Past 90°, only kb4 projects: equidistant has no projection for rays at or past 90°; kb4 has one.

- Equidistant stalled on the one past-90° lens we tested: on BF2M, up to 97° off axis, it stayed at its
starting values, 15–24 px off TUM in fx, even on a recording where it dropped no corner.

- kb4 converged there: from the same start, kb4 came within 0.4 px of TUM in fx. We have not found why
equidistant stalls.

- No cost below 90°: fisheye and kannala_brandt mean kb4.

- Kalibr export: a camera–IMU result with kb4 exports to Kalibr as pinhole-equi, exact for rays in front
of the camera. On export MVIS warns when the fit used corners past 90°, which Kalibr cannot project.

- Fold warning: MVIS warns when the kb4 polynomial folds inside the image, as it does on BF2M: no ray lands
past about 712–743 px from the centre.

How to choose it: Choose a fisheye model (T265 example).

## The setup: two models

Both models map the angle $\theta$ of a ray off the optical axis to a distance $r$ from the principal point, with
the same four coefficients:

$r = f\,\theta\,(1 + k_1\theta^2 + k_2\theta^4 + k_3\theta^6 + k_4\theta^8)$
They differ only in how they get $\theta$ from a 3D point $(x, y, z)$:

Model | $\theta$ from | Rays at or past 90° ($z \le 0$) |
equidistant (Kalibr pinhole-equi) | $\theta = \arctan(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}/z)$ | Cannot be projected |
kb4 (Kannala–Brandt, as in Basalt) | $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\, z)$ | Projected, up to the polynomial’s first fold |

## 1. Below 90°, they are the same

Where few or no corners pass 90°, the two models give the same calibration:

Data | Solves | kb4 − equidistant |
Intel T265, VI-Rig, 7 recordings, camera-only | 28 pairs | mapping gap p95 ≤ $1.9\times10^{-6}$ px, intrinsics ≤ $7.8\times10^{-7}$ px |
Intel T265, VI-Rig, 7 recordings, camera–IMU | 28 pairs | rotation ≤ $1.0\times10^{-11}$ rad, lever ≤ $1.9\times10^{-9}$ mm, td ≤ $1.5\times10^{-10}$ ms |
TUM-VI, imu1–4, camera–IMU | 8 pairs | rotation ≤ $2.2\times10^{-13}$ rad |
TUM-Fisheye, 4 lenses, 12 recordings; largest corner 58–89° by TUM’s calibration | 24 pairs, one and all corners | same fx to 0.01 px |

- Older results: published T265 results solved with equidistant hold for kb4 too.

- Code: MVIS main 644f7a2 and 197549a, not re-run on newer code.

## 2. On a lens past 90°, equidistant stalled

- Lens: the TUM-Fisheye BF2M2020S23 sees the board up to 94–97° off axis, by MVIS’s kb4 fit.

- Corners: each recording has 13–19 thousand detected corners, 11.8–18.3 thousand of them in the kb4 solve.

- Reference: TUM’s own calibrations of the same images. They are another tool’s results, not ground truth.

Recording | Largest angle (kb4) | equidistant fx − TUM | kb4 fx − TUM | Mean error, equidistant / kb4 |
1 | 94.0° | +23.88 px | +0.06 px | 1.35 / 0.16 px |
2 | 97.0° | +15.51 px | +0.31 px | 0.95 / 0.20 px |
3 | 96.1° | +22.07 px | +0.33 px | 1.48 / 0.20 px |

All corners, camera-only, MVIS main f902d39, 2026-11-11.

- Two corners per tag: with the MVIS default, the equidistant intrinsics are the same, mean error within
0.01 px. kb4 is +0.12 to +0.39 px off TUM in fx.

- Same start: both models start from fx = fy = 404.98 / 396.51 / 402.95 px, the principal point at the
image centre (639.5, 511.5) and zero distortion.

- What happens: kb4 moves from there. Equidistant does not: the solver gives up at the first step with the
error unchanged, so every intrinsic ends at its starting value. The 15–24 px fx offsets are that start.

- Where it gives up: every trial step raises the cost. On recording 1 the cost is 15,541 at the start, and
85,047 down to 42,972 for the trial steps as the damping $\lambda$ rises from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{1}$.

- The damping cap: the solver stops at MVIS’s cap, $\lambda = 10^{2}$; GTSAM’s default is $10^{5}$. We have
not tested whether a higher cap lets equidistant converge.

- kb4’s other intrinsics: cx is 0.30–0.48 px low, cy within 0.1 px and fy within 0.37 px of TUM.

- Corners past 90° are not the whole story: equidistant’s stalled fit drops only 0, 3 and 1 corners as past
90°. On recording 1, at its starting values, it puts no corner past 90°, where kb4’s fit puts its largest at
94°. It still stalls the same way.

- Cause unknown: we have not tested whether the corners near or past 90° block the first step.

- Past-90° warning: MVIS warns when corners lie at or past 90° with equidistant and suggests kb4. That fires
on recordings 2 and 3.

- No stall warning: nothing in MVIS flags the stall. On recording 1 the only signs are the solver library’s
“Levenberg-Marquardt giving up” line, an error that does not change (15541.4565 -> 15541.4565), and a mean
error about 8× kb4’s.

## 3. Earlier runs on BF2M

MVIS 197549a, 2026-11-04, not repeated on the section 2 code.

- Corners past 90°: by TUM’s calibration, 36, 37 and 45 corners lie past 90°. We counted them on the frames
of the kb4 all-corner run, which has the same corner totals as the kb4 solve in section 2.

- Same stall then: the three all-corner equidistant solves gave the same values to 4 decimals.

- One corner per tag converged: with one corner per tag, equidistant converged on the same recordings:
fx −0.00 / +0.91 / +2.72 px from TUM, kb4 −0.00 / +0.14 / +0.15.

- The stall depends on the corner set: on the other four TUM-Fisheye lenses equidistant converged with one
and with all corners (section 1).

- Kalibr did not do better: its pinhole-equi failed to converge on all 3 BF2M recordings, even seeded with
TUM’s fx, and on 1 of the 12 other recordings.

- Kalibr DS and EUCM converged: on all 3, after a patched initial guess on a second attempt.

## 4. Choosing kb4 costs nothing below 90°

- Same pixels below 90°: section 1 shows it, so nothing changes on a lens that never gets there.

- Kalibr export: a camera–IMU result with kb4 is written to Kalibr’s camchain-imucam as pinhole-equi,
with the same $k_1$–$k_4$. It is exact for rays in front of the camera.

- Camera-only: camera-only results have no Kalibr export.

- The fold is checked: a KB polynomial can turn back, so $r$ stops growing with $\theta$. MVIS reports the
fold angle of every fit and flags corners past it.

- TUM-VI folds beyond every corner: with all corners, 13 of 16 fits fold inside the image, 12 of 16 with two
corners per tag. The smallest margin is 22.2°, so no corner lies past the fold, but MVIS warns that the fold is
inside the image.

- BF2M folds inside the image too: every kb4 fit folds at 120–128°, 712–743 px from the principal point; the
image corner is 822 px away. No corner lies past the fold (the largest is at 97°), but pixels beyond that
radius have no ray, and MVIS warns about it in every run.

Conclusion:

- Same where both work: kb4 is the same model as equidistant where both work.

- kb4 keeps working past 90°: on the one past-90° lens we tested, where equidistant stalled.

- Default: fisheye and kannala_brandt mean kb4. Use equidistant only when you want that name, on a
lens whose corners stay under 90°.

## Limits

- Past-90° evidence is thin: one lens, BF2M, with 3 recordings and 36–45 corners past 90° each, plus
TUM-VI.
- TUM-VI counts are not re-checked: there, 96 corners past 90° are detected and about 40 reach the
solve; Basalt detects 2,481. These counts come from a one-off survey with our own solver.
- Reference: TUM’s calibration, not ground truth.
- Why equidistant stalls: not found. At its starting values, recording 1’s fit puts no corner past
90°.
- Another start: not tested, such as starting equidistant from TUM’s fx.
- A higher damping cap: not tested. MVIS stops at lambda 102; GTSAM’s default is
105.
- Older runs: the one-corner-per-tag runs, where equidistant converged, and the section 1 rows were
not re-run on the section 2 code.
- The fold downstream: how much the kb4 fold near the image corners matters downstream is not
tested.
- Who ran it: we ran every solve.

## Data

- Runs:

- Section 1: the T265 and TUM-VI rows from MVIS main 644f7a2, the TUM-Fisheye row from 197549a.

- Section 2: MVIS main f902d39 (2026-11-11), all corners and two corners per tag.

- Section 3: MVIS 197549a (2026-11-04).

- Section 4: the TUM-VI fold counts from MVIS b03d456, all corners.

- The equidistant past-90° warning came with commit 5d28769 (2026-11-05).

- fisheye and kannala_brandt mean kb4 since MVIS 29daf90.

- TUM-Fisheye: the 15 released MVIS calibrations (two corners per tag, MVIS 197549a; kb4 on BF2M,
equidistant on the other lenses) are on the Hub,
calibench-vi/results → runs/tum-fisheye/2026-11-04.
The section 2 runs and the one- and all-corner runs behind section 1 are diagnostic runs, not published. The
images are from the Double Sphere paper’s data (Usenko et al., 2018); please cite it.

- T265: virig-5imus-4cams (results). Please cite the VI-Rig dataset and MVIS.

- TUM-VI: TUM-VI.

# Why calibrate rolling shutter | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/why/rolling-shutter/

This page shows what rolling shutter does to a real calibration. You need no setup.
Data: our runs on the VI-Rig dataset virig-4imus-4cams.

The answer first:

- The ELP is rolling shutter: it reads its rows one after another, over about 16.6 ms.

- Calling it global costs fit: on recording 01 the median reprojection error grew by 25 % (1.04 → 1.30 px).

- td hides the error: the camera–IMU time offset td moves by about half the readout to absorb it.

- No warning: the solve still converges, and the shifted td looks like a normal time offset.

How to turn it on: Rolling-shutter calibration.

## The setup

- Readout tr: the time a camera takes to read all its rows.

- Reprojection error: the distance in pixels between a detected board corner and where the calibration
predicts it.

- Cameras: two ELP cameras, ELP left and ELP right, 640×480 at 25 Hz as recorded (about 20–22 Hz after restamping), rolling shutter.

- Solve: MVIS solves the readout with the other camera terms, in the camera-only step and again in the
camera–IMU step.

## 1. The ELP reads its rows over about 16.6 ms

- Example run, recording 01: readout 16.68 ms for ELP left and 16.73 ms for ELP right. See the
worked example.

- All 15 recordings, median: with ELP stereo and two IMUs (T8), ELP left reads 16.618 ms (sd 0.122) and ELP right
16.594 ms (sd 0.111).

- Left and right agree: within 0.05 ms.

- What it means: the top and bottom rows of one image are taken about 16.6 ms apart. If the rig moves, they
see the board from slightly different poses.

## 2. Called global, the fit gets worse and the time offset moves

We ran the same camera–IMU solve twice: once with rolling shutter, once with the ELP called global shutter.
Setup: ELP pair, T265 IMU as base IMU, Xsens as aux IMU, recording 01.

Older code
This test ran on October 2026 code, before three later changes: the ELP stamp correction (the image stamps moved
onto the camera’s own frame clock; see Recordings),
board-shape estimation and vision_pose: imu. Its absolute errors, about 1 px, are much
worse than the 0.16–0.18 px median on the ELP in the results (batch 2026-11-10a). Read the change between the two
columns, not the values.

Recording | Median reprojection, RS (px) | Median reprojection, called global (px) | ELP left td shift (ms) | Readout in the RS run (ms) |
01 | 1.043 | 1.303 | +9.5 | 16.2 |

- Fit: the median error grows by 0.26 px.

- td moves by about half the readout: a global-shutter model stamps the whole image at one time, so the
solver moves td until that time sits near the middle row.

- The IMU barely notices: the base gyro scale moved by 0.5 % or less. A wrong shutter model mainly corrupts
the camera timing.

- The real risk: the shifted td is right only for the middle row. The top and bottom rows are off by up to
half the readout, about 8 ms.

## 3. MVIS repeats the readout tighter than Kalibr

The results compare MVIS and Kalibr on all 15 recordings; see
VI-Rig: 4 IMUs + 4 cameras.

Camera-only (ELP stereo + readout, T2):

Camera | MVIS readout (ms) | Kalibr readout (ms) |
ELP left | 14.604 (sd 0.404, n = 15) | 16.354 (sd 2.00, n = 15) |
ELP right | 14.601 (sd 0.404, n = 15) | 17.369 (sd 1.42, n = 13) |

- MVIS repeats 3–5× tighter across recordings than Kalibr’s rolling-shutter model.

- One camera at a time: Kalibr’s rolling-shutter model has no ELP stereo baseline.

- Lens models differ: MVIS uses the equidistant model on the ELP, Kalibr radtan, so only the readout is
compared.

- Kalibr was not re-run after the ELP stamp correction.

- With the IMU: the MVIS readout spread drops to about 0.1 ms (section 1).

Camera–IMU, mixed rig (T265 left + ELP left + two IMUs, T7):

Camera | MVIS median reprojection (px) | Kalibr median reprojection (px) |
ELP left | 0.181 (rolling shutter) | 0.795 (taken as global shutter) |
T265 left | 0.200 | 0.367 |

- Kalibr’s camera–IMU solver is global shutter only: it takes ELP left as global, with readout fixed at 0.

- Not a clean on/off test: MVIS uses two corners per tag, non-base cameras at 4 Hz or lower and an
estimated board shape. Kalibr uses none of these.

- Part of the gap is settings: the gap on the global-shutter T265 suggests so.

Conclusion:

- Model the shutter: the ELP is rolling shutter, and calling it global makes the fit worse.

- The error goes into td: it moves by about half the readout, with no warning.

- MVIS repeats the readout: tighter than Kalibr across recordings, and tighter still with the IMU.

## Limits

- Camera-only and camera–IMU disagree: MVIS gets 14.6 ms camera-only and 16.6 ms with the IMU,
about 2 ms apart.
- Readout needs help to be seen: a high enough frame rate or IMU support. On a low-rate camera with
no IMU, the readout can follow the solver’s starting value, not the data.
- Check repeatability, not one run: calibrate several recordings and compare the readout. A value
that moves a lot between recordings is not well observed.
- A round trip cannot test it: mvis apply-calib corrects frame stamps only. It does
not unwarp image rows, so a round-trip validation says nothing about the
readout.
- Older on/off code: section 2 is one recording on October 2026 code.
- Who ran it: we ran every solve, Kalibr included.

## Data

- Recordings: virig-4imus-4cams, all 15 recordings.

- Section 1: the worked example and the
results page, batch 2026-11-10a.

- Section 2: a diagnostic on/off run on October 2026 code, before the ELP stamp correction, board-shape
estimation and vision_pose: imu.

- Section 3: the results page, batch 2026-11-10a. Kalibr was not
re-run after the ELP stamp correction.

- Citation: please cite the VI-Rig dataset and MVIS.

## Related

- Rolling-shutter calibration

- Camera model: how readout sits in the one camera factor.

- Notation

- Why calibrate t_ga: another timing error that a tool without the parameter pushes into td.

- Why calibrate the board shape

# Why calibrate cameras together | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/why/multi-camera/

This page shows what you gain from putting several cameras into one solve. You need nothing to follow along.
Data: every number comes from the VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cams dataset.

The answer first:

- Sub-mm extrinsics: solving all cameras in one graph gives camera-to-camera extrinsics that repeat to a
fraction of a millimetre over 15 recordings.

- One td per camera: each camera gets its own camera–IMU time offset td. The two camera pairs on this
rig are about 116–118 ms apart.

- Not every rig bundles: solve a global-shutter camera and an unsynchronised rolling-shutter camera one by one
in the camera-only step.

How to turn it on: Solve the cameras in pairs, then
join them in Camera–IMU calibration.

## The setup

The rig has two camera pairs:

- T265 left / right: global-shutter fisheye, 848×800, 30 Hz.

- ELP left / right: rolling shutter, 640×480, 25 Hz as recorded (about 20–22 Hz after restamping).

The lever is the translation between a camera and the IMU.

## 1. Cameras do not share a clock

Example run on recording 01: all 4 cameras and 4 IMUs in one camera–IMU
solve.

Camera | td (ms) |
T265 left (cam0) | −5.41 |
T265 right (cam1) | −7.47 |
ELP left (cam2) | −123.25 |
ELP right (cam3) | −123.30 |

- Pairs agree inside: the two offsets of each pair are close.

- Pairs disagree: the ELP pair sits about 116–118 ms behind the T265 pair.

- One shared offset fails: one td for the whole rig would be wrong by over 100 ms for one pair. Give each
camera its own td.

## 2. Extrinsics repeat to a fraction of a millimetre

Results over 15 recordings, batch 2026-11-10a (full tables).
Median and standard deviation (sd) of the camera-to-camera distance. MVIS is the results page’s “MVIS” column, not
“MVIS (K-IMU)“:

Camera pair | Run | MVIS | Kalibr | Basalt |
T265 left – T265 right | T1, camera-only | 63.667 mm (sd 0.036) | 63.468 mm (sd 0.099) | 63.555 mm (sd 0.135) |
ELP left – ELP right | T8, camera–IMU | 59.207 mm (sd 0.084) | not run | — |
T265 left – ELP left | T7, camera–IMU | 153.51 mm (sd 0.17), 14 of 15 recordings | — | — |

- T265 pair: the MVIS spread is about 3× tighter than Kalibr’s and 4× tighter than Basalt’s.

- Mixed pair: a fisheye and a rolling-shutter camera on different clocks still repeat to 0.17 mm.

- Kalibr in T7: its camera baselines there are inputs from an MVIS export, so we do not compare them.

## 3. A wide camera can help a narrow one

What we expect, not measured here:

- Narrow view: the ELP sees about 92° across. A board seen by the ELP alone constrains its lever weakly along
some axes.

- Wide view: the T265 fisheyes see the board over a much wider range of angles. In one graph their poses pin
the rig, which should help the ELP. We have not measured the ELP lever with and without the T265.

- Time offsets across lenses: with estimate.camera.td: true (older configs: optimize_time_offset), MVIS estimates the camera-to-camera offsets
two ways, from PnP board poses and from homography cross-correlation. See
What the pipeline does.

## 4. When not to bundle

Joint is not always better:

-
Hybrid rigs: we tested a global-shutter camera plus an unsynchronised rolling-shutter camera, T265 left + ELP left.
On recordings 03–05 a joint camera-only bundle gave:

- 2.4–2.5 px rms reprojection

- readout scatter of 15–19 ms

- lever z shifts of 5 mm

One mono solve per camera gave 0.43 px and 0.1 ms readout scatter.

-
What we do: solve each such camera on its own in the camera-only step, then join them in the camera–IMU
solve, which gives the extrinsics and each camera’s td.

-
Synced pairs are fine: hardware-synced, same-shutter pairs such as ELP left + right work as a joint camera-only
solve.

-
A bad camera can pull a solve: in an older test, adding ELP left as a global-shutter camera to a Kalibr T265
run pulled the T265 gyro scale up about 3 % on two axes. We later traced the cause to the ELP frame stamps,
which the published bags now correct (see Recordings).
Check each camera’s residuals before you trust a joint result.

Conclusion:

- Own offset: give each camera its own td.

- Bundle what shares a clock and a shutter: solve hybrid cameras one by one in the camera-only step and join
them in the camera–IMU solve.

- Check residuals: one bad camera can pull the joint result.

## Limits

- One rig: every number is from our own runs on one rig, VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cams.
- Time offsets from one recording: the per-camera offsets in section 1 come from the example run on
recording 01.
- Mixed pair: the T265 left – ELP left row covers 14 of 15 recordings.
- Kalibr and Basalt coverage: Kalibr was not run on the ELP pair, and in T7 its camera baselines are
inputs from an MVIS export.
- Hybrid test: the joint against mono comparison used recordings 03–05 only.
- Who ran it: we ran every solve, Kalibr and Basalt included.

## Data

- Dataset: VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cams, our own recordings on the Hub,
calibench-vi/datasets.

- Section 1: the example run on recording 01.

- Section 2: results batch 2026-11-10a, in the full tables.

- Section 3: no measurement; an expectation.

- Section 4: our own diagnostic runs, October 2026, on older MVIS code.

- Citation: please cite the VI-Rig dataset and MVIS.

## Related

- Why calibrate rolling shutter

- Why calibrate IMUs together

- VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 4 cams results

- Camera-only calibration

- Camera–IMU calibration
