td ms | −20.909 |
Reprojection px | 0.562 |
Readout ms | +31.24 |
IMU |
t_ga ms | −0.36 ± 0.07 |

## Limits

- The tab with both lenses is put together from two solves, not one joint solve: each lens is placed in the IMU frame by its own recording. Its IMU values and its calibration-process view are those of the front-lens recording.
- The distance between the lenses, 36.2 mm here, comes from two camera-to-IMU results, not from one joint solve. It agrees with a direct estimate from the camera-pair recording without the IMU (36–37 mm) and with four 60 s windows (34.6–38.0 mm). The organisers' Kalibr chain gives 40.1 mm. Using the whole recordings, including the first 100–130 s where the camera turns about one axis only, gives about 34 mm; that difference isn't fully explained.
- The 7×12 calibration board isn't flat: it bows about 12 mm across its 2.2 m width, the same in both recordings. Treating it as flat moves each lens by up to 10 mm, so the board shape is estimated here; see Board shape.
- The organisers publish a Kalibr calibration (EUCM model, IMU intrinsics fixed). It isn't an independent reference: it comes from the same recordings.
- The board reaches about 95° from the lens axis, so the outermost part of each 200° image is extrapolated.
- The images are JPEG-compressed, which can shift detected corners slightly.

## How it was run

- Each lens alone with the IMU, then both placed in the one IMU frame. Only the well-excited part of each recording is used: the camera turns about all three axes from 130 s (front) and 100 s (back), and the last 10 s, where it is put down, are left out; 92 s and 97 s. Camera intrinsics (enhanced unified model, EUCM, as in the organisers' calibration) start from a single-camera solve and stay free; the shape of the 7×12 board, rolling-shutter readout, camera time offset, IMU scale and misalignment and the gyro-to-accel offset t_ga are estimated. IMU noise measured on the camera-pair recording, where the camera stands still, and widened about 2.8×. Solved 2026-11-12.


---

# Datasets | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/datasets/

This page lists every dataset we use to test and benchmark MVIS, where to get it, and its licence.

- Where the data lives: the calibench-vi/datasets
repository on Hugging Face. Calibench-VI is our visual-inertial calibration benchmark.

- What it hosts: our own VI-Rig recordings, recordings from two partners, and third-party sets whose licence
allows us to share them again (CC BY 4.0). Our calibration results are in a separate repository,
calibench-vi/results, under CC BY 4.0.

- What it does not host: all other third-party sets. For those, a download recipe fetches the files from the
original site.

- Results: the reference results for each set are on the Leaderboard and in
calibench-vi/results.

## VI-Rig: our own recordings

We built the VI-Rig to research calibration of rigs with several cameras and several IMUs. An IMU (inertial
measurement unit) is a gyroscope plus an accelerometer. Each dataset below is one sensor setup on the same frame,
recorded as ROS1 bags (one bag per recording) while we move the rig in front of a calibration board.

Dataset | Cameras | IMUs | Board | Recordings | Size | Results |
4 IMUs + 3 cameras | Blackfly + T265 pair, all global shutter | 4, 100–500 Hz | AprilGrid | 10, 131–161 s | 76 GB | results · example |
4 IMUs + 3 cameras, ArUco | same 3 cameras | 4 IMUs (3 in recordings 11–17) | ArUco tags | 17, 102–139 s | 117 GB | not benchmarked |
4 IMUs + 4 cameras | T265 pair (global) + ELP stereo (rolling) | 4, 100–500 Hz | AprilGrid | 15, 131–152 s | 113 GB | results · example |
5 IMUs + 4 cameras | two T265 pairs, all global shutter | 5, 100–500 Hz | AprilGrid | 7, 41–64 s | 28 GB | results · example |

Terms used in the table:

- Global shutter: the camera exposes every row of the image at the same time.

- Rolling shutter: the camera reads the image out row by row, so each row has its own capture time.

- AprilGrid: a printed grid of AprilTags, square codes that the software finds and identifies in each image.

- ArUco: another family of square marker tags.

### Licence and access

- Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included. Use, share and adapt
the recordings for any purpose, with attribution.

- Gated: log in to Hugging Face and accept the terms on the
dataset page. Access is granted at once. The gate adds
no restriction.

- Since 2026-11-25: from 2026-09-11 until then these recordings were CC BY-NC 4.0. A copy downloaded in that time
may now be used under CC BY 4.0 as well.

### Download

Accept the terms on the Hub first, then set HF_TOKEN to a read token from your Hugging Face settings (or log in once with hf auth login, after pip install huggingface_hub).

mvis datasets list # every dataset key, recording and size

mvis datasets download --select mvis_4imus_3cams/april_01 # one recording, 6.9 GB

- Where files land: in $MVIS_DATASETS (default ~/Datasets). The example configs refer to the data as
${MVIS_DATASETS}/....

- Checks: mvis datasets checks each file’s size and SHA-256 checksum.

- Without MVIS: use the Hugging Face CLI; each dataset page gives the exact command.

## Partner recordings on the Hub

Two partners agreed to share their recordings under the same terms as the VI-Rig sets (CC BY 4.0, commercial
use included, gated; CC BY-NC 4.0 from 2026-11-03 to 2026-11-25). Please acknowledge Looper Robotics and GiLabs when
you use them.

Dataset | Rig | Recordings | Hub folder | On this site |
Looper Robotics Insight 9 | 2 global-shutter mono cameras + 1 rolling-shutter colour camera + 400 Hz IMU | 10 ROS1 bags, AprilGrid | looper-insight9 | device · results · example |
GiLabs examples | GI Ego1 and GI EGO1GS head-worn cameras: 2 cameras + IMU | 3 MCAP recordings, not in the benchmark | gilabs-examples | GI Ego1 · GI EGO1GS |

## Third-party datasets

These sets come from other groups. Each keeps its own licence and citation; please cite the original authors.

- Hosted: the calibration recordings of sets under CC BY 4.0, converted to ROS1 bags. A .provenance.json
beside each bag records the source address, the source checksum and the conversion steps.

- Recipe: we never copy these files. The Hub’s
recipes/download.py fetches them
from the original site and checks them.

- Key: mvis datasets download --dataset <key> also fetches from the original site and checks each file. For
the hosted sets it gets the original archives; mvis datasets convert then turns them into ROS1 bags. Urban
fisheye and part of PennCOSYVIO have no checksum in the catalog; add --allow-unverified to fetch them
unchecked.

Dataset | Rig | Licence | How to get it | Original source | On this site |

TUM-VIE, frame cameras | stereo 1024² + BMI160 IMU | CC BY 4.0 | hosted: converted/tum_event · key tum_event | TUM | – |
UZH-FPV | DAVIS346 + IMU; Snapdragon stereo + IMU | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | keys uzh_fpv_davis, uzh_fpv_snapdragon | UZH | results · example |

# VI-Rig: 4 IMUs + 3 cameras | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/datasets/virig-4imus-3cams/

Three global-shutter cameras and four IMUs on one frame, recorded in front of an AprilGrid. The
Quickstart uses this set.

- Hub folder: calibench-vi/datasets → virig-4imus-3cams

- Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included; gated. See
Licence and access.

- Results: results page ·
worked example

## The rig

Rates are measured from the bags. Shutter: every camera here is global shutter.

Sensor | Type | Rate | Image size | ROS topic |
FLIR Blackfly S BFS-U3-16S2M | camera, standard lens | 30 Hz | 720×540 (2×2 binned) | /blackfly/image_raw |
RealSense T265, left | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265/fisheye1/image_raw |
RealSense T265, right | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265/fisheye2/image_raw |
Xsens MTi-100 | IMU | 400 Hz | – | /imu/data |
MicroStrain 3DM-GX3-25 | IMU | 500 Hz | – | /gx3_25/data |
MicroStrain 3DM-GX3-35 | IMU | 100 Hz | – | /gx3_35/imu/data |
RealSense T265 IMU (BMI055) | IMU | 200 Hz | – | /t265/imu |

- Board: AprilGrid, 6×6 tags of family t36h11, tag size 88 mm, spacing 0.3 of the tag size. The target file
april.yaml
is in the folder.

- Board shape: the printed board is not flat (about 2.4 mm rms). Our runs estimate its shape; see
Why calibrate the board shape.

- Drivers: we recorded with these ROS drivers.

- More on the T265: device page.

## Recordings

- Count: 10 ROS1 bags, virig_4imus_3cams_april_01.bag to virig_4imus_3cams_april_10.bag.

- Length: 131 to 161 s each, 24 minutes in total.

- Size: 6.9 to 8.5 GB each, 76 GB in total.

### Time-offset sweep

The folder also holds tga-sweep/:
11 versions of recording 01, cut to a shorter window, with the T265 accelerometer delayed by a known amount (−50 to +50 ms). They test whether
a tool can find the delay between gyroscope and accelerometer ($t_{ga}$). Each copy is 3.3 GB. A README, the MVIS
calibration used for the correction and a provenance.json are beside them. See
Why calibrate t_ga.

## Download

Accept the terms on the Hub page and set
HF_TOKEN to a read token from your Hugging Face settings (or run hf auth login once,
after pip install huggingface_hub). Then either:

# with MVIS: checks size and SHA-256, saves to $MVIS_DATASETS/mvis_4imus_3cams/

mvis datasets list --dataset mvis_4imus_3cams

mvis datasets download --select mvis_4imus_3cams/april_01 # one recording, 6.9 GB

mvis datasets download --dataset mvis_4imus_3cams # all 10, 76 GB

# with the Hugging Face CLI: the 10 recordings and the board file, without the sweep

hf download calibench-vi/datasets --repo-type dataset \

--include " virig-4imus-3cams/virig_*.bag " " virig-4imus-3cams/april.yaml " \

--local-dir ./calibench

## Results

We ran MVIS and Kalibr on every recording, and Basalt on the camera-only runs (batch 2026-11-10a). The
results page shows every value and its spread.

Run | Recordings solved |
Camera only. Kalibr: the 3 cameras together. MVIS and Basalt: the Blackfly alone and the T265 pair, so no baseline to the Blackfly | MVIS 10 of 10 · Kalibr 10 of 10 · Basalt 10 of 10 |
Camera + IMU, 3 cameras + 4 IMUs | MVIS 10 of 10 · Kalibr 10 of 10 · Basalt not run (one IMU per run) |

A few MVIS values from the camera + IMU runs. Each is the median over the 10 recordings, ± the standard deviation
between recordings. This shows how well MVIS repeats, not that it is right.

- Blackfly focal length $f_x$: 448.30 ± 0.61 px

- Lever arm of the GX3-25 from the Xsens: 131.31 ± 0.20 mm

- Time offset of the T265 IMU to the Xsens: 2.83 ± 0.21 ms

- Reprojection error, median: 0.35 px (Blackfly), 0.23 and 0.24 px (T265 pair)

The worked example shows one full run with its config.

### Sensor order in the results files

The reference results in calibench-vi/results (CC BY 4.0) hold one
file per tool, batch and run (for example MVIS/2026-11-10a/T6.json) and the configs behind them in configs/T6/
(camera + IMU) and configs/T6c/ (camera only). Kalibr and MVIS name the sensors in the same order. The base IMU is
the one the other sensors are referred to.

Sensor | Blackfly | T265 left | T265 right | Xsens MTi-100 | GX3-25 | GX3-35 | T265 IMU |
Kalibr | cam0 | cam1 | cam2 | imu0 | imu1 | imu2 | imu3 |
MVIS | cam0 | cam1 | cam2 | base IMU | aux IMU 1 | aux IMU 2 | aux IMU 3 |

## Run it yourself

- Start here: the worked example has the camera + IMU config we ran.

- Steps: a camera-only run first (mvis cam -c <config>), then camera + IMU (mvis cam-imu -c <config>). See
Camera-only calibration and
Camera–IMU calibration.

## Cite

Please cite Calibench-VI and the MVIS paper. The BibTeX is on the overview page.

# VI-Rig: 4 IMUs + 3 cameras, ArUco tags | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/datasets/virig-4imus-3cams-aruco/

The same rig as 4 IMUs + 3 cameras, recorded in front of printed ArUco tags
instead of one AprilGrid. ArUco tags are square marker codes, like AprilTags, from another family. The tags are
printed on several boards set at different angles, so their corners spread in 3D rather than lying on one plane.

- Hub folder: calibench-vi/datasets → virig-4imus-3cams-aruco

- Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included; gated. See
Licence and access.

- Results: none published. This set is not part of the benchmark.

## What it is for

- Feature mode: the tag corners serve as image features whose 3D positions are not given. The calibration
estimates those positions together with the sensor parameters, as a visual-inertial system does in the field.
No board layout is used.

- In MVIS: the MVIS dataset catalog lists this set for camera + IMU calibration in feature mode only.
mvis cam-imu 0.1.0 has no feature mode. One-off study scripts in examples/experiments/ of the
repository used it (run_board_vs_feature.py,
run_feature_ablation_aruco.py); they are kept to reproduce those studies and are not supported.

## The rig

The cameras are the same as in 4 IMUs + 3 cameras: a FLIR Blackfly and a
RealSense T265 fisheye pair, all global shutter, at 30 Hz. The IMUs differ between two groups of recordings (rates
measured from the bags):

Recordings | IMUs and topics |
01–10 | all four: Xsens MTi-100 400 Hz /imu/data, GX3-25 500 Hz /gx3_25/data, GX3-35 100 Hz /gx3_35/imu/data, T265 IMU 200 Hz /t265/imu |
11–17 | three: Xsens MTi-100 400 Hz /imu/data, GX3-25 500 Hz /gx3_25/data, and the T265 gyroscope (200 Hz, /t265/gyro/sample) and accelerometer (about 63 Hz, /t265/accel/sample) on separate topics. No GX3-35. |

## Recordings

- Count: 17 ROS1 bags, virig_4imus_3cams_aurco_01.bag to virig_4imus_3cams_aurco_17.bag. The file names
spell “aurco”; we kept them as recorded.

- Length: 102 to 139 s each, 37 minutes in total.

- Size: 5.4 to 7.3 GB each, 117 GB in total.

## Download

Accept the terms on the Hub page and set
HF_TOKEN to a read token from your Hugging Face settings (or run hf auth login once,
after pip install huggingface_hub). Then either:

# with MVIS: checks size and SHA-256, saves to $MVIS_DATASETS/mvis_4imus_3cams/data_arucotags/

mvis datasets list --dataset mvis_4imus_3cams_aruco

mvis datasets download --select mvis_4imus_3cams_aruco/aruco_01 # one recording, 6.6 GB

mvis datasets download --dataset mvis_4imus_3cams_aruco # all 17, 117 GB

# with the Hugging Face CLI

hf download calibench-vi/datasets --repo-type dataset \

--include " virig-4imus-3cams-aruco/* " --local-dir ./calibench

## Cite

Please cite Calibench-VI and the MVIS paper. The BibTeX is on the overview page.

# VI-Rig: 4 IMUs + 4 cameras | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/datasets/virig-4imus-4cams/

Two global-shutter and two rolling-shutter cameras with four IMUs on one frame, recorded in front of an AprilGrid.
The guides use this set as their running example, because it has every hard case in one rig: fisheye lenses,
rolling shutter, several cameras and several IMUs.

- Hub folder: calibench-vi/datasets → virig-4imus-4cams

- Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included; gated. See
Licence and access.

- Results: results page ·
worked example

## The rig

The same frame as in 4 IMUs + 3 cameras, with an ELP stereo module in place of the
Blackfly. Rates are measured from the bags.

Sensor | Type | Shutter | Rate | Image size | ROS topic |
RealSense T265, left | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | global | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265/fisheye1/image_raw |
RealSense T265, right | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | global | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265/fisheye2/image_raw |
ELP stereo, left | camera, standard lens | rolling | 25 Hz as recorded, about 20–22 Hz after restamping | 640×480 | /elp/split_sync_image_node/left/image_raw |
ELP stereo, right | camera, standard lens | rolling | 25 Hz as recorded, about 20–22 Hz after restamping | 640×480 | /elp/split_sync_image_node/right/image_raw |
Xsens MTi-100 | IMU | – | 400 Hz | – | /imu/data |
MicroStrain 3DM-GX3-25 | IMU | – | 500 Hz | – | /gx3_25/data |
MicroStrain 3DM-GX3-35 | IMU | – | 100 Hz | – | /gx3_35/imu/data |
RealSense T265 IMU (BMI055) | IMU | – | 200 Hz | – | /t265/imu |

- Board: AprilGrid, 6×6 tags of family t36h11, tag size 88 mm, spacing 0.3 of the tag size. The target file
april.yaml
is in the folder.

- Board shape: the printed board is not flat (about 2.4 mm rms). Our runs estimate its shape; see
Why calibrate the board shape.

- More on the T265: device page.

## Recordings

- Count: 15 ROS1 bags, 4imus_4cams_01.bag to 4imus_4cams_15.bag.

- Length: 131 to 152 s each, 35 minutes in total.

- Size: 7.1 to 8.3 GB each, 113 GB in total.

The ELP stamps in the bags as recorded are the times the computer received each frame, not when the camera took
it. Both ELP cameras run on one shared frame clock (about 29.6 Hz), and the driver delivers about 25 of those frames
per second. So each recording comes in two versions:

- 4imus_4cams_NN.bag (restamped, for board calibration): each ELP frame is moved onto the camera’s own frame
clock, the same for both ELP cameras. The fit uses the board detections, so the tool removes the frames it
cannot place: fit outliers, frames with no board detection and frames outside the solved window. About 20 to 22 frames
per second are left. A .sensor_clock_provenance.yaml beside each bag records the fit and the frames removed.
Our benchmark runs use these bags.

- 4imus_4cams_NN_raw.bag (as recorded): every frame, with the original ELP stamps. Use it for anything other
than board calibration.

## Download

Accept the terms on the Hub page and set
HF_TOKEN to a read token from your Hugging Face settings (or run hf auth login once,
after pip install huggingface_hub). Then either:

# with MVIS: checks size and SHA-256, saves to $MVIS_DATASETS/mvis_4imus_4cams/

mvis datasets list --dataset mvis_4imus_4cams

mvis datasets download --select mvis_4imus_4cams/bag_01 # one recording, 8.1 GB

mvis datasets download --dataset mvis_4imus_4cams # all 15, 113 GB

# with the Hugging Face CLI: the 15 restamped recordings, their provenance files and the board file

hf download calibench-vi/datasets --repo-type dataset \

--include " virig-4imus-4cams/4imus_4cams_??.bag* " " virig-4imus-4cams/april.yaml " \

--local-dir ./calibench

mvis datasets fetches the restamped bags only. Add "virig-4imus-4cams/*_raw.bag" to the hf command for the
raw ones.

## Results

We ran MVIS and Kalibr on every recording, and Basalt on the camera-only runs (batch 2026-11-10a). The
results page shows every value and its spread.

Run | Recordings solved |
Camera only, T265 pair | MVIS 15 of 15 · Kalibr 15 of 15 · Basalt 15 of 15 |
Camera only, ELP pair with readout time | MVIS 15 of 15 · Kalibr 15 of 15 on ELP left, 13 of 15 on ELP right, one camera at a time · Basalt 15 of 15 as global shutter, no readout time (shown only) |
Camera + IMU, T265 left + ELP left, T265 IMU + Xsens | MVIS 15 of 15 · Kalibr 14 of 15 · Basalt not run (one IMU per run, no rolling-shutter model) |
Camera + IMU, ELP pair, T265 IMU + Xsens | MVIS 15 of 15 · Kalibr 3 of 15, from earlier runs · Basalt not run (no rolling-shutter model) |

A few MVIS values. Each is the median over the 15 recordings, ± the standard deviation between recordings. This
shows how well MVIS repeats, not that it is right.

- T265 stereo baseline (camera only): 63.667 ± 0.036 mm

- ELP stereo baseline (camera + IMU, ELP pair): 59.21 ± 0.08 mm

- ELP readout time (camera + IMU, ELP pair): 16.6 ± 0.1 ms. The readout time is how long the camera takes to
read the image from the first row to the last. The camera-only runs give 14.6 ± 0.4 ms; the
results page shows both.

- Reprojection error, median (camera + IMU, ELP pair): 0.16 px (left), 0.18 px (right)

The worked example shows one full run with its config.

How we ran Kalibr on the rolling-shutter ELP cameras (stock Kalibr, Docker image kalibr:noetic):

- Camera only: kalibr_calibrate_rs_cameras, one ELP camera at a time, so it gives no ELP stereo baseline.
These runs predate the ELP restamping.

- Camera + IMU: Kalibr’s camera + IMU solver is global-shutter only, so its runs treat ELP left as a
global-shutter camera with readout time 0.

See Methodology for how the tools are compared.

### Sensor order in the results files

The reference results in calibench-vi/results (CC BY 4.0) hold one
file per tool, batch and run (for example MVIS/2026-11-10a/T8.json) and the configs behind them in
configs/<run>/. Each run names its own sensors; Kalibr and MVIS use the same order. The base IMU is the one the
other sensors are referred to. The GX3-25 and GX3-35 are in the bags but in none of these runs.

Run (folder) | Cameras | IMUs |
Camera only, T265 pair (T1) | cam0 T265 left, cam1 T265 right | – |
Camera only, ELP pair (T2) | MVIS: cam0 ELP left, cam1 ELP right. Kalibr: one ELP camera per run | – |
Camera + IMU, T265 left + ELP left (T7) | cam0 T265 left, cam1 ELP left | imu0 / base: T265 IMU, imu1 / aux: Xsens MTi-100 |
Camera + IMU, ELP pair (T8) | MVIS: cam0 ELP left, cam1 ELP right. Kalibr (earlier runs of recordings 1–3): cam0 T265 left | imu0 / base: T265 IMU, imu1 / aux: Xsens MTi-100 |

## Run it yourself

- Start here: the worked example has the camera + IMU config we ran.

- Step by step: the guides walk through this set, from
Camera-only calibration and Rolling shutter to
Camera–IMU calibration and Multi-IMU calibration.

- Why it matters: rolling shutter, several cameras and
several IMUs are each shown on this set.

## Cite

Please cite Calibench-VI and the MVIS paper. The BibTeX is on the overview page.

# VI-Rig: 5 IMUs + 4 cameras | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/datasets/virig-5imus-4cams/

Two RealSense T265 units and five IMUs on one frame, recorded in front of an AprilGrid. The two units are not
synced to each other, so the only link between their clocks is the motion that every sensor sees. This makes it
a test of time offsets across many sensors.

- Hub folder: calibench-vi/datasets → virig-5imus-4cams

- Licence: CC BY 4.0, commercial use included; gated. See
Licence and access.

- Results: results page ·
worked example

## The rig

Rates are measured from the bags. Every camera is a global-shutter fisheye.

Sensor | Type | Rate | Image size | ROS topic |
T265 unit A, left | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265_01/fisheye1/image_raw |
T265 unit A, right | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265_01/fisheye2/image_raw |
T265 unit B, left | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265_03/fisheye1/image_raw |
T265 unit B, right | camera, fisheye (about 163°) | 30 Hz | 848×800 | /t265_03/fisheye2/image_raw |
Xsens MTi | IMU | 400 Hz | – | /mti/sensor/imu_raw |
MicroStrain 3DM-GX3-25 | IMU | 500 Hz | – | /gx3_25/data |
MicroStrain 3DM-GX3-35 | IMU | 100 Hz | – | /gx3_35/imu/data |
T265 unit A IMU (BMI055) | IMU | 200 Hz | – | /t265_01/imu |
T265 unit B IMU (BMI055) | IMU | 200 Hz | – | /t265_03/imu |

- Sync: the two cameras inside one T265 are hardware-synced. The two units are not synced to each other.

- Board: the same AprilGrid as the other VI-Rig sets (6×6 tags of family t36h11, tag size 88 mm). The target
file april.yaml
is in the folder.

- Board shape: the printed board is not flat. Our camera + IMU runs estimate its shape; see
Why calibrate the board shape.

- More on the T265: device page.

## Recordings

- Count: 7 ROS1 bags, 5imus_4cams_01.bag to 5imus_4cams_07.bag.

- Length: 41 to 64 s each, about 6 minutes in total.

- Size: 3.3 to 5.2 GB each, 28 GB in total.

## Download

Accept the terms on the Hub page and set
HF_TOKEN to a read token from your Hugging Face settings (or run hf auth login once,
after pip install huggingface_hub). Then either:

# with MVIS: checks size and SHA-256, saves to $MVIS_DATASETS/vi_sensor_rigs_5imus/

mvis datasets list --dataset vi_sensor_rigs_5imus

mvis datasets download --select vi_sensor_rigs_5imus/bag_01 # one recording, 5.2 GB

mvis datasets download --dataset vi_sensor_rigs_5imus # all 7, 28 GB

# with the Hugging Face CLI: recordings, board file and our results

hf download calibench-vi/datasets --repo-type dataset \

--include " virig-5imus-4cams/* " --local-dir ./calibench

## Results

This set has a separate study (2026-11-02), outside the leaderboard batch. We ran MVIS only; Kalibr and Basalt
were not run on it, so nothing is compared.

Run | Recordings solved |
Camera only, one T265 pair per run | MVIS 7 of 7 (each pair) |
Camera + IMU, 4 cameras + 5 IMUs in one run | MVIS 7 of 7 |

- How we ran it: each camera-only run holds one T265 pair, with no time offset, because the two units share
no clock. The camera + IMU runs hold all four cameras and all five IMUs, with the Xsens as base IMU. Their
camera intrinsics start from the median of the 7 camera-only runs.

- Results files on the Hub: the folder
calibench-vi/results → runs/virig-5imus-4cams/2026-11-02/
holds the run configs, the camera-only calibrations, the camera intrinsics prior and, per recording, the camera +
IMU result (cam_imu.json, the calibration YAML, a Kalibr-style camchain and the estimated board shape). It has
numbers only, no images, under CC BY 4.0.

A few MVIS values from the camera + IMU runs. Each is the median over the 7 recordings, ± the standard deviation
between recordings. This shows how well MVIS repeats, not that it is right.

- Gyro-to-accelerometer delay $t_{ga}$ of the T265 IMUs: −6.59 ± 0.08 ms (unit A), −6.65 ± 0.10 ms (unit B).
The other three IMUs stay within 0.6 ms of zero. The T265 delay depends on how fast the rig moves, so read it as
a compromise value; see Why calibrate t_ga.

- T265 unit A stereo baseline: 63.66 ± 0.12 mm

- Reprojection error, median: 0.21 to 0.23 px over the four cameras

- Start here: the worked example has the camera + IMU config we ran.

Camera–IMU calibration.

# Notation & glossary | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/notation/

Use this page to look up a symbol, a frame or a sign convention.
Every equation on this site uses the symbols below.

The frame and transform conventions follow OpenVINS.
Result files use their own XtoY names (below).

## Frames

A frame is a coordinate system attached to the world, a sensor or the board.
We write it in braces, e.g. $\{I\}$.

Symbol | Frame | Notes |
$\{G\}$ | global | gravity-aligned; yaw and position are unobservable |
$\{I\}$ | base IMU | the reference clock and the trajectory’s body frame |
$\{w\}$, $\{a\}$ | gyroscope triad, accelerometer triad | inside one IMU; which one $\{I\}$ coincides with depends on the IMU convention |
$\{I_{s_j}\}$ | auxiliary IMU $j$ | rigidly attached to $\{I\}$ |
$\{C_i\}$ | camera $i$ | optical frame: $x$ right, $y$ down, $z$ forward |
$\{B\}$ | calibration board | fixed in $\{G\}$ |

## Transforms

A rotation is written ${}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R}$.
It takes a vector expressed in $\{B\}$ into $\{A\}$.
A translation ${}^{A}\mathbf{p}_{B}$ is the origin of $\{B\}$ expressed in $\{A\}$.
Together they form the transform ${}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{T}$:

${}^{A}\mathbf{p} = {}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R}\, {}^{B}\mathbf{p} + {}^{A}\mathbf{p}_{B}$
Result files and code use a different spelling
Code and result files name a transform T_XtoY: it takes points from $\{X\}$ into $\{Y\}$.
So T_CtoI is ${}^{I}_{C}\mathbf{T}$, R_wtoI is ${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}$, R_atoI is ${}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}$
and T_IstoI is ${}^{I}_{I_{s}}\mathbf{T}$.
A position is p_XinY, the origin of $\{X\}$ in $\{Y\}$: p_CinI_mm is ${}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{C}$ and p_IsinI_m is ${}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{I_{s}}$.
W in a name is the global frame $\{G\}$ (gravity-aligned, $z$ up), as in T_BinW.
One exception: T_cam_imu in the camera–IMU YAML and the Kalibr export keeps Kalibr’s direction.
It maps base-IMU points into the camera, ${}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{T}$, the inverse of T_CtoI.
See Result formats.

## Rotations as vectors

We report a rotation as its rotation vector $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathrm{Log}(\mathbf{R}) \in \mathbb{R}^3$, in rad.
Its direction is the rotation axis and its norm is the angle.
We never report roll, pitch and yaw angles.

Symbol | Meaning |
$\boldsymbol{\theta}^\wedge$ | the $3\times3$ skew-symmetric matrix of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, so $\boldsymbol{\theta}^\wedge \mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{v}$ |
$\mathrm{Exp}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ | rotation vector to rotation matrix: $\mathbf{I} + \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\boldsymbol{\theta}^\wedge + \frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta^2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^\wedge)^2$, with $\theta = \lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\rVert$ |
$\mathrm{Log}(\mathbf{R})$ | the inverse of $\mathrm{Exp}$; the rotvec fields of a result |

## Calibration state

The calibration state is the set of quantities we estimate.
Intrinsics describe a sensor itself; extrinsics give its pose in the base-IMU frame $\{I\}$.
The Per column says whether a quantity exists once per camera, per rolling-shutter (RS) camera, per IMU or per auxiliary IMU.

Symbol | Quantity | Dimension | Per |
$\mathbf{f}_i = [f_u\ f_v\ c_u\ c_v]$ | camera intrinsics (focal lengths, principal point; fx fy cx cy in files) | 4 | camera |
$\mathbf{d}_i$ | distortion coefficients | 1 to 5, by camera model | camera |
${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{T}$ | camera extrinsics | 6 | camera |
$t_{d,i}$ | camera–IMU time offset | 1 | camera |
$t_{r,i}$ | rolling-shutter readout | 1 | RS camera |
$\mathbf{D}_w$ | gyroscope correction: scale and misalignment | 6, or 9 in calyx | IMU |
$\mathbf{D}_a$ | accelerometer correction: scale and misalignment | 6 | IMU |
${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}$ or ${}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}$ | rotation between the gyro and accel triads | 3 (kalibr, rpng) | IMU |
$\mathbf{T}_g$ | g-sensitivity: how specific force leaks into the gyro | 9 | IMU |
$t_{ga}$ | gyro–accel time offset inside one IMU | 1 | IMU |
${}^{I}_{I_{s_j}}\mathbf{T}$ | auxiliary IMU extrinsics | 6 | aux IMU |
$t_{d,j}$ | IMU–IMU time offset | 1 | aux IMU |
$\mathbf{b}_g,\ \mathbf{b}_a$ | gyro / accel biases | 3 each | IMU |
${}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k}$ | velocity of $\{I\}$ in $\{G\}$ at state $k$ (part of the trajectory, not a calibration value) | 3 | IMU state |
$\mathbf{x}_{in}$ | one IMU’s intrinsics stacked into one solver variable ($\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$, $\mathbf{T}_g$, triad rotation) | 24 | IMU |
$h_m$ | height of board corner $m$ along the board normal | 1 | board corner, with board_points on |

$\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$ and $\mathbf{T}_g$ are correction matrices: they map a raw reading to the true value.
IMU model gives the equations.

The full state $\mathbf{x}$ stacks the trajectory with all of the above.
The cost that acts on it is in Camera–IMU calibration math.

Indices: $i$ camera, $j$ auxiliary IMU, $k$ IMU state (or the interval from
state $k$ to $k+1$), $f$ frame, $m$ board corner.

## Measurements

What the sensors report, and the terms we build from those readings:

Symbol | Measurement |
$\boldsymbol{\omega}_m$ | measured angular velocity (raw gyro reading) |
$\mathbf{a}_m$ | measured specific force (raw accel reading) |
${}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}$ | true angular velocity of $\{I\}$, expressed in $\{I\}$ |
${}^{I}\mathbf{a}$ | true specific force in $\{I\}$: ${}^{I}\mathbf{a} = {}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R}\,({}^{G}\mathbf{a}_I - {}^{G}\mathbf{g})$ |
${}^{G}\mathbf{g}$ | gravity in $\{G\}$, $[0\ 0\ {-9.81}]^\top$ m/s² |
$\mathbf{n}_g,\ \mathbf{n}_a$ | gyro / accel white noise (densities sigma_g, sigma_a) |
$\mathbf{n}_{bg},\ \mathbf{n}_{ba}$ | bias random-walk noise (densities sigma_bg, sigma_ba) |
$\mathbf{z}_{i,m}$ | pixel observation of board corner $m$ in camera $i$ |
$\Pi(\cdot)$ | camera projection: point in $\{C_i\}$ to pixel (Camera model) |
$\mathbf{r}$ | residual (subscripted by factor type) |
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ | measurement covariance |
$\mathbf{P}_k$ | covariance of the IMU preintegration over interval $k$ (Base IMU factor) |

## Time

Every stamp is mapped onto one reference clock, the base-IMU clock.

Symbol | Meaning |
$t_I$ | timestamp on the base-IMU clock, the reference |
$t_C$ | timestamp as reported by a camera driver |
$t_d$ | offset such that $t_I = t_C + t_d$ |
$t_r$ | whole-frame readout time of a rolling-shutter camera |
$\eta(v)$ | row factor of image row $v$: the share of $t_r$ after the frame stamp (Rolling shutter) |
$t_{ga}$ | gyro–accel offset: the accel reading stamped $t$ was sampled at $t - t_{ga}$ |

A board corner seen in row $v$ of camera $i$ was captured at

$t_I = t_C + t_{d,i} + \eta(v)\, t_{r,i}$
The sign convention matters.
td is added to the sensor’s own stamp to reach base-IMU time.
A positive td means the camera stamps run early: the image was captured later than its stamp says.
mvis apply-calib re-stamps each message as stamp + td.

## Conventions worth stating once

- Quaternions: result files store rotations as matrices and log(R)
rotation vectors, not quaternions. Simulator trajectory files
(mvis.simulation) use JPL quaternions $q_{GtoI}$, as in OpenVINS. The
Basalt export uses Hamilton quaternions, as Basalt does.

- Error states (the small corrections around the current estimate) are defined:

- multiplicatively for rotations,
$\mathbf{R} \approx \hat{\mathbf{R}}\,\mathrm{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta})$;

- additively for everything else.

- Units in result files: metres, radians and seconds; summaries add _mm and
_ms copies where the name says so.

- Board points are flat and known by default (estimate.board_points: false).
Board errors then go into the calibration: a wrong tag_size gives a scale bias
on translations, and a bent board biases the focal length, gyro scale and lever
(Why calibrate the board shape). With
estimate.board_points: true, MVIS solves one height $h_m$ per corner.

## Glossary

- Factor: one term of the cost the solver minimises.

- Residual: the error a factor measures, predicted minus observed.

- Jacobian: the derivative of a residual with respect to a state variable.

- Lever arm: the translation between two sensors, e.g. ${}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{C_i}$.

- Incidence angle: the angle of a ray off the camera’s optical axis.

- Specific force: what an accelerometer measures, acceleration minus gravity.

- Pre-integration: IMU readings between two states combined into one relative motion.

- Base / auxiliary IMU: the base IMU sets the clock and the body frame; every other IMU is auxiliary.


---

# Camera model | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/camera-model/

Use this page to pick the camera model for each camera in your rig, and to see
the exact equations MVIS uses.

A camera model $\Pi$ maps a 3D point $\mathbf{P} = [X\ Y\ Z]^\top$ in the camera
frame $\{C_i\}$ to a pixel $[u\ v]^\top$: a projection plus a lens distortion.
Symbols follow Notation & glossary.

Each model lives in one class under
src/mvis/camera/.
The class holds the projection, its Jacobians (the derivatives the optimiser
uses) and the unprojection. So every model works:

- in camera-only and camera–IMU calibration;

- with a calibration board of known corner positions, and in feature mode,
where the corners’ 3D positions are not given and are solved as well
(example: VI-Rig 4 IMUs + 3 cams, ArUco);

- mixed across cameras in one rig.

## The eight models

Model | Config value | Origin | Distortion coefficients, in file order | Suits |
Pinhole + radial-tangential | radtan | Brown–Conrady | k1 k2 p1 p2 | Normal lenses |
Kannala–Brandt KB4 | kb4 (also fisheye, kannala_brandt) | Kannala–Brandt, $\theta$ from atan2 | k1 k2 k3 k4 | Fisheye, including corners past 90° |
Equidistant | equidistant | Kannala–Brandt on $X/Z, Y/Z$ | k1 k2 k3 k4 | Fisheye with every corner under 90° |
FOV | fov | Devernay–Faugeras | omega | Wide-angle, one parameter |
Double Sphere | double_sphere | Usenko et al. (Basalt) | xi alpha | Very wide field of view |
EUCM | eucm | Khomutenko et al. | alpha beta | Very wide field of view |
UCM | ucm | Unified model (Mei), $\alpha$ form | alpha | Very wide field of view; Kalibr omni / none |
Omni + radtan | omni_radtan | Mei, experimental | xi k1 k2 p1 p2 | Catadioptric, ultra-wide |

Every model shares the four intrinsics $f_u, f_v, c_u, c_v$ (fx fy cx cy).
The distortion coefficients follow them.

config.yaml
cameras :

- camera_id : 0

distortion_model : kb4

## Projection equations

Each model ends with the same affine step from a normalised point
$[m_x\ m_y]^\top$ to pixels:

$u = f_u\, m_x + c_u, \qquad v = f_v\, m_y + c_v$
What differs is how $[m_x\ m_y]$ comes from $\mathbf{P}$.
A point outside a model’s valid domain has no pixel. That corner is left out
of the error statistics and, in camera–IMU, out of the cost. Left uncounted,
it would make the error look smaller than it is. So the result counts dropped
corners:

- past_fold: a Kannala–Brandt corner past the fold;

- other_invalid: anything else, such as $Z \le 0$ under equidistant.

### radtan

Source: src/mvis/camera/pinhole_radtan.py (GTSAM Cal3DS2).

$x = \frac{X}{Z},\quad y = \frac{Y}{Z},\quad r^2 = x^2 + y^2$
$\begin{aligned}
m_x &= x\,(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) + 2 p_1 x y + p_2\,(r^2 + 2x^2) \\
m_y &= y\,(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) + p_1\,(r^2 + 2y^2) + 2 p_2 x y
\end{aligned}$
Valid: $Z > 0$.

### kb4 and equidistant

Both use the Kannala–Brandt odd polynomial in the incidence angle $\theta$
(the angle of the ray off the optical axis):

$\theta_d = \theta\,(1 + k_1\theta^2 + k_2\theta^4 + k_3\theta^6 + k_4\theta^8)$
$m_x = \frac{\theta_d}{\rho}\, X, \qquad m_y = \frac{\theta_d}{\rho}\, Y, \qquad \rho = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$
The two differ only in how they get $\theta$:

Model | $\theta$ | Valid domain |
kb4 | $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\rho, Z)$ | $0 \le \theta < \pi$ and $\theta$ below the first fold $\theta_f$ |
equidistant | $\theta = \arctan(\rho / Z)$, after dividing by $Z$ | $Z > 0$, so $\theta < 90°$ |

The first fold $\theta_f$ is the smallest $\theta > 0$ where
$\mathrm{d}\theta_d / \mathrm{d}\theta = 1 + 3k_1\theta^2 + 5k_2\theta^4 + 7k_3\theta^6 + 9k_4\theta^8 = 0$
($\pi$ when there is none). Past it, $\theta_d$ falls again and two rays share
one pixel, so the inverse is no longer unique.

- Below 90° the two models give the same pixels for the same coefficients.

- At or past 90° only kb4 has a pixel. This is why fisheye means kb4
(Why kb4 for fisheye).

- After a solve MVIS logs the fold angle and the radius in pixels where the
valid domain ends. It warns when that radius lies inside the image.

Source: src/mvis/camera/kb4.py,
src/mvis/camera/kb_domain.py,
src/mvis/camera/pinhole_equidistant.py (GTSAM Cal3Fisheye).

### fov

Source: src/mvis/camera/fov_model.py.

$x = \frac{X}{Z},\quad y = \frac{Y}{Z},\quad r_u = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2},\quad
r_d = \frac{1}{\omega}\arctan\!\Big(2\, r_u \tan\frac{\omega}{2}\Big)$
$m_x = \frac{r_d}{r_u}\, x, \qquad m_y = \frac{r_d}{r_u}\, y$
On the optical axis the scale $r_d / r_u$ is its limit $2\tan(\omega/2)/\omega$.
As $\omega \to 0$ the model becomes a plain pinhole.
Valid: $Z > 0$.

### double_sphere

Source: src/mvis/camera/double_sphere.py.

$d_1 = \lVert \mathbf{P} \rVert, \qquad
d_2 = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2 + (\xi d_1 + Z)^2}$
$w = \alpha\, d_2 + (1 - \alpha)(\xi d_1 + Z), \qquad
m_x = \frac{X}{w}, \quad m_y = \frac{Y}{w}$
Valid: $w > 0$. Expected ranges: $\xi \in [-1, 1]$, $\alpha \in [0, 1]$.

### eucm

Source: src/mvis/camera/eucm.py.

$d = \sqrt{\beta\,(X^2 + Y^2) + Z^2}, \qquad
w = \alpha\, d + (1 - \alpha) Z, \qquad
m_x = \frac{X}{w}, \quad m_y = \frac{Y}{w}$
Valid: $w > 0$. Expected ranges: $\alpha \in [0, 1]$, $\beta > 0$.

### ucm

Source: src/mvis/camera/ucm.py.
UCM is EUCM with $\beta = 1$:

$d = \lVert \mathbf{P} \rVert, \qquad
w = \alpha\, d + (1 - \alpha) Z, \qquad
m_x = \frac{X}{w}, \quad m_y = \frac{Y}{w}$
Valid: $Z > -w_f\, d$, with
$w_f = (1-\alpha)/\alpha$ for $\alpha > 0.5$, else $w_f = \alpha/(1-\alpha)$.
Past that bound the image folds back. Expected range: $\alpha \in [0, 1)$.

Kalibr’s omni camera with distortion none is the same model in $\xi$ form.
MVIS converts on import and export only:

$\xi = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{f}{1 - \alpha}$

### omni_radtan (experimental)

Source: src/mvis/camera/omni_radtan.py.
A projection onto the unit sphere with mirror parameter $\xi$, then radtan
distortion on the normalised plane:

$d = \lVert \mathbf{P} \rVert, \qquad
x = \frac{X}{Z + \xi d}, \quad y = \frac{Y}{Z + \xi d}$
then $m_x, m_y$ from $x, y$ exactly as in radtan.
Valid: $Z + \xi d > 0$. Expected range: $\xi \in [0, 5]$.
This is Kalibr’s omni / radtan.

All projection kernels outside GTSAM are in
src/mvis/calibration/factors/custom_projections.py,
with analytical Jacobians.

## Choosing one

More parameters are not better. A model richer than the lens needs fits
noise. On wide field-of-view data it can slide into a basin (a wrong local
minimum) that looks converged and is not.

Choose by the largest incidence angle of the board corners, not by the lens’s
advertised field of view. Every result reports this angle
(max_theta_deg, and max_theta_used_deg for the corners the fit kept), and
counts any corners past the model’s valid domain.

- Normal lens: radtan.

- Fisheye: kb4, which is what fisheye and kannala_brandt select. It
stays valid past 90° up to its first fold (why).

- Every corner under 90°, and you want equidistant by name: equidistant.
It gives the same pixels as kb4 there.

- Very wide field of view, a different shape: eucm, ucm or double_sphere.

- Catadioptric (lens plus mirror): omni_radtan. It is experimental.

### When a fit diverges

Wide-FoV models can diverge on stereo
In our TUM-VI runs, stereo double_sphere and eucm fits can diverge into a
basin where the focal length and $\xi$ or $\alpha$ trade off, while the
single-camera fit is stable. The working recipe has two steps:

- Fit each camera alone.

- Pin those intrinsics for the joint solve
(examples/configs/tumvi_cam_imu/).

You recognise a diverged fit by an implausible focal length or very large
distortion coefficients, not by a large residual.

Camera-only calibration runs two passes: a first solve, then a second one
after outlier rejection. A guardrail keeps the first-pass result if the
second pass lands on any of these
(src/mvis/calibration/pipeline_cam.py):

- a focal length of 1 px or less;

- $f_u$ and $f_v$ more than 30 % apart;

- a distortion coefficient above 2 in magnitude (for ucm: $\alpha$ outside
$[0, 1)$; for omni_radtan: $\xi$ outside $[0, 5]$);

- a 95th-percentile reprojection error more than 1.5 times the first pass’s,
on a camera whose $f_u$ moved less than 5 %;

- a mean RMS reprojection error over all cameras more than 1.5 times the first
pass’s.

It is a backstop, not a substitute for picking the right model.

## Kalibr export

The camchain written for Kalibr uses these names:

MVIS | Kalibr camera_model / distortion_model |
radtan | pinhole / radtan |
equidistant | pinhole / equidistant |
kb4 | pinhole / equidistant: exact for $Z > 0$; MVIS warns when the fit used corners at or past 90°, which Kalibr cannot project |
fov | pinhole / fov |
double_sphere | ds / none |
eucm | eucm / none |
ucm | omni / none, converted to $\xi$ form |
omni_radtan | omni / radtan |

## Rolling shutter

A rolling-shutter camera exposes its rows one after another, so one image
spans a range of times. The readout $t_r$ is the time from the first row to
the last.

A corner observed in row $v$ of an image of height $H$ was captured at

$t_I = t_C + t_d + \eta(v)\, t_r$
The row factor $\eta(v)$ depends on which row the driver stamps.
In a camera–IMU config, set it with camera_input.rolling_mode (default 0), or per camera with camera_input.cameras[i].rolling_mode.
A camera-only run has no such key and always uses the top row, $\eta(v) = v/H$.

rolling_mode | Frame stamp at | $\eta(v)$ |
0 | top row | $v / H$ |
1 | middle row | $v / H - 0.5$ |
2 | bottom row | $(v - H) / H$ |

Source: src/mvis/core/shutter.py.
For a global-shutter camera $t_r = 0$, so every corner of a frame shares one time.

The camera–IMU vision factor uses that per-corner time directly. It takes the
pose of $\{I\}$ at $t_I$ from the base IMU, composes the extrinsics, and then
projects:

$\mathbf{z}_{i,m} = \Pi\big({}^{C_i}\mathbf{p}_{m}(t_I)\big) + \mathbf{n}$
where ${}^{C_i}\mathbf{p}_m(t_I)$ is board corner $m$ in the camera frame at
the corner’s capture time. Projection, time offset, readout and extrinsics sit
in one factor, so $t_d$ and $t_r$ get Jacobians and are solved with everything
else, not corrected afterwards. The HTML report uses the same projection code,
so the residuals it shows are the ones the optimiser minimised.

Turn it on per camera:

config.yaml
input :

cameras :

- camera_id : 0

shutter_type : rolling

In a camera–IMU config, use camera_input.estimate_readout: true (or per camera in camera_input.cameras[i]), or estimate.camera.tr: true.
Practical guidance: Rolling shutter.


---

# IMU model | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/imu-model/

Use this page to see how MVIS models an IMU, which convention to pick, and how
to correct raw IMU readings with a calibration result.

MVIS solves the IMU intrinsics rather than taking them from a datasheet. IMU
intrinsics are the sensor’s own error terms:

- Scale and misalignment of the gyroscope and the accelerometer
($\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$)

- The rotation between the two triads (the gyro and accel axes are not
exactly parallel)

- G-sensitivity $\mathbf{T}_g$: specific force leaking into the gyro (optional)

- Biases $\mathbf{b}_g$, $\mathbf{b}_a$

- The gyro–accel time offset $t_{ga}$ inside one IMU

Symbols follow Notation & glossary. The code is in
src/mvis/imu/:
imu_model.py holds the shared equations, kalibr.py, rpng.py and
calyx.py the three layouts.

## Measurement model

$\mathbf{D}_w$ and $\mathbf{D}_a$ are correction matrices: they turn a raw
reading into a true value. The raw readings are therefore their inverses applied
to the truth. With ${}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}$ the true angular velocity and
${}^{I}\mathbf{a}$ the true specific force, both in the IMU frame $\{I\}$:

$\mathbf{a}_m(t) = \mathbf{D}_a^{-1}\, {}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}^{\top}\, {}^{I}\mathbf{a}(t - t_{ga}) + \mathbf{b}_a + \mathbf{n}_a$
$\boldsymbol{\omega}_m(t) = \mathbf{D}_w^{-1}\, {}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}^{\top}\, {}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}(t) + \mathbf{T}_g\, {}^{I}\mathbf{a}(t) + \mathbf{b}_g + \mathbf{n}_g$

- ${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}$ and ${}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}$ rotate the gyro triad
$\{w\}$ and the accel triad $\{a\}$ into $\{I\}$. kalibr and rpng each
fix one of them to the identity; calyx fixes both.

- $t_{ga}$ is the gyro–accel offset of the
accel against the gyro clock.

- $\mathbf{n}_g$, $\mathbf{n}_a$ are white noise. The biases follow a random
walk, $\dot{\mathbf{b}}_g = \mathbf{n}_{bg}$, $\dot{\mathbf{b}}_a = \mathbf{n}_{ba}$.
Their densities are the config’s sigma_g, sigma_a, sigma_bg, sigma_ba.

## Inverse model (correction)

The correction is the exact inverse. The accel comes first, because the gyro’s
g-sensitivity term needs the corrected specific force:

${}^{I}\mathbf{a}(t) = {}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}\, \mathbf{D}_a \big(\mathbf{a}_m(t + t_{ga}) - \mathbf{b}_a\big)$
${}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}(t) = {}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}\, \mathbf{D}_w \big(\boldsymbol{\omega}_m(t) - \mathbf{b}_g - \mathbf{T}_g\, {}^{I}\mathbf{a}(t)\big)$
This is the correction the IMU factor applies to every sample inside the solve
(src/mvis/calibration/factors/aci.py),
the ACI3 integration (cite ACI2).
The simulator uses the forward model above to make raw readings, so the two are
exact inverses without noise.

## Three conventions

cam_imu.yaml
estimate :

imu :

model : calyx # kalibr | rpng | calyx (default calyx)

solve.imu_intrinsics_model is the same setting under its low-level name.

The two triads and $\{I\}$ have 3 + 3 + 3 rotational degrees of freedom, but
the data only sees the rotation between the triads. So one rotation must be
pinned. What is pinned, and the shape of each matrix, is the convention:

The matrix shapes, the free rotation, the frame $\{I\}$ and the parameter count
of each convention are in one table on
Base IMU factor. Each
has 24 intrinsic parameters.

On top of those 24, every convention has the two biases (3 + 3) and $t_{ga}$ (1).

### kalibr

$\mathbf{D}_w = \begin{bmatrix} d_{w1} & 0 & 0 \\ d_{w2} & d_{w4} & 0 \\ d_{w3} & d_{w5} & d_{w6} \end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf{D}_a = \begin{bmatrix} d_{a1} & 0 & 0 \\ d_{a2} & d_{a4} & 0 \\ d_{a3} & d_{a5} & d_{a6} \end{bmatrix},
\quad
{}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$
${}^{I}\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{D}_a(\mathbf{a}_m - \mathbf{b}_a), \qquad
{}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega} = {}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{D}_w(\boldsymbol{\omega}_m - \mathbf{b}_g - \mathbf{T}_g\,{}^{I}\mathbf{a})$
This is the structure of Kalibr’s scale-misalignment IMU model. Kalibr’s
imu.yaml maps onto it as $\mathbf{D}_w = \mathbf{M}_g^{-1}$,
$\mathbf{D}_a = \mathbf{M}_a^{-1}$, ${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{C}_{gyro\_i}^{\top}$
and $\mathbf{T}_g = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{C}_{gyro\_i}$
(src/mvis/io/kalibr.py).
Pick it when you compare against Kalibr.

### rpng

$\mathbf{D}_w = \begin{bmatrix} d_{w1} & d_{w2} & d_{w4} \\ 0 & d_{w3} & d_{w5} \\ 0 & 0 & d_{w6} \end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf{D}_a = \begin{bmatrix} d_{a1} & d_{a2} & d_{a4} \\ 0 & d_{a3} & d_{a5} \\ 0 & 0 & d_{a6} \end{bmatrix},
\quad
{}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$
${}^{I}\mathbf{a} = {}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{D}_a(\mathbf{a}_m - \mathbf{b}_a), \qquad
{}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega} = \mathbf{D}_w(\boldsymbol{\omega}_m - \mathbf{b}_g - \mathbf{T}_g\,{}^{I}\mathbf{a})$
The convention of the RPNG group’s VINS work (the
OpenVINS lineage). Here $\{I\}$ is the gyro
triad, so the camera–IMU extrinsics are relative to the gyro axes.

### calyx

$\mathbf{D}_w = \begin{bmatrix} d_{w1} & d_{w2} & d_{w3} \\ d_{w4} & d_{w5} & d_{w6} \\ d_{w7} & d_{w8} & d_{w9} \end{bmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf{D}_a \text{ upper-triangular as in } \texttt{rpng},
\quad
{}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R} = {}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$
${}^{I}\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{D}_a(\mathbf{a}_m - \mathbf{b}_a), \qquad
{}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega} = \mathbf{D}_w(\boldsymbol{\omega}_m - \mathbf{b}_g - \mathbf{T}_g\,{}^{I}\mathbf{a})$
The full $\mathbf{D}_w$ is linear in its nine entries, so the solve needs no
rotation variable. After the solve, MVIS splits it into a rotation and an
upper-triangular matrix with a positive diagonal (a QR decomposition):

$\mathbf{D}_w = {}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}\; \mathbf{U}_w$
The result reports both: R_wtoI, U_w, and Dw_decomposed with the
per-axis gyro scale (Dw_scale, the diagonal of $\mathbf{U}_w$), the
cross-coupling (Dw_shear, its upper off-diagonals) and
gyro_misalign_rotvec $= \mathrm{Log}({}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R})$ in rad.
Read the scale from Dw_scale, not from Dw_diag: in calyx the diagonal of
$\mathbf{D}_w$ mixes scale with rotation.

### How they compare

- Same physics, different bookkeeping. All three describe the same
sensor. They differ in which frame $\{I\}$ is and where the triad rotation sits.

- Not a quality lever. Before the 0.1.0 release we checked this on TUM-VI
and on the Monado SLAM calibration set MIC (Valve Index, see
Datasets), with camera intrinsics pinned or freed. All three
recovered the same extrinsics and camera intrinsics. Choose the one that matches what you compare against.

- Not comparable entry by entry. A kalibr $\mathbf{D}_w$ and an rpng
$\mathbf{D}_w$ of the same IMU differ. Before concluding that two calibrations
disagree, check they used the same convention.

- Default staging differs. The default estimate.imu.intrinsics: dw_da
frees $\mathbf{D}_w$ and $\mathbf{D}_a$ only. In calyx that already
includes the triad rotation (it lives in $\mathbf{D}_w$). In kalibr and
rpng the rotation stays at the identity until you choose dw_da_r.

Which blocks each estimate.imu.intrinsics setting frees, and their priors:
Which intrinsics are solved.

## Correct readings with a result

mvis cam-imu writes a calibration YAML next to its JSON summary (for
cam_imu.json, the file is cam_imu_calib.yaml). Each entry of its imus:
list has:

Key | Meaning |
name, role, topic | IMU name, base or aux, and its topic when known |
model | kalibr, rpng or calyx |
Dw, Da | the correction matrices, $3\times3$ |
imu_intr_xi | the 24 intrinsics as an offset from the identity, in the convention’s order; it also carries $\mathbf{T}_g$ and the triad rotation |
b_g, b_a | biases, rad/s and m/s² |
t_ga, t_ga_sigma | gyro–accel offset and its 1-sigma, s |
Dw_diag, Da_diag | the diagonals, for a quick look only; in calyx Dw_diag is not a scale |
Dw_decomposed | calyx only (base and aux): scale, shear and misalignment rotation |
R_wtoI, U_w | calyx, base IMU only: the split above |
td | aux only: IMU–IMU time offset, s |
p_IsinI_m | aux only: lever arm to the base IMU, m |
gyro_only | aux only, present when the IMU was calibrated gyro-only |

The layout of imu_intr_xi:

Convention | $\mathbf{D}_w$ | $\mathbf{D}_a$ | $\mathbf{T}_g$ (column-major) | rotation vector |
kalibr | [0:6] | [6:12] | [12:21] | [21:24], ${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}$ |
rpng | [0:6] | [6:12] | [12:21] | [21:24], ${}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}$ |
calyx | [0:9] | [9:15] | [15:24] | none |

### With MVIS

mvis.recalib.load_rig_calib reads any convention
and applies the inverse model above:

from mvis.recalib import load_rig_calib

imu = load_rig_calib ( " cam_imu_calib.yaml " ).base_imu

w, a = imu.intr. correct ( w_m , a_m , imu.b_g , imu.b_a ) # true omega, true specific force in {I}

### With numpy only

Read the YAML with yaml.safe_load and pass one imus: entry. The Dw and
Da matrices come straight from the file; $\mathbf{T}_g$ and the rotation come
from imu_intr_xi. w_m and a_m are length-3 arrays of one sample, with the
accel already shifted by $t_{ga}$ (below).

kalibr
import numpy as np

from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation

def correct_kalibr ( w_m , a_m , imu ) :

xi = np. asarray ( imu [ " imu_intr_xi " ])

Dw, Da = np. asarray ( imu [ " Dw " ]), np. asarray ( imu [ " Da " ]) # lower-triangular

Tg = xi[ 12 : 21 ]. reshape ( 3 , 3 , order = " F " )

R_wtoI = Rotation. from_rotvec ( xi [ 21 : 24 ]). as_matrix ()

a = Da @ (a_m - imu[ " b_a " ]) # accel triad = {I}

w = R_wtoI @ Dw @ (w_m - imu[ " b_g " ] - Tg @ a)

return w, a

rpng
import numpy as np

from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation

def correct_rpng ( w_m , a_m , imu ) :

xi = np. asarray ( imu [ " imu_intr_xi " ])

Dw, Da = np. asarray ( imu [ " Dw " ]), np. asarray ( imu [ " Da " ]) # upper-triangular

Tg = xi[ 12 : 21 ]. reshape ( 3 , 3 , order = " F " )

R_atoI = Rotation. from_rotvec ( xi [ 21 : 24 ]). as_matrix ()

a = R_atoI @ Da @ (a_m - imu[ " b_a " ])

w = Dw @ (w_m - imu[ " b_g " ] - Tg @ a) # gyro triad = {I}

return w, a

calyx
import numpy as np

def correct_calyx ( w_m , a_m , imu ) :

xi = np. asarray ( imu [ " imu_intr_xi " ])

Dw, Da = np. asarray ( imu [ " Dw " ]), np. asarray ( imu [ " Da " ]) # full, upper-triangular

Tg = xi[ 15 : 24 ]. reshape ( 3 , 3 , order = " F " )

a = Da @ (a_m - imu[ " b_a " ]) # accel triad = {I}

w = Dw @ (w_m - imu[ " b_g " ] - Tg @ a) # Dw already holds the triad rotation

return w, a

We checked all three against ImuModel.correct in MVIS on random
intrinsics; they agree to machine precision.

### Shifting the accel by t_ga

Do this first, on the whole recording: re-sample the accel channel at each
stamp plus $t_{ga}$, so that gyro and accel describe the same instant.

import numpy as np

def shift_accel ( t , acc , t_ga ) :

""" t: (N,) stamps in s, sorted; acc: (N, 3) raw accel. Returns acc at t + t_ga. """

return np. stack ( [ np. interp ( t + t_ga , t , acc [ :, k ]) for k in range ( 3 ) ], axis = 1 )

### What mvis apply-calib does

mvis apply-calib writes a corrected copy of a ROS1 bag
(src/mvis/recalib/apply.py).
On each IMU message, in this order:

- t_ga: the accel is linearly re-interpolated at header stamp + $t_{ga}$
(--no-t-ga skips it).

- Intrinsics and bias: the inverse model above subtracts the saved
$\mathbf{b}_g$, $\mathbf{b}_a$ and removes $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$,
$\mathbf{T}_g$ and the triad rotation. --keep-bias leaves the biases in;
--no-imu-intrinsics removes only the biases.

- td: the header stamp becomes stamp + td (--no-td keeps the original).

An auxiliary IMU entry without imu_intr_xi is read with identity intrinsics,
so only its saved bias (if any) and its stamps change.

## t_ga: the gyro–accel offset

$t_{ga}$ is the time offset between the gyroscope and accelerometer channels
inside one IMU.

Many drivers publish gyro and accel together under one stamp, yet the two
channels are sampled at different rates and instants. MVIS takes the shared
stamp as the gyro clock and models the accel stored at $t$ as sampled at
$t - t_{ga}$.

cam_imu.yaml
solve :

estimate_t_ga : true # default in camera–IMU runs

sigma_t_ga : 0.010 # weak prior, s

- In the solve: a first-order correction inside the IMU factor, with
re-integration when $t_{ga}$ moves far
(details).

- Reported in the calibration YAML, the cam_imu.json summary
(t_ga_ms) and the report.

- Corrected by mvis apply-calib, as above.

- Checked by mvis roundtrip: after correction a
re-calibration should find $t_{ga}$ near zero.

Why it matters: a tool without $t_{ga}$ puts part of that delay into the
camera $t_d$. On real devices a single $t_{ga}$ can also depend on the motion.
Both are shown in Why calibrate t_ga.

## Gyro-only auxiliaries

The other answer to an untrustworthy accelerometer is to skip it:

cam_imu.yaml
input :

imus :

- {} # base IMU

- { gyro_only : true } # auxiliary IMU

What a gyro-only IMU solves and holds, and its factor:
Gyro-only mode. It is
not allowed on the base IMU, which needs its accelerometer for gravity and
metric scale. The result marks each such IMU with gyro_only: true.

We built it for the Intel T265 (Bosch BMI055), whose 62.5 Hz accel the driver
interpolates to 200 Hz. We calibrated, corrected the bag and calibrated again.
Without gyro-only, the T265’s td moved from +8.6 ms to −9.0 ms between the two
runs. With gyro-only it moved from +0.9 ms to +0.4 ms.

## Which to reach for

Both address an accelerometer that is out of step with its gyro:

Option | What it does | Prefer it for |
estimate_t_ga | Measures the offset | The base IMU, which must use its accel; the value itself is worth having |
gyro_only | Avoids the accelerometer | An auxiliary IMU whose accel adds nothing you need |

## What is observable

Each term needs the right motion:

- Scale and misalignment need rotation and acceleration on every axis.

- The triad rotation needs rotation about several axes while the
accelerometer sees gravity from several directions.

- G-sensitivity $\mathbf{T}_g$ needs rotation and strong linear
acceleration at the same time. Most hand-held motions do not produce that,
which is why the default leaves it out.

- $t_{ga}$ needs the specific force to change quickly, so that a time shift
changes the reading.

When a freed term returns near its start value with a wide covariance, it was
not observed. See Observability and
Degeneracy.


---

# Camera–IMU calibration math | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/camera-imu-math/

Use this page to see what the camera–IMU solve minimises and how a board corner
ties the cameras to the IMU trajectory. The two IMU factors have their own pages:

- Base IMU factor: links consecutive
states of the base IMU. Its intrinsics, biases and t_ga sit inside it.

- Auxiliary IMU factor: each extra IMU
sees the same motion through its own extrinsic, time offset and intrinsics.

A factor is one term of the cost. A residual is the error one factor
measures. The base IMU is the first IMU in the config; its clock is the
reference clock, and the trajectory is its pose over time. Symbols follow
Notation & glossary.

## The cost

The solve finds the one set of values that makes every measurement fit best,
given the priors. It minimises:

$\min_{\mathbf{x}}\;
\sum_{i,f}\rho\!\left(\big\|\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}^{i,f}\big\|^2_{\sigma_{px}}\right)
+\sum_{k}\big\|\mathbf{r}_{\text{imu}}^{k}\big\|^2_{\mathbf{P}_k}
+\sum_{j,k}\big\|\mathbf{r}_{\text{aux}}^{j,k}\big\|^2_{\mathbf{P}_{j,k}}
+\sum_{p}\big\|\mathbf{r}_{\text{prior}}^{p}\big\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p}$

- $\mathbf{x}$: everything solved: the IMU states, the board pose, and every
calibration value. The full list is on Calibration graph.

- $i, f$: camera, frame. $m$: a board corner.

- $\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}^{i,f}$: the residuals of all corners $m$ of frame $f$
in camera $i$, stacked into one vector (2 rows per corner).

- $k$: an interval between two IMU states. $j$: an auxiliary IMU.

- $\rho$: the Huber loss. It acts on a frame’s stacked residual, not on single
corners: past a whitened norm of 2 (2 px at $\sigma_{px}$ = 1 px) the error grows
linearly instead of quadratically, so a frame with a large total error is
down-weighted as a whole (solve.huber_px, default 2.0).

- $\|\mathbf{r}\|^2_{\boldsymbol\Sigma} = \mathbf{r}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{r}$:
the squared error weighted by its covariance. Pixels use $\sigma_{px}$ = 1 px
(solve.sigma_px). The IMU terms use $\mathbf{P}$, the covariance the
integration propagates from the IMU noise densities.

The solver is Levenberg–Marquardt (a damped Gauss–Newton method) with analytic
Jacobians (the derivatives of each residual with respect to each variable).

## The reprojection factor

The reprojection factor asks: given the current estimate, where should board
corner $m$ appear in the image, and how far is that from where it was detected?

### When was the corner captured?

A frame carries one stamp $t_C$ on the camera clock. Two things move the real
capture time of each corner:

- Time offset $t_{d,i}$: the camera clock runs offset from the base-IMU clock.

- Rolling shutter: a rolling-shutter camera exposes its rows one after
another. The whole frame takes the readout time $t_{r,i}$. A corner on row
$v_m$ of an image $H$ rows high is captured later than the first row.

$t_m = t_C + t_{d,i} + \eta(v_m)\, t_{r,i},
\qquad
\eta(v_m) = \frac{v_m}{H}$
$\eta(v)$ is the row factor of Notation. $\eta(v_m) = v_m/H$
is for a stamp at the top row, the default. With camera_input.rolling_mode: 1
(stamp at the middle row) $\eta(v_m) = v_m/H - 0.5$; with
camera_input.rolling_mode: 2 (stamp at the bottom row) $\eta(v_m) = v_m/H - 1$.
The table is in Camera model. The readout $t_{r,i}$ is solved only for a
rolling-shutter camera with estimate.camera.tr: true (off by default). Otherwise
the camera is treated as global shutter and $t_{r,i}$ is held at 0.

### Where was the IMU at that time?

The IMU states sit at discrete times $t_k$ (30 Hz by default, solve.state_hz).
A corner’s capture time $t_m$ almost never lands on one. MVIS gets the pose at
$t_m$ from the IMU itself. This is solve.vision_pose: imu, the default.

Take the state $k$ at or just before the frame (the anchor). Integrate the
raw base-IMU samples from $t_k$ over the signed interval $\Delta_m = t_m - t_k$:

${}^{G}_{I}\mathbf{R}(t_m) = {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}\;\Delta\mathbf{R}_m$
${}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I}(t_m) = {}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_k} + {}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k}\,\Delta_m
+ \tfrac12\,{}^{G}\mathbf{g}\,\Delta_m^2 + {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}\;\Delta\mathbf{p}_m$

- $\Delta\mathbf{R}_m$, $\Delta\mathbf{p}_m$: the rotation and position change
integrated from the IMU readings over $\Delta_m$, in the anchor’s frame. They
use the corrected readings: current biases, $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$,
$\mathbf{T}_g$ and t_ga (see Base IMU factor).

- ${}^{G}\mathbf{g} = [0,\ 0,\ -9.81]^\top$ m/s²: gravity in the global frame,
which is gravity-aligned.

- A negative $\Delta_m$ is integrated backwards in time. The window follows
the current $t_{d,i}$ and $t_{r,i}$, so it moves as they change.

The corner pose therefore follows the measured motion between states (for
example 200 Hz IMU samples between 30 Hz states). There is no interpolation
error for the calibration values to absorb. The IMU velocity and intrinsics enter
the reprojection factor too, so the gyro scale is fitted by the camera and the
IMU terms together.

To save time the factor integrates once and corrects the result to first order
as the estimate moves (solve.vision_imu_linearized, default on). It integrates
again when a capture time has moved more than 1 ms.

The older model: interpolation
solve.vision_pose: interp places the corner on the straight path between the
two neighbouring states. With $\lambda = (t_m - t_k)/(t_{k+1} - t_k)$:
${}^{G}_{I}\mathbf{R}(t_m) = {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}\,\mathrm{Exp}\!\big(\lambda\,\mathrm{Log}({}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}^\top\,{}^{G}_{I_{k+1}}\mathbf{R})\big),
\qquad
{}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I}(t_m) = (1-\lambda)\,{}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_k} + \lambda\,{}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_{k+1}}$Its error grows with angular acceleration times the state spacing squared. On
fast motion the time offsets, gyro scale and lever arm absorb it.

### Project and compare

With the IMU pose at $t_m$, chain the transforms from the board to the camera:

${}^{C_i}\mathbf{p}_m =
\big({}^{G}_{I}\mathbf{T}(t_m)\;{}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{T}\big)^{-1}\;
{}^{G}_{B}\mathbf{T}\;\big({}^{B}\mathbf{p}_m + h_m\,\mathbf{e}_z\big)$
$\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}^{i,f,m} =
\Pi\big({}^{C_i}\mathbf{p}_m;\ \mathbf{f}_i,\ \mathbf{d}_i\big) - \mathbf{z}_{i,m}$

- ${}^{B}\mathbf{p}_m$: the corner’s position on the board, from the board
config.

- $h_m$: the corner’s height off the flat board, along the board normal
$\mathbf{e}_z$. It is 0 unless estimate.board_points: true
(Why calibrate the board shape).

- ${}^{G}_{B}\mathbf{T}$: the board pose. The board stays still, so it is one
pose for the whole recording.

- $\Pi$: the camera model, with intrinsics $\mathbf{f}_i$ and
distortion $\mathbf{d}_i$ (Camera model).

- $\mathbf{z}_{i,m}$: the detected pixel.

One factor holds all corners of one frame. It touches the anchor pose, the
anchor velocity and biases, the board pose, the camera’s calibration
(${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{T}$, $t_{d,i}$, $t_{r,i}$, $\mathbf{f}_i$, $\mathbf{d}_i$),
the IMU intrinsics, t_ga, and the board heights when they are solved.

### How the time offsets get their gradient

The time offsets have a derivative because the pose depends on the capture time:

$\frac{\partial\,{}^{G}_{I}\mathbf{T}(t_m)}{\partial t_{d,i}} \;\propto\;
\begin{bmatrix} {}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}(t_m) \\ {}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I}(t_m) \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\,\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}}{\partial t_{r,i}} = \eta(v_m)\,\frac{\partial\,\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}}{\partial t_{d,i}}$
So $t_{d,i}$ is seen only while the rig turns or moves, and $t_{r,i}$ only when
corners on different rows move differently. Observability
works this through.

## Why calibration sits inside the factors

One could integrate the IMU with fixed values and correct the result later. The
solver could not move those values then: the correction has no derivative with
respect to them.

MVIS puts every calibration value inside the residual instead:

- the IMU intrinsics $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$, $\mathbf{T}_g$ and the biases;

- the extrinsics ${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{T}$ and ${}^{I}_{I_{s_j}}\mathbf{T}$;

- the time offsets $t_{d,i}$, $t_{d,j}$, t_ga and the readout $t_{r,i}$.

Each then has a Jacobian, and the optimiser can move it. The price: the IMU
integrals depend on the values being solved. The factors carry first-order
corrections for small changes and integrate again when a value moves far.

## What each factor constrains

Factor | Constrains directly | Constrains through the others |
Reprojection | camera intrinsics, ${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{T}$, $t_{d,i}$, $t_{r,i}$, board pose and shape | the trajectory, and the gyro scale through the corner poses |
Base IMU | biases, $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$, $\mathbf{T}_g$, t_ga | metric trajectory, gravity direction |
Auxiliary IMU | ${}^{I}_{I_{s_j}}\mathbf{T}$, $t_{d,j}$, its own intrinsics and t_ga | the base trajectory, through the shared motion |

No single factor sees the whole state. Which values the data can fix depends on
the motion: see Observability and
Degeneracy.

## What this means for your recording and setup

- Turn and move while the board is in view. The time offsets and the readout
get their signal only from motion.

- Fill the image rows. The readout is fitted from how the error changes from
the top row to the bottom row.

- Give the solve a good camera prior. The camera intrinsics are refined here,
but they start from the camera-only result
(step 3).

- Use the cleanest camera as the first camera. Its frames set the state times.
A global-shutter, low-latency camera is best
(step 4).


---

# Calibration graph | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/calibration-graph/

Use this page to see everything MVIS solves at once, and in what order it gets
there.

A factor graph links the unknowns (variables) to the measurements and
priors that constrain them (factors). Each factor adds one term to the cost;
the solver moves all variables together until the total is smallest. That joint
solve is what lets a camera’s time offset, an IMU’s scale and a lever arm be
fitted from one recording.

Symbols follow Notation & glossary. The factor equations are
on Camera–IMU calibration math,
Base IMU factor and
Auxiliary IMU factor.

## The camera–IMU graph

The camera–IMU graph for one camera, one auxiliary IMU and five states. Each
state holds the base-IMU pose, velocity and biases. Not drawn, to keep it
readable: the reprojection factors also touch the anchor’s velocity and biases,
the IMU intrinsics and t_ga; the auxiliary IMU has its own velocity and bias at
each of its knots. The IMU calibration variables have priors; camera calibration
gets one only on what is held (see Priors below).

## Variables

Variable | Symbol | Size | How many |
IMU pose | ${}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{T}$ | 6 | one per state, at solve.state_hz (30 Hz) on the first camera’s frames |
IMU velocity and biases | ${}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k}$, $\mathbf{b}_{g,k}$, $\mathbf{b}_{a,k}$ | 9 | one per state |
Board pose | ${}^{G}_{B}\mathbf{T}$ | 6 | one; the board stays still |
Board shape | $h_m$, one per board corner $m$ | 1 per corner | only with estimate.board_points: true |
Camera calibration | ${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{T}$, $t_{d,i}$, $t_{r,i}$, $\mathbf{f}_i$, $\mathbf{d}_i$ | 8 + intrinsics | one per camera |
Base IMU intrinsics | $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$, $\mathbf{T}_g$ (and a triad rotation) | 24 | one |
Gyro-to-accel offset | $t_{ga}$ | 1 | one per IMU, when estimate_t_ga is on (the default) |
Auxiliary IMU calibration | ${}^{I}_{I_{s_j}}\mathbf{T}$, $t_{d,j}$, its intrinsics | 31 | one per auxiliary IMU |
Auxiliary IMU velocity and biases | ${}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_{s_j}}$, $\mathbf{b}_{g,s}$, $\mathbf{b}_{a,s}$ | 9 (3 if gyro-only) | one per auxiliary knot |

$\mathbf{x}$ stacks all of them. A 60 s recording at 30 Hz has 1800 states,
each with a pose, a velocity and two biases.

## Factors

Factor | Links | Weight |
Reprojection | one frame’s corners to its anchor state, the board, the camera calibration, the IMU intrinsics and t_ga | 1 px per axis; Huber past 2 on the frame’s stacked residual |
Base IMU | two consecutive states, the IMU intrinsics, t_ga | the integration covariance |
Auxiliary IMU | two base states 3 intervals apart, the auxiliary states and calibration | the integration covariance |
Priors | single variables (below) | per prior |

Rates. Each camera adds about 10 reprojection factors per second
(solve.factor_hz, settable per camera). The state rate stays 30 Hz, so the
trajectory stays dense even when the cameras are thinned.

Priors:

- Gauge on the first pose: a gauge prior fixes directions the data cannot
see. Here it holds the first pose’s position and its rotation about gravity.
The tilt (the direction of gravity in the IMU frame) stays free, since the
accelerometer sees gravity.

- First velocity and biases: weak (0.5 m/s, 0.01 rad/s, 0.1 m/s²).

- IMU intrinsics: a tight prior on the pinned blocks, a weak one on the freed
blocks (which blocks).

- t_ga: zero-mean, 10 ms.

- Camera calibration: free, except a tight prior on whatever is held: $t_{r,i}$
on a global-shutter camera, and any estimate.camera.*: false.

- Board shape: each height has a 3 mm prior. A gauge prior holds the mean height
and the two tilts at 0, so the board pose keeps the plane and the heights keep
only the shape.

## The cost

The solve minimises the weighted sum of all factor errors, given on
Camera–IMU calibration math.
After the solve, MVIS computes the marginal covariance of every calibration
variable. Its square root is the 1σ (one standard deviation) printed next to
each value. A wide 1σ is how a weakly observed value shows itself.

## Stages of a camera–IMU run

mvis cam-imu reaches the joint solve in steps. Each step gives the next a
starting point close enough to converge.

Stage | What happens | What is estimated |
1. Window | Bags longer than 80 s: keep the 80 s with the most gyro and accelerometer excitation (input.window_mode: motion). Shorter bags: from 3 s in (input.t0). | — |
2. Detection | Board corners in every frame. | — |
3. Frame selection | Keep frames with enough corners and a valid board pose (PnP: the camera pose from known board points); thin each camera to factor_hz. | the board pose per frame, from the camera prior |
4. Start values | Per camera: time offset from angular rates, rotation and gyro bias from a rotation fit, then a linear solve for gravity, scale, velocities and lever arm; the accelerometer bias starts at 0. Per auxiliary IMU: offset, rotation and gyro bias from gyro-to-gyro. | rough $t_{d,i}$, ${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{R}$, ${}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{C_i}$, gyro bias, gravity direction; ${}^{I}_{I_{s_j}}\mathbf{R}$, $t_{d,j}$ |
5. Joint solve | The graph above, Levenberg–Marquardt, up to 50 iterations. t_ga re-integration as needed. | everything at once |
6. Clock retiming (opt-in) | For cameras marked retime_sensor_clock: a first solve gives each frame its own capture offset, a regular sensor clock is fitted to them, the frames are re-stamped, and the joint solve runs again. | per-frame offsets, then everything |
7. Results | Residuals; χ² per degree of freedom per factor type (the weighted squared error divided by its degrees of freedom, about 1 when the noise model fits); 1σ for every value. | — |

Checks on the way:

- Start values: a lever-arm start with 1σ over 5 cm starts at 0 instead. The start reports its
gravity magnitude and scale (both should come out near 9.81 m/s² and 1) and how
sharp the time-offset minimum is.

- The joint solve: Levenberg–Marquardt can stop at its damping cap far from
a minimum, which looks like convergence. MVIS spots this from the step the
linear system still predicts, solves again from the same start with a different
damping, and keeps that result only if its cost is lower. A solve whose linear
system cannot be solved (no step at all) is marked not ok.

## Stages of a camera-only run

mvis cam has no IMU. Its graph holds one board pose per timestamp, the
intrinsics of every camera, the extrinsic of every camera to the first one, the
rolling-shutter readout, the board shape when asked, and time offsets between
cameras when optimize_time_offset is on (off by default).

Stage | What happens | What is estimated |
1. Detection | Board corners in every frame. | — |
2. Start values | Per camera: OpenCV intrinsics (radtan) or a vanishing-point start (other models), and a board pose per frame. | intrinsics, board poses |
3. Gating | Drop frames with too few tags (6) or too small a spread, poses with a PnP error over 10 px, corners seen in too few frames. | — |
4. Per-camera solve | One graph per camera. | intrinsics, distortion, board poses, readout of rolling-shutter cameras |
5. Alignment | Align the board-pose tracks of the cameras. | camera-to-camera extrinsics, time offsets |
6. Joint solve | All cameras in one graph. | everything at once |
7. Outlier rerun | Drop corners and frames whose error is over 2 px and above the 99th percentile; solve again from the previous values. On by default. | everything again |

The camera-only solves after the start values thin the corners to two per tag
(corner_subsample: two_anti); the start values use every corner. The camera–IMU solve keeps all of them.

## What this means for your recording

- Record about 60 s. Past 80 s, MVIS keeps the 80 s with the most motion.

- Read the 1σ, not only the residual. A small residual with a wide 1σ means
the value was not observed: see Degeneracy.

- Leave solve.state_hz at 30 Hz. Lower rates undersample fast motion
(step 4).


---

# Observability | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/observability/

Use this page to see which motion makes which calibration value measurable, and
why.

A value is observable when the measurements change if the value changes. If
they do not, the data cannot tell a right value from a wrong one, however long
you record. The solver then returns roughly its start value, with a wide 1σ.

Whether a calibration value is observable depends on the motion. The MVIS paper
analyses this for the full multi-camera, multi-IMU state, and the earlier
papers below give the degenerate motions for the time offset, extrinsics and IMU
intrinsics:

- Y. Yang, P. Geneva, G. Huang,
Multi-visual-inertial system: Analysis, calibration, and estimation,
The International Journal of Robotics Research 43(13), pp. 1995–2026, 2024.

- Y. Yang, P. Geneva, K. Eckenhoff, G. Huang,
Degenerate motion analysis for aided INS with online spatial and temporal sensor calibration,
IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 4(2), pp. 2070–2077, 2019.

- Y. Yang, P. Geneva, X. Zuo, G. Huang,
Online IMU intrinsic calibration: Is it necessary?,
Robotics: Science and Systems XVI, 2020.

This page gives the short reason for each value. Symbols follow
Notation & glossary; the factors are on
Camera–IMU calibration math.

## Never observable: four directions

The measurements are relative: the cameras see the board, the IMUs feel motion
and gravity. Moving the whole scene (board and trajectory) or turning it about
gravity changes nothing they measure. So four directions are never observable:

- global position (3);

- rotation about gravity (1).

MVIS holds them with a prior on the first state’s position and its rotation
about gravity. The tilt (the direction of gravity in the IMU frame) stays free:
the accelerometer sees gravity, so it is observable. Metric
scale is observable too: the board has a known size, and the accelerometer
measures in m/s².

## What each value needs

Value | Needs | Short reason |
Camera intrinsics $\mathbf{f}_i$, $\mathbf{d}_i$ | the board seen at many distances, angles and across the whole image | from the board alone |
Extrinsic rotation ${}^{I}_{C_i}\mathbf{R}$ | rotation about at least 2 axes | camera and gyro see the same angular velocity, rotated |
Lever arm ${}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{C_i}$ | rotation about at least 2 axes, with changing angular velocity | it shows up only through rotation |
Time offset $t_{d,i}$ | angular velocity that changes, and some translation | a time shift moves a pose by its velocity |
Readout $t_{r,i}$ | fast rotation about the camera’s x or y axis, board spread over many rows | each row is shifted by its own share of the readout |
Gyro scale and misalignment $\mathbf{D}_w$ | rotation about every axis, at varied rates | each column multiplies one axis of the angular velocity |
Accel scale and misalignment $\mathbf{D}_a$, bias $\mathbf{b}_a$ | gravity along every axis (tilts), plus linear acceleration changes | each column multiplies one axis of the specific force |
G-sensitivity $\mathbf{T}_g$ | strong linear acceleration while rotating on all axes | the gyro error must vary with acceleration, apart from rotation |
t_ga | quickly changing acceleration (brisk reversals) | it enters only through the rate of change of acceleration |
Auxiliary IMU rotation and $t_{d,j}$ | rotation about at least 2 axes | the two gyros see the same angular velocity |
Auxiliary IMU lever arm | rotation about at least 2 axes, with changing angular velocity | centripetal and tangential acceleration |

The motion in step 2: record the dataset is built
