The runner and its baselines stay with the maintainers, not in the public repository; the commands
below are how we run it. See Regression testing for the tests you can run.

python scripts/run_regression.py --mode all --level fast # the gate

python scripts/run_regression.py --only-collection mvis_4imus_3cams/april_01

python scripts/run_regression.py --mode all --level all --dry # compare existing results only

--level | Runs |
fast | The first recording of each family: the gate for every change |
mid | Three recordings per family |
full | Every recording of every family |
optional | Rows outside the gates, such as camera-model variants |
all | full and optional |

--help prints the current row counts.
--update-baseline rewrites the stored baselines after an intended change; the baseline diff
then shows every number the change moved.
How the suite is built: Regression testing.


---

# Submit results | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/contribute/submit-results/

Use this page if you want results from your calibration tool next to MVIS,
Kalibr and Basalt on the Leaderboard.

Open submissions are paused
We are replacing the old submission process with a new one. Until it opens,
pull requests to the submissions repository are not merged and no outside
results appear on the leaderboard. You can still send us results through an
issue (see below).

## How the leaderboard is built today

- Who runs it: we run MVIS, Kalibr and Basalt ourselves on the same
recordings. The current numbers are from batch 2026-11-24a.

- What it shows: each calibration parameter per tool, as the median and
spread over the recordings of one test family (a group of recordings of one
rig, solved with one setup). Real recordings have no ground truth, so a gap
between tools shows where they disagree, not which one is right. See
Methodology.

- Where the data lives: every record is public in the Hugging Face dataset
calibench-vi/results
under the CC BY 4.0 licence.

The results repository has this layout:

Path | Contents |
<Tool>/<batch>/<family>.json | one record per tool and test family: per method, the number of recordings, the median reprojection error, and each parameter’s median, spread, count and status |
configs/<family>/<Tool>/ | the configuration files behind each record |
schemas/ | the JSON schema of a record |
datasets.json, sensors.json | the dataset and sensor catalogues |
families.json | datasets to families, with each family’s recordings, sensors and caveats |
runs/<dataset>/<date>/ | separate studies outside the leaderboard batch, one folder per dataset and date (for example runs/virig-5imus-4cams/2026-11-02/) |

## Compare your tool now

You do not need us to compare your tool against the leaderboard.

- Get the data. Download the recordings from
calibench-vi/datasets
(see Datasets). The VI-Rig sets are gated: accept the terms on
the Hugging Face page first.

- Use the same recordings. Take the recording list of a family from
families.json in calibench-vi/results.

- Run your tool on those recordings.

- Compare your values with the MVIS, Kalibr and Basalt records of that
family and batch.

## Send us your results

Open an issue in
openmvis/calibench-submissions.
Include:

- Tool: name, version and commit hash, and a link to the code or paper.

- Configs: the exact configuration files and command-line flags, per
dataset. Attach the files; do not describe them in prose.

- Recordings: the dataset and recordings you ran, and which ones you used
for calibration.

- Outputs: your calibration outputs, not scores: intrinsics, distortion,
extrinsics and time offsets per run. Add each parameter’s standard deviation
(σ) if your tool reports it.

- Statistic: for any metric you report yourself, its exact definition, for
example “median reprojection error over all corners of all frames”.

- Runtime and hardware: wall-clock time per dataset, CPU, RAM, GPU if used,
and operating system.

- Licence: a statement that your outputs may be published under CC BY 4.0.

Rotations: give them as the log(R) rotation vector in radians, or as a rotation
matrix or quaternion. Do not give roll, pitch and yaw angles.

We reply on the issue. When the new submission process opens, this page and the
README of openmvis/calibench-submissions describe it.

## Related pages

- Leaderboard

- Methodology

- Evaluation & metrics

- Submit a dataset

# Regression testing | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/contribute/regression-testing/

Use this page before you change MVIS code. It lists the test tiers you can run
from a clone of github.com/openmvis/openmvis
and tells you which one to run when.

## Set up

git clone https://github.com/openmvis/openmvis

cd openmvis

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Python 3.11 or 3.12, Linux or macOS

pip install -e " .[apriltag,aruco,ros1,dev] "

The dev extra installs pytest. See Installation
for the other extras.

## The four tiers

Run the smallest tier that covers your change. Each one is a single command
from the repository root.

Tier | Command | What it runs | Time | When |
Unit | scripts/test.sh unit | every test except the slow and integration ones | about 4 min | while coding |
Solver | scripts/test.sh solver | five real solves: a simulated camera–IMU solve, the t_ga term end to end, two checks on one digital twin, and a check that the fast linearised IMU factor matches the exact one | about 1 min | with unit; CI runs it |
Integration | scripts/test.sh integration | digital twins, and a simulated camera whose frames are stamped by polling the sensor clock, through the full solver | about 3 min | before you commit a solver change |
Full | scripts/test.sh full | everything in tests/ | about 20 min | before a merge |

- t_ga: the time offset between the gyroscope and the accelerometer of one
IMU. See Why t_ga.

- Times are approximate and depend on your machine.

- What scripts/test.sh does: it pins the linear-algebra library (BLAS) to
one thread, so results repeat. It tests the src/ of this checkout, not an
installed copy.

- Extra arguments go to pytest: scripts/test.sh unit -k imu.

- Interpreter: set PYTHON to choose it.

## What CI runs

- When: on every pull request and every push to main.

- What: the unit and solver tiers only.

- What it skips: the slow and integration tests. Run
scripts/test.sh full yourself before you ask for a merge.

## Tests that need recordings

Some tests read real recordings. They skip when the data is missing, so a
clean clone passes without any download.

To run them:

- Log in with hf auth login, or set HF_TOKEN. The VI-Rig sets are gated: accept their terms on the
dataset page first.

- Pick a folder for the data and set MVIS_DATASETS to it. Without it, MVIS
uses ~/Datasets.

- Download what you need with mvis datasets download. Use mvis datasets list
to see the catalogue, and --dataset <key> to fetch one dataset.

hf auth login

export MVIS_DATASETS = / path / to / datasets

mvis datasets list

mvis datasets download --dataset <key>

scripts/test.sh full

See Datasets for what each set contains and its licence.

## Digital-twin tests

A digital twin is a simulated copy of a real recording. The integration tier
solves twins of two real stereo camera–IMU recordings, without images:

Twin | Covers |
twin_gs | global-shutter cameras, 470 Hz IMU, t_ga +5.3 ms |
twin_rs | rolling-shutter cameras with negative readout (rows read bottom to top), 200 Hz IMU, t_ga −7.4 ms |

How a twin works:

- The truth: a real solve, moved by a fixed random step so that no real
device calibration ships in the test files. Focal length moves by up to 1 %,
the principal point by 4 px, other intrinsics by 5 %, the extrinsic rotation by
10 mrad and the lever arm by 5 mm per axis, td (the time offset between the
camera and IMU clocks) by 1 ms and t_ga by 0.5 ms.

- What it keeps: the real frame times, corner ids, IMU timestamps and solve
settings.

- The precise check: the solve without noise. Any error left there is bias
in the estimator.

- The limits: set just above the measured errors, so a failure means
something changed.

- Iteration check: each test also checks that the optimiser iterated. A
result flagged ok alone does not show that it solved.

The noise is Gaussian, and a twin has no lens or timing model errors. So the
twin tests check the estimator, not a real recording. The fixtures are in
tests/data/twins/. Making a new fixture needs the recording; running the tests
needs only the fixture.

To simulate your own rig, see Digital-twin check.

## Where new tests go

- Place: tests/<area>/test_<topic>.py, one folder per area: camera,
detection, calibration, cam_imu, simulation, config, io, mvisdb,
datasets, cli, recalib and integration.

- Helpers: shared helpers go in tests/helpers/. A test module does not
import from another test module.

- Library code belongs in src/mvis. Tests import from scripts/ only to
test a script’s own command line.

- Do not refactor tests/_reference/. It is a frozen copy of earlier code
that the speed-up tests compare against bit for bit.

- Slow tests: tests/slow_tests.txt lists the tests that take over 5 s, and
tests/conftest.py marks them slow. Add a new slow test to that list by
hand; no marker is needed in the test file.

## Beyond the test tiers

We also run two larger suites: real benchmark recordings, and digital twins of
them, each compared parameter by parameter with earlier approved results. They
need the full dataset collection and many hours of compute, so they are not
part of the tiers above. The same recordings, solved with MVIS, Kalibr and
Basalt, make the Leaderboard; Methodology
explains how we run them and Evaluation & metrics
defines the metrics.

## Related pages

- CONTRIBUTING.md:
pull-request rules and the licence header for new files

- Governance


---

# Submit a dataset | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/contribute/submit-dataset/

Use this page to give us a calibration recording of your rig. A rig we have not
seen is worth more than another run on one we have. We credit every dataset we
host.

The steps:

- Check that it is usable.

- Package it in a format MVIS reads.

- Write a dataset card.

- Choose the licence.

- Send it.

## 1. Check that it is usable

We can only calibrate from a recording that has:

- Raw sensor streams: no rectified (pre-undistorted) images and no
vendor-corrected IMU output. The IMU (inertial measurement unit) is the
gyroscope and accelerometer. A correction we cannot undo hides the intrinsics,
the sensor’s own parameters, so they cannot be calibrated.

- A calibration board in view for most of the recording. MVIS reads
AprilGrid, chessboard and ArUco boards. See Set up the board.

- Motion on every axis: rotation about all three axes and translation along
them, not just one kind. See Record the dataset
and Degeneracy.

- Timestamps from one clock for all streams, or a stated offset between
clocks.

Run mvis inspect <path> on your recording before you send it. It reports
which MVIS modes can read it, each camera stream (rate, resolution, encoding),
each IMU stream (rate, units, timestamp order) and how long the camera and IMU
streams overlap.

## 2. Package it

MVIS reads these inputs. Pick one that fits what you recorded:

- ROS1 bag: Image messages, or PNG or JPEG CompressedImage. Reading it
needs no ROS install.

- ROS2 bag.

- EuRoC / ASL folder: the mav0 layout used by EuRoC and TUM-VI.

- Image folder, or timestamped images: camera only. These carry no IMU
data, so use one of the formats above for a camera–IMU recording.

mvis inspect lists the modes (cam, cam-imu) that can read your
recording.

Configuration lists the input fields for each.

MVIS does not read video files. Convert video to images first.

Send these details with the data:

Item | What to give |
Board | type, rows and columns, tag or square size in metres, tag spacing, tag family |
Sensors | model, rate, resolution and topic of each camera and IMU |
Shutter | global or rolling for each camera; for rolling shutter, the readout direction if you know it |
Timing | hardware-synchronised or not, and how timestamps are taken |
Reference | any existing calibration, and the tool that produced it |

Send a reference calibration even if it is rough, and say how you got it. Then a
method can be checked against your recording, not only run on it.

## 3. Write a dataset card

Add one short page (a README.md) next to the data:

- Rig: what it is and what makes it different.

- Recording: how and where you recorded it.

- Known problems: dropped frames, clock jumps, saturated IMU segments,
streams synchronised in software.

- Licence: the licence, and how to cite the data.

- Contact: who answers questions about it.

Say what is wrong with it
The known-problems section matters most. A documented flaw leaves a usable
dataset. An undocumented one gives results nobody can explain, and every later
user repeats the same debugging.

## 4. Licence

The licence must let us publish results computed on the data. For us to host a
copy, it must also allow redistribution.

- Hosted by us: recordings we host in the Hugging Face dataset
calibench-vi/community
use CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial, attribution required). Downloads need a free
Hugging Face login with automatic approval.

- Hosted by you: if your data must stay under another licence, keep it where
it is. We add a download recipe that points to your copy.

- People and private spaces: blur faces, screens, documents and anything
else private before you send the data. We do not publish recordings that
still show them.

- Your rights: you must own the data or have the right to grant the licence.

## 5. Send it

Open an issue on openmvis/mvis_pages.
In it:

- describe the rig in one or two sentences

- link the data (any download link works)

- attach or link the dataset card

We reply on the issue and arrange hosting from there. Data we host ends up in
calibench-vi/community;
open the request on the issue tracker, not there.

## Credit

We credit every dataset we host. What that includes is listed in
Governance › Credit. To send results on an
existing dataset instead, see Submit results.


---

# Governance | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/contribute/governance/

Use this page to know what to expect before you put effort into a contribution.

## Repositories

Repository | Holds | Where to contribute |
openmvis/openmvis | the MVIS toolbox (code, tests, docs) | issues and pull requests |
openmvis/mvis_pages | this site | issues and pull requests; dataset offers |
openmvis/calibench-submissions | leaderboard submissions | issues while submissions are paused; see Submit results |
calibench-vi/datasets and calibench-vi/community on Hugging Face | the recordings | see Submit a dataset |
calibench-vi/results on Hugging Face | the leaderboard records | written by us only |

## Maintainers

- Who: the maintainers are listed on Contributors.

- What they do: review and merge pull requests, run the benchmark, host the
datasets and make releases.

- Releases: only maintainers can create release tags. A tag builds the
package and publishes it to PyPI after a maintainer approves it.

- Support: MVIS is research code, maintained on a best-effort basis.

## How contributions are reviewed

Contribution | What we check |
Code | correct behaviour, a test that fails before and passes after, the CI tiers pass, no unintended change in benchmark results |
Documentation | the facts are right and the page stays its type (see below) |
Dataset | format, dataset card, licence, no private content (see Submit a dataset) |
Results | the configs, outputs and provenance needed to reproduce them (see Submit results) |

CI (the checks that run automatically on GitHub) tests what it can. A maintainer
reviews the rest.

For code, read CONTRIBUTING.md
first. In short:

- One topic per pull request, with a test that fails before the change and
passes after it.

- Keep CI green: scripts/test.sh unit and scripts/test.sh solver. Run
scripts/test.sh full before you ask for a merge. See
Regression testing.

- Licence header: new source files start with the same licence header as the
files in src/. A test checks it.

- Bug reports: include the config YAML, the full log, mvis --version, your
operating system and Python version, and a link to the data if you can share it.

## Page types on this site

Each page declares a pageType in its frontmatter and keeps to it:

Type | Contains | Does not contain |
tutorial | one ordered path from start to result | alternatives, options, theory |
guide | the steps for one task | derivations (link to a concept page) |
concept | explanation, maths, figures | commands (link to a guide) |
reference | complete lists, one anchor per entry | narrative |
example | a real run, with its checks | concepts introduced for the first time |

When a page drifts, split it instead of mixing the two types:

- A guide that starts explaining means a concept page is missing.

- A concept page that starts giving commands means a guide is missing.

We review documentation pull requests against this table.

## Licence of contributions

A pull request to openmvis/openmvis comes with the contributor terms in
CONTRIBUTING.md:
you keep the copyright, and grant the copyright holder the right to offer your
contribution under the commercial licence too. How the code, datasets and
results are licensed: License.

## Conduct

Be civil and assume good faith. We do not accept:

- harassment

- personal attacks

- submissions made in bad faith

Maintainers may close issues, reject contributions and restrict participation
when these rules are broken. Report a problem to contact@openmvis.com.

## Security problems

Do not open a public issue for a security problem. Email contact@openmvis.com
with the affected version (mvis --version), the steps to reproduce and, if you
have one, a fix. We acknowledge reports within a week. The full policy is in
SECURITY.md.

## Credit

- Code contributors are listed in the AUTHORS file of openmvis/openmvis.

- Datasets we host get:

- a citation entry in the dataset card

- a named entry on Contributors

- where we calibrate it, a page for the rig in the Device wiki
with the results

- Security reports are credited in the changelog unless you ask us not to.

# Changelog | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/about/changelog/

Use this page to see what changed in the toolbox, on the documentation site and
in the datasets. Notable changes come newest first.

- Toolbox releases: listed below and in the toolbox’s
CHANGELOG.md;
the full
commit history has every change.

- Site changes: see the
site repository.

## MVIS 0.1.0

The first public release. There is no earlier public version, so the list
describes the toolbox as it ships. Released on 2026-11-15, on
PyPI and Zenodo.

- Package: pymvis (import and command mvis), Linux and macOS (Windows
tentative), Python 3.11 and 3.12.

### Calibration

- Camera-only (mvis cam): one or more cameras; intrinsics, distortion,
extrinsics, camera–camera time offset and rolling-shutter readout (the time
the sensor takes to read the image row by row).

- Camera–IMU (mvis cam-imu): camera–IMU extrinsics, time offset td,
readout, camera intrinsics, IMU intrinsics, biases, the gyro–accel offset
t_ga (for the base IMU and every auxiliary IMU that is not gyro_only),
and the extrinsics and time offsets of further IMUs.

- Camera models: eight, usable in both modes and mixed within one rig:
radtan, equidistant, kb4, fov, double_sphere, eucm, ucm and
omni_radtan (experimental). fisheye means kb4.

- IMU conventions: kalibr, rpng and calyx, with scale and
misalignment (Dw, Da) and optional g-sensitivity (Tg).

- estimate: block: chooses what is solved and what is held, including the
board shape (board_points).

- One command for both modes: mvis run runs either mode from one config
(mode: cam or mode: cam-imu).

- Batch: input.bags calibrates a whole set of recordings from one config.

### Input and output

- Inputs: image folders, timestamped images, ROS1 bags (Image, and PNG or
JPEG CompressedImage), ROS2 bags and EuRoC / ASL folders.

- ROS2 without ROS: ROS2 bags (a bag folder, or one .db3 or .mcap file)
are read with the pure-Python rosbags, with no ROS install.

- Boards: AprilGrid, chessboard and ArUco.

- Kalibr interop: read and write Kalibr camchains.

- Output: YAML calibration files, JSON results and self-contained HTML
reports for both modes.

- Datasets: mvis datasets lists, downloads and verifies the Calibench-VI
datasets on Hugging Face.

### Tools

- mvis apply-calib: writes a corrected copy of a ROS1 bag: IMU intrinsics
and bias removed, streams re-stamped by td, accelerometer shifted by t_ga,
images optionally undistorted.

- mvis roundtrip: calibrates, applies the result, calibrates again, and
gives a PASS/FAIL report. ROS1 bags only.

- mvis check, mvis inspect, mvis verdict: check the environment and
config, summarise a dataset, and grade a finished result.

- Simulator (mvis.simulation): digital twins of real recordings.

## Site

### Release preparation (2026-11-12)

- Datasets section: Datasets is now its own section. The old
/reference/datasets/ addresses redirect.

- Continuous-time page removed: its address redirects to
Calibration graph.

- Pages updated for 0.1.0: install steps, defaults and licences follow the
release; benchmark figures come from batch 2026-11-10a.

### New addresses (2026-11-09 and 2026-11-10)

- Device wiki: now at /devices/ (2026-11-10).

- Benchmark: its own section (2026-11-09), with results at /benchmark/results/,
examples at /benchmark/examples/.

- Old addresses redirect.

### Why calibrate (2026-11-10 and 2026-11-12)

A section on what each calibrated quantity changes: IMU,
t_ga, board shape,
fisheye model (kb4), rolling shutter,
multi-camera and multi-IMU.

### Leaderboard shows results, not scores (2026-11-03)

Each dataset shows the results of MVIS, Kalibr and Basalt side by side, with
the differences between them. There are no scores or ranks. See
Methodology.

### Move to Astro + Starlight (August 2026)

The site moved from jemdoc to Astro + Starlight, with search, dark mode and
KaTeX maths. The old openmvis.com/*.html pages redirect.

## Datasets

The datasets are on
Hugging Face. Each set
and its licence is listed on Datasets.

- VI-Rig recordings (ours): multi-camera, multi-IMU recordings, CC BY 4.0
and gated.

- Partner recordings: Looper and GiLabs, on the same terms.

- Converted third-party sets: Monado MIC, MGC and MOC, and the TUM-VIE frame
cameras, CC BY 4.0.

- Now CC BY 4.0, commercial use included: every recording in
calibench-vi/datasets:
the VI-Rig sets, looper-insight9 and gilabs-examples, like the converted
sets before. Access stays gated.

- Before: the VI-Rig sets were CC BY-NC 4.0 from 2026-09-11, the Looper and
GiLabs sets from 2026-11-03. A copy downloaded then may now be used under
CC BY 4.0 as well.

- Unchanged: device recordings in
calibench-vi/community
keep each folder’s licence, CC BY-NC 4.0 unless the folder says otherwise. See
License.

# Roadmap | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/about/roadmap/

Use this page to see what we plan after MVIS 0.1.0. These are intentions, not
commitments with dates. What shipped is on the Changelog.

## Toolbox

Item | Status |
pip install pymvis from PyPI | done: pypi.org/p/pymvis |
Public code repository | done: github.com/openmvis/openmvis |
omni_radtan | experimental in 0.1.0 |
Stable config schema | not before 1.0: 0.x releases may change it |
Windows | tentative: MVIS has run there, but GTSAM has no Windows wheels, so the install steps are not written up yet |
Python 3.13 | blocked upstream: the NumPy 1.x that GTSAM 4.2 needs has no 3.13 wheel |

## Documentation

The CLI, Configuration and
Python API pages were checked against MVIS 0.1.0.
When they differ from the code, mvis <command> --help and mvis check are
authoritative.

## Benchmark and datasets

Item | Status |
New results submission process | being set up; see Submit results |
Verified results (a maintainer re-runs a submission) | planned |
Contributed datasets | open; see Submit a dataset |

## Not planned

- Replacing Kalibr for single-IMU rigs. Kalibr is mature and widely used.
MVIS adds what Kalibr does not cover, such as rolling-shutter readout on
several cameras, camera–camera time offsets, the gyro–accel offset t_ga and
the board shape. See
Comparison.

- A single combined score on the leaderboard. How to weigh one parameter
against another is the reader’s call, not the benchmark’s. See
Methodology.

Missing something you need? Open an issue on
the toolbox repository (or on
the site repository for this site).

# FAQ & troubleshooting | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/about/faq/

Use this page to learn what OpenMVIS is, or when MVIS does not install, a run
fails, or a result looks wrong. Each entry gives the short answer first, then
the reason.

## About OpenMVIS

### What is OpenMVIS?

Answer: open-source multi-visual-inertial sensor calibration.

- OpenMVIS: the project.

- MVIS: the calibration toolbox, installed as the Python package pymvis;
the import and the command are mvis. It calibrates cameras (intrinsics,
distortion, extrinsics, time offsets, rolling-shutter readout) and cameras
with one or more IMUs (extrinsics, time offsets, IMU intrinsics, biases and
t_ga).

- Calibench-VI: our datasets and results on
Hugging Face.

More: Overview and
Contributors & citation.

### Is MVIS a Kalibr alternative that runs without ROS?

Answer: yes. MVIS is pure Python: it installs with pip and reads ROS1 and
ROS2 bags itself, with no ROS install and no C++ build.

- Kalibr: needs a ROS workspace (ROS 1, or Docker).

- Basalt: runs without ROS, but needs a C++ build.

- Kalibr files: MVIS reads and writes Kalibr camchains and reads Kalibr
AprilGrid target files, so a Kalibr calibration can be its start.

Kalibr is mature and widely validated, and MVIS does not aim to replace it
where it works well. The full feature matrix:
Comparison vs Kalibr / Basalt.

### Can MVIS calibrate rolling-shutter cameras with an IMU?

Answer: yes. MVIS solves the rolling-shutter readout in camera-only and in
camera–IMU solves, one readout per camera.

- Mixed rigs: global-shutter and rolling-shutter cameras and IMUs go into
one solve.

- Kalibr: its rolling-shutter tool is camera-only, a separate tool.

- Basalt: solves no readout.

How to run it: Rolling-shutter calibration. Why it matters:
Why calibrate rolling shutter.

### Can MVIS calibrate several IMUs at once?

Answer: yes. MVIS puts every IMU in one graph. The first IMU is the base
IMU; each auxiliary IMU gets its extrinsics, time offset and intrinsics.

- Gyro-only mode: an auxiliary IMU whose accelerometer is unreliable can be
calibrated from its gyroscope alone (gyro_only: true).

- Kalibr: also solves several IMUs in one run, without a gyro-only mode.

- Basalt: takes one IMU per run, so a four-IMU rig is calibrated IMU by IMU
and composed.

How to run it: Multi-IMU calibration. Why it pays
off: Why calibrate IMUs together.

### Should I use MVIS, Kalibr or Basalt?

Answer: pick by what your rig and your workflow need.

- Kalibr: mature and widely used. If it already works on your rig, there is
no need to switch.

- MVIS: adds what Kalibr and Basalt do not cover: the gyro–accel offset
t_ga, the board shape, rolling-shutter readout in the camera–IMU solve, a
gyro-only mode per auxiliary IMU, corrected-bag export (mvis apply-calib)
and a PASS/FAIL round-trip check (mvis roundtrip). It needs no ROS.

- Basalt: a C++ build with no ROS, for one IMU per run.

We ran all three on public data; the per-dataset results are side by side on
the Leaderboard, with no scores or ranks. Details:
Comparison vs Kalibr / Basalt.

### What is the licence, and how do I cite it?

Answer: MVIS is GPL-3.0-only, or a commercial licence.

- GPL-3.0-only: free for everyone, companies included, for research,
teaching and internal use. Software you distribute that includes or is
derived from MVIS must be released under GPL-3.0.

- Commercial licence: for closed-source products. Write to
licensing@openmvis.com.

- Your results: results you compute on your own recordings are yours.
Results on our datasets are CC BY 4.0.

- Datasets: the recordings in calibench-vi/datasets (VI-Rig, Looper,
GiLabs and the converted third-party sets) are CC BY 4.0, commercial use
included, and gated. Community device recordings are CC BY-NC 4.0 unless
their folder says otherwise.

- Citing: cite the MVIS paper; cite the OpenMVIS project
(Zenodo DOI) for the toolbox, the
site and the benchmark results; cite Calibench-VI when your results depend
on our datasets.

Full terms: License. BibTeX entries:
Contributors & citation.

## Install

### Which platforms and Python versions work?

Answer: Linux or macOS (x86-64 or arm64), Python 3.11 or 3.12.

- Windows: tentative. MVIS has run there, but GTSAM, the optimisation
library MVIS builds on, publishes no Windows wheels, so the install steps
are not written up yet.

- No Python 3.13: MVIS needs NumPy 1.x (see below), and NumPy 1.x has no
3.13 wheel.

- No Python 3.10 or older: GTSAM publishes wheels for 3.11 and newer only.

### How do I install it?

Answer: from PyPI, into a Python 3.11 or 3.12 virtual environment.

python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

pip install " pymvis[apriltag,ros1] "

mvis check --env --smoke # checks the environment and runs a small solve

Add the aruco extra for ArUco boards. The package is pymvis; the import
and the command are mvis. Full steps, including an install from source:
Installation.

### Which extras do I need?

Answer: only the ones for your board and your input.

- apriltag: AprilGrid boards (the grid of square AprilTag markers).

- aruco: ArUco boards. It installs opencv-contrib-python; install it in
a fresh environment, because it and opencv-python both provide cv2.

- ros1: ROS1 and ROS2 bags, through the pure-Python rosbags reader.

- viz: the optional Rerun 3D viewer.

- mcap: converting MCAP episodes with H.265 video (it installs PyAV).
ROS2 bags stored as .mcap need only ros1.

Chessboards, image folders and EuRoC folders need no extra.

### Do I need ROS to read a bag?

Answer: no, for ROS1 or ROS2 bags. The ros1 extra installs rosbags, a
pure-Python reader, so you need no ROS installation or catkin workspace.

-
ROS2 bags: give the bag folder with its metadata.yaml, or one .db3 or
.mcap file.

-
ROS1 only: mvis apply-calib and mvis roundtrip work on ROS1 bags only.

-
Image topics: sensor_msgs/Image, and sensor_msgs/CompressedImage in
PNG or JPEG.

-
JPEG: lossy, so it can shift corners. MVIS warns once per topic.

-
Rejected: compressedDepth and video codecs stop the run with an error.

### Can I calibrate from a video file?

Answer: not directly. Extract the frames into an image folder first.

The inputs are image folders, timestamped image folders, ROS1 bags, ROS2 bags
and EuRoC / ASL folders.

### Segfault when MVIS builds a pose

Answer: you have NumPy 2. Install NumPy 1.x.

pip install " numpy<2 "

GTSAM 4.2 from pip is built against the NumPy 1.x ABI. With NumPy 2,
constructing a gtsam.Pose3 crashes instead of raising an error. pymvis pins
numpy<2, so this only happens when something else upgrades NumPy later. The
same pin keeps OpenCV below 4.12, whose wheels need NumPy 2.

### Does it work on macOS?

Answer: yes. We test on Apple silicon (arm64) with Python 3.11. Intel Macs
are not tested.

## Choosing settings

### Which camera model should I use?

Answer: pick by the lens.

- Ordinary (non-fisheye) lens: radtan, the pinhole model with
radial-tangential distortion.

- Fisheye: kb4, the Kannala-Brandt model. fisheye and kannala_brandt
mean kb4. It stays valid past 90° from the optical axis.

- equidistant: the same polynomial, but it stops at 90°. It gives the same
pixels as kb4 when every corner is under 90°. MVIS warns you to switch to
kb4 when a fit has corners past 90°.

- Others: fov, double_sphere, eucm, ucm and omni_radtan
(experimental) are there to match a downstream system that expects them.

Why kb4 is the fisheye default: Fisheye model (kb4). The
equations: Camera model.

### Which IMU convention should I use?

Answer: the one your downstream estimator reads. The default is calyx.

The convention sets how the IMU intrinsics are written down, not how well they
fit. We calibrated TUM-VI (4 raw recordings) and Monado MIC (8 recordings) with
each of the three. The reprojection error, lever arm, baseline, td and the
corrected readings agreed across conventions; only the way the matrices are
laid out differs.

- kalibr: lower-triangular scale and misalignment matrices Dw (gyro)
and Da (accel), plus a free gyro-to-IMU rotation.

- rpng: upper-triangular Dw and Da, plus a free accel-to-IMU rotation.

- calyx: a full 3×3 Dw and an upper-triangular Da, with no separate
rotation. The gyro rotation is recovered from Dw after the solve.

All three can add Tg, the gyro’s sensitivity to linear acceleration. Set the
convention with estimate.imu.model or solve.imu_intrinsics_model. How to
correct raw readings with each one: IMU model.

### Which sign does td have?

Answer: td is the camera–IMU time offset. An image stamped $t_\text{cam}$
sees the IMU pose at $t_\text{cam} + t_d$.

- Kalibr: timeshift_cam_imu uses the same sign
($t_\text{imu} = t_\text{cam} + \text{shift}$), so compare the two values as
they are.

- Basalt: the same sign as well.

- Aux IMUs: their td is relative to the base IMU, with the same sign as
Kalibr’s per-IMU time_offset.

### What is t_ga, and why is it on by default?

Answer: t_ga is the time offset between an IMU’s gyroscope and its
accelerometer. MVIS estimates it in every camera–IMU run
(solve.estimate_t_ga: true).

- Meaning: the accelerometer sample stamped $t$ was taken at
$t - t_\text{ga}$; the gyroscope defines the IMU clock.

- Why it matters: some drivers merge a slower accelerometer into the gyro
stream by interpolation. The Intel T265 is one: its 62.5 Hz accelerometer is
resampled to 200 Hz. Without t_ga, that delay goes into td.

- Correcting it: mvis apply-calib shifts the accelerometer channel by
t_ga; --no-t-ga turns that step off.

Kalibr and Basalt have no t_ga. That is why the MVIS td can differ from
theirs on the same recording. See Why calibrate t_ga.

### Should I estimate the board shape?

Answer: yes, unless you know the board is flat. Set
estimate.board_points: true.

A printed board is never flat. Held flat in the solve, a bent board pulls the
focal length and, in camera–IMU runs, the gyro scale and the lever arm. With
board_points on, MVIS estimates a height per corner along the board normal,
with a 3 mm prior. It is off by default; our VI-Rig runs turn it on. See
Why calibrate the board shape.

## Running

### Few or no detections

Answer: check the board settings against the board you printed.

- AprilGrid: rows and cols count tags; check tag_size (metres),
tag_spacing (gap over tag size) and tag_family.

- Chessboard: rows and cols count inner corners; check square_size.

- ArUco: check marker_size, marker_separation and aruco_dict.

Then run mvis inspect <dataset path> for a summary of what MVIS sees in the
recording, and mvis check -c config.yaml to lint the config. MVIS detects at
several scales, so far and near boards both work. It cannot fix a wrong tag
family. Board set-up: Set up the board.

### Every translation is off by the same factor

Answer: the board size in the config does not match the print. Measure a tag
(or square) with calipers and set tag_size or square_size in metres.

### Quality gating drops most of my frames

Answer: the recording is too sparse. Get closer to the board, keep more of
it in view, or move more slowly.

Quality gating removes frames and corners that would be poorly constrained:

- Per frame: at least 6 tags.

- Per corner: at least 5 views across all cameras, and at least 3 in each
camera.

- Shared frames: a reference frame needs at least 20 % of the tags across
the cameras.

### Initialisation fails on a wide fisheye

Answer: use kb4.

- Why: with equidistant, corners past 90° can make the first estimate
unusable.

- What MVIS does: it checks the first estimate of each camera. If the
principal point falls outside the image or the distortion is extreme, it logs
a warning naming the camera and restarts from a plain guess (focal length half
the longer image side, principal point at the centre).

- If the warning appears: switch the camera to kb4 and run again.

### A wide-field stereo fit diverged

Answer: fit each camera alone, then use those intrinsics in the stereo or
camera–IMU solve.

On TUM-VI, stereo camera-only fits with double_sphere, eucm or fov can
drift into a wrong solution, where the focal length trades against the model’s
shape parameter. Single-camera fits stay stable. The two-step recipe is in
examples/configs/tumvi_cam_imu/.

### It is slow

Answer: check these, in order.

- BLAS threads: the mvis command pins the numerical library (BLAS) to one
thread, because the solve works on small matrices and extra threads only spin.
If you import mvis from your own Python, set OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1,
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 and MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 before NumPy loads.
MVIS_BLAS_THREADS=<n> changes the CLI’s choice. Details:
doc/blas_threads.md.

- Detection cache: set input.cache_dir. Re-runs on the same recording then
skip detection, and a camera-only and a camera–IMU run share it.

- Frame rate in the solve: factor_hz sets how many frames per second enter
the camera factors. Lower it to cut the solve time.

- Corner subsampling: camera-only runs already keep two diagonal corners per
tag (two_anti). Do not drop to one corner (top_left): it shifts the
principal point by up to about 0.8 px.

- Window: by default (input.window_mode: motion), a camera–IMU run
solves the 80 s segment with the most IMU motion. Lower
input.segment_length to cut the time, or set window_mode: manual with
t0 and window (seconds) to choose the span yourself. Recordings shorter
than segment_length are used whole.

### Results did not change after I changed detection settings

Answer: clear the detection cache. The cache is keyed on the recording, the
image topic and the board, so other detection changes reuse the old detections.
Delete the cache_dir folder and run again.

## Results that look wrong

### Reprojection error is low but the extrinsics look off

Answer: check that the motion constrained them. Read the motion-excitation
grade in the HTML report, and for camera–IMU runs on a ROS1 bag also run
mvis roundtrip.

A low reprojection error means the solution explains its own observations. A
parameter the motion never constrained stays near its starting value without
raising the error. See Degeneracy.

### The round trip fails

Answer: treat it as a real finding. (mvis roundtrip works on ROS1 bags
only.) Common causes:

- Wrong camera model: on a fisheye, use kb4.

- An interpolated accelerometer: keep estimate_t_ga on, or set
gyro_only: true for that auxiliary IMU.

- Too little motion: record again with rotation about every axis and
changes of speed.

See Round-trip validation.

### td or the lever arm look wrong on a fast-moving rig

Answer: keep state_hz at its default, 30 Hz.

state_hz is how many pose states per second the camera–IMU solve places along
the trajectory. Below 30 Hz, reprojection, lever arm and td get worse on fast
motion. Slow, gentle recordings barely notice.

### One IMU’s accelerometer is unreliable

Answer: set gyro_only: true for that IMU under input.imus.

MVIS then calibrates that IMU from its gyroscope alone: rotation, td, gyro
scale (Dw) and gyro bias. Its lever arm, Da and Tg stay fixed. This works
for auxiliary IMUs only; the base IMU needs its accelerometer for gravity and
metric scale.

### IMU intrinsics come back at their starting values

Answer: the motion did not constrain them.

- Scale and misalignment: need rotation and acceleration on every axis.

- Tg: needs rotation and strong linear acceleration at the same time.

See Degeneracy.

### Results differ from Kalibr’s

Answer: check these, in order.

- IMU convention: kalibr, rpng and calyx write different matrices for
the same device. Compare like with like.

- Transform direction and sensor numbering: MVIS stores T_cam_imu like
Kalibr; check which camera and IMU each value belongs to.

- t_ga: Kalibr has none, so td can differ on IMUs with a gyro–accel
offset.

- Board shape: Kalibr holds the board flat. With
estimate.board_points: true, MVIS does not, and that alone moves the focal
length on a bent board.

mvis.io.kalibr reads and writes Kalibr camchains, which is the reliable way to
compare. Our side-by-side results are on the Leaderboard.

### Results differ between recordings of the same rig

Answer: the parameters that differ were not well constrained by the motion
in some recordings.

Calibrate every recording from one config with input.bags (see
Camera–IMU calibration) and compare the
spread. Without ground truth, the spread across recordings is the most honest
accuracy measure.

## Still stuck

Open an issue on
github.com/openmvis/openmvis.
Include:

- Your config YAML

- The full log

- The output of mvis --version

- Your OS, CPU and Python version

- A link to the data, if you can share it

Report security problems privately to contact@openmvis.com, not in an issue.

# Auxiliary IMU factor | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/camera-imu-math/aux-imu/

Use this page to see how MVIS calibrates every IMU after the first one.

An auxiliary IMU is any IMU after the first in input.imu_topics. It is
rigidly mounted, so it feels the same motion as the base IMU, seen from another
place, along other axes and on another clock. MVIS solves, for each one:

- Extrinsic ${}^{I}_{I_{s_j}}\mathbf{T}$: its rotation and position in the
base-IMU frame. The position part is its lever arm.

- Time offset $t_{d,j}$: an auxiliary sample stamped $t$ is the motion at
base-IMU time $t + t_{d,j}$.

- Its own intrinsics: $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$, $\mathbf{T}_g$, in the
same convention as the base IMU.

- Its own t_ga and its own biases.

Below we write $I_s$ for $I_{s_j}$. Symbols follow
Notation & glossary. The base factor this builds on is
Base IMU factor.

## Variables

Variable | Size | Where |
calibration: ${}^{I}_{I_s}\mathbf{T}$, $t_{d,j}$, 24 intrinsics | 6 + 1 + 24 = 31 | one per auxiliary IMU |
velocity ${}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_s}$, biases $\mathbf{b}_{g,s}$, $\mathbf{b}_{a,s}$ | 9 | at the auxiliary knots |
t_ga of this IMU | 1 | one per auxiliary IMU |

The auxiliary IMU has no pose states of its own. Its poses come from the base
trajectory, so every auxiliary factor pulls on the base states too.

Knots: one auxiliary factor spans 3 base intervals by default
(solve.aux_imu_stride: 3). Fewer factors make the solve faster. The stride is not
accuracy-neutral: the lever arms shift with it. When the lever arm matters, solve
again with solve.aux_imu_stride: 1 (one factor per interval, slower) and compare.

## From the base pose to the auxiliary pose

At each knot $k$ MVIS builds the auxiliary IMU’s pose from the base state, the
extrinsic and the time offset:

${}^{G}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}_k = {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}\;\mathrm{Exp}\!\big({}^{I}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}\;{}^{I_s}\boldsymbol{\omega}_k\;\delta t_{d}\big)\;{}^{I}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}$
${}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_s,k} = {}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_k} + {}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k}\,\delta t_{d}
+ {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}\;\mathrm{Exp}\!\big({}^{I}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}\;{}^{I_s}\boldsymbol{\omega}_k\;\delta t_{d}\big)\;{}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{I_s}$

- ${}^{I_s}\boldsymbol{\omega}_k$: the auxiliary IMU’s corrected angular
velocity at the knot.

- $\delta t_d = t_{d,j} - \bar t_{d,j}$: only the part of the time offset not
yet absorbed. MVIS cuts the auxiliary samples for interval $[t_k, t_{k+1}]$ at
stamps $[t_k - \bar t_{d,j},\ t_{k+1} - \bar t_{d,j}]$, with $\bar t_{d,j}$ the
starting value. The pose then needs only a small shift, which keeps the
first-order propagation accurate even for offsets of tens of ms.

## The residual

The auxiliary IMU’s own readings are preintegrated over the knot interval,
exactly as for the base IMU: corrected by its own biases, intrinsics and t_ga.
The residual is the same 15-row residual as the
base factor, evaluated on the
auxiliary poses above and the auxiliary velocity and biases:

$\mathbf{r}_{\text{aux}}^{j,k} =
\mathbf{r}_{\text{imu}}\Big(
{}^{G}_{I_s}\mathbf{T}_{k},\ {}^{G}_{I_s}\mathbf{T}_{k'},\
{}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_s,k},\ {}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_s,k'},\
\mathbf{b}_{s,k},\ \mathbf{b}_{s,k'};\
\mathbf{x}_{in,s},\ t_{ga,s}\Big)$
with $k'$ the next knot. The Jacobians chain the base-factor Jacobians through
the pose map above, so they reach the base poses, the base velocities, the
extrinsic and $t_{d,j}$. All are analytic and checked against finite differences.

### Why the lever arm needs rotation

A point at ${}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{I_s}$ on a rigid body feels the base acceleration
plus two rotation terms:

${}^{I_s}\mathbf{a} = {}^{I}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}^\top\Big({}^{I}\mathbf{a}
+ \big({}^{I}\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\big)^\wedge{}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{I_s}
+ \big(({}^{I}\boldsymbol\omega)^\wedge\big)^2\,{}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{I_s}\Big)$
$(\cdot)^\wedge$ is the cross-product (skew-symmetric) matrix of Notation. With no rotation both terms vanish
and the lever arm leaves no trace. The rotation of the extrinsic and $t_{d,j}$
come from the gyro alone: two gyros on one body read the same angular velocity,
rotated and shifted in time.

## Starting values

Before the joint solve, MVIS initialises each auxiliary IMU from its gyro and the
base gyro alone. Both are direct angular-rate measurements at 100 Hz or more, so
this is sharper than going through a camera.

- Time offset: scan $t_{d,j}$ and keep the value where the two gyro signals,
aligned by the best rotation, agree best. A parabola refines the minimum.

- Rotation: the best rotation between the two gyro signals at that offset
(the Kabsch method, a closed-form least-squares rotation fit).

- Gyro bias from the means of the two signals.

- Lever arm: 0. Only the joint solve can see it.

The start is accepted when the minimum is sharp (the error at
$\pm$ half the search window is more than 1.5 times the minimum) and the two
streams overlap by more than 10 s.

## Priors

- First knot: velocity and biases, as for the base IMU (0.5 m/s, 0.01 rad/s,
0.1 m/s² by default).

- Extrinsic and time offset: free. estimate.imu.extrinsics: false or
estimate.imu.td: false holds them at their start.

- Intrinsics: staged as for the base IMU (estimate.imu.intrinsics).

- t_ga: the same weak 10 ms prior as the base IMU.

## Gyro-only mode

Some accelerometers are noisy or interpolated by their driver. Mark such an IMU
gyro_only: true and MVIS calibrates it from its gyro alone:

cam_imu.yaml
input :

imus :

- {} # base IMU: always full

- { gyro_only : true } # second IMU: gyro only

The factor keeps only the rotation and gyro-bias rows:

$\mathbf{r}_{\text{gyro}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathrm{Log}\!\Big(\Delta\mathbf{R}^\top\;{}^{G}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}_k^\top\,{}^{G}_{I_s}\mathbf{R}_{k'}\;\mathrm{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\Big)\\[2pt]
\mathbf{b}_{g,s,k'} - \mathbf{b}_{g,s,k}
\end{bmatrix}$

| Gyro-only IMU |
Solved | extrinsic rotation (unless estimate.imu.extrinsics: false), $t_{d,j}$ (unless estimate.imu.td: false), gyro bias, and $\mathbf{D}_w$ unless estimate.imu.intrinsics: pinned |
Held | lever arm, $\mathbf{D}_a$, $\mathbf{T}_g$ and the triad rotation (kalibr, rpng), at their start values; no t_ga is solved |
States | the gyro bias at each knot; no velocity or accel bias |

The base IMU cannot be gyro-only: it needs its accelerometer for gravity and
metric scale.

## What this means for your recording

- Rotate about at least two axes, briskly. The auxiliary rotation and time
offset come from angular velocity; the lever arm from angular velocity and
angular acceleration.

- Record long enough for the gyro start: the two IMUs must overlap by more
than 10 s.

- Mount the IMUs rigidly. The model assumes one rigid body.

How we run multi-IMU rigs: step 6: multi-IMU calibration.
Why it pays off: Why calibrate IMUs together.

# Base IMU factor | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/concepts/camera-imu-math/base-imu/

Use this page to see how MVIS turns the base IMU’s raw readings into a factor
between two trajectory states, with the IMU’s own errors solved inside it.

- Base IMU: the first IMU in the config. Its clock is the reference clock and
its pose is the trajectory.

- State: the IMU pose, velocity and biases at one time $t_k$. States sit at
solve.state_hz (30 Hz by default) on the first camera’s frames.

- Preintegration: the IMU readings between two states, combined into one
relative rotation, velocity change and position change.

Symbols follow Notation & glossary. The IMU conventions
(calyx, kalibr, rpng) are on IMU model.

## Corrected readings

The gyroscope gives $\boldsymbol{\omega}_m$ and the accelerometer
$\mathbf{a}_m$. MVIS corrects each reading before it integrates it:

${}^{I}\mathbf{a} = {}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}\;\mathbf{D}_a\,\big(\mathbf{a}_m - \mathbf{b}_a\big)$
${}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega} = {}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}\;\mathbf{D}_w\,\big(\boldsymbol{\omega}_m - \mathbf{b}_g - \mathbf{T}_g\,{}^{I}\mathbf{a}\big)$

- $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$: correction matrices. Their diagonal fixes
the scale of each axis; the rest fixes misalignment (axes not quite at right
angles). They multiply the raw reading, so a diagonal of 0.998 means the raw
axis read 0.2 % high.

- $\mathbf{T}_g$: g-sensitivity, the part of the gyro reading caused by
linear acceleration.

- $\mathbf{b}_g$, $\mathbf{b}_a$: the biases, solved at every state.

- ${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}$, ${}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}$: the gyro and accelerometer
triad rotations into the IMU frame. Each convention frees at most one of them:

Convention | $\mathbf{D}_w$ | $\mathbf{D}_a$ | Free rotation | $\{I\}$ is | Intrinsic parameters |
calyx (default) | full 3×3 (9) | upper-triangular (6) | none; folded into $\mathbf{D}_w$ | the accel triad | 9 + 6 + 9 ($\mathbf{T}_g$) = 24 |
kalibr | lower-triangular (6) | lower-triangular (6) | ${}^{I}_{w}\mathbf{R}$ (3) | the accel triad | 6 + 6 + 9 + 3 = 24 |
rpng | upper-triangular (6) | upper-triangular (6) | ${}^{I}_{a}\mathbf{R}$ (3) | the gyro triad | 6 + 6 + 9 + 3 = 24 |

All three give the solver one 24-value intrinsics variable $\mathbf{x}_{in}$.
It starts at identity (no correction).

An IMU slower than 200 Hz is first upsampled (cubic, the real samples kept)
before integration (solve.imu_min_rate_hz).

## Preintegration

Between two states at $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$ ($\Delta t = t_{k+1} - t_k$), the
corrected readings give the motion in the frame of the first state:

$\Delta\mathbf{R}_{k} = {}^{I_k}_{I_{k+1}}\mathbf{R},
\qquad
\Delta\mathbf{v}_{k} = \int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}} {}^{I_k}_{I_\tau}\mathbf{R}\;{}^{I}\mathbf{a}_\tau\,d\tau,
\qquad
\Delta\mathbf{p}_{k} = \int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}\!\!\int_{t_k}^{s} {}^{I_k}_{I_\tau}\mathbf{R}\;{}^{I}\mathbf{a}_\tau\,d\tau\,ds$
MVIS evaluates these with ACI3: analytic combined IMU integration
(ACI2, Yang et al., ICRA 2020) extended with the
IMU intrinsics in the MVIS paper. Between two
samples it takes the midpoint of the two corrected readings as constant and
integrates the rotation and the rotated acceleration in closed form. The same
pass gives:

- the Jacobians of $\Delta\mathbf{R}$, $\Delta\mathbf{v}$, $\Delta\mathbf{p}$
with respect to the biases, the 24 intrinsics and t_ga;

- the 15×15 covariance $\mathbf{P}_k$, from the noise densities (solve.sigma_g,
sigma_a) and the bias random-walk densities (sigma_bg, sigma_ba).

The integration runs once, at the biases and intrinsics of the start point.
Small changes after that are applied through the Jacobians. A detection gap is
bridged by one factor over the whole gap.

## The gyro-to-accel offset t_ga

Many drivers publish gyro and accelerometer on one stamp, though the two were
sampled at different instants. MVIS takes the stamp as gyro time. The
accelerometer value that belongs to gyro time $t$ is the one stamped
$t + t_{ga}$. Over one integration step from sample 0 to sample 1, to first order:

$\bar{\mathbf{a}}_m = \tfrac12\big(\mathbf{a}_{m,0} + \mathbf{a}_{m,1}\big) + t_{ga}\,\dot{\mathbf{a}}_m,
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf{a}}_m = \frac{\mathbf{a}_{m,1} - \mathbf{a}_{m,0}}{\delta t}$

- One more Jacobian column: $\partial\bar{\mathbf{a}}_m/\partial t_{ga} = \dot{\mathbf{a}}_m$,
carried through $\mathbf{D}_a$ and, through $\mathbf{T}_g$, into the gyro.

- Re-integration: after the first two iterations, when t_ga has moved more
than 3 ms from the value the factors were integrated at, MVIS integrates that
IMU again with its accelerometer resampled at $t + t_{ga}$
(solve.tga_relin_threshold_s, default 0.003 s). The linear term then covers
only what is left.

- Prior: a weak zero-mean prior, 10 ms (solve.sigma_t_ga).

estimate_t_ga is on by default in camera–IMU runs. What the offset is and when
it matters: Why calibrate t_ga.

## The residual

The factor links state $k$ (pose ${}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{T}$, velocity
${}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k}$, biases) to state $k+1$. It predicts the measured
preintegration from the two states and compares.

Write $\delta\boldsymbol{\beta}$ for the change since integration:
$\delta\mathbf{b}_g$, $\delta\mathbf{b}_a$, $\delta\mathbf{x}_{in}$ and
$\delta t_{ga}$. First-order corrections, built from the Jacobians above:

$\delta\boldsymbol\theta = \mathbf{J}_{R}\,\delta\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
\delta\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{J}_{v}\,\delta\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
\delta\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{J}_{p}\,\delta\boldsymbol\beta$
The 15 residual rows are:

$\mathbf{r}_\theta = \mathrm{Log}\!\Big(\Delta\mathbf{R}_k^\top\;{}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}^\top\,{}^{G}_{I_{k+1}}\mathbf{R}\;\mathrm{Exp}(\delta\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\Big)$
$\mathbf{r}_p = {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}^\top\Big({}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_{k+1}} - {}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I_k} - {}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k}\,\Delta t - \tfrac12\,{}^{G}\mathbf{g}\,\Delta t^2\Big) - \delta\mathbf{p} - \Delta\mathbf{p}_k$
$\mathbf{r}_v = {}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}^\top\Big({}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_{k+1}} - {}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I_k} - {}^{G}\mathbf{g}\,\Delta t\Big) - \delta\mathbf{v} - \Delta\mathbf{v}_k$
$\mathbf{r}_{b} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{b}_{g,k+1} - \mathbf{b}_{g,k}\\ \mathbf{b}_{a,k+1} - \mathbf{b}_{a,k}\end{bmatrix}$
The cost is $\|\mathbf{r}\|^2_{\mathbf{P}_k}$ with
$\mathbf{r} = [\mathbf{r}_\theta;\ \mathbf{r}_p;\ \mathbf{r}_v;\ \mathbf{r}_b]$.

- Bias random walk: $\mathbf{r}_b$ is the random-walk term. Biases may drift
between states, by as much as the random-walk densities allow. There is no
separate bias factor.

- No robust loss: the IMU residual is plain least squares. Only the
reprojection factor uses Huber.

- The covariance follows the correction: $\mathbf{P}_k$ is rotated by the
current $\delta\boldsymbol\theta$ before it weights the residual.

## Jacobians

Every block is analytic and checked against finite differences in the test
suite.

Variable | Rows it touches | Comes from |
pose $k$ | $\mathbf{r}_\theta$, $\mathbf{r}_p$, $\mathbf{r}_v$ | the predicted relative motion, rotated into frame $k$ |
pose $k+1$ | $\mathbf{r}_\theta$, $\mathbf{r}_p$ | the same, at the end point |
velocity $k$, $k+1$ | $\mathbf{r}_p$, $\mathbf{r}_v$ | ${}^{G}_{I_k}\mathbf{R}^\top$, times $\Delta t$ in $\mathbf{r}_p$ |
biases $k$ | all | the bias Jacobians of the integration; identity in $\mathbf{r}_b$ |
biases $k+1$ | $\mathbf{r}_b$ | identity |
intrinsics $\mathbf{x}_{in}$ | $\mathbf{r}_\theta$, $\mathbf{r}_p$, $\mathbf{r}_v$ | the intrinsic Jacobians of the integration |
t_ga | $\mathbf{r}_\theta$, $\mathbf{r}_p$, $\mathbf{r}_v$ | the t_ga column of the integration |

## Which intrinsics are solved

estimate.imu.intrinsics frees blocks of $\mathbf{x}_{in}$. A pinned block gets a
very tight prior at its start value; a freed block gets a weak one, so a direction
the motion does not excite stays near its start instead of drifting.

Setting | Free | Weak prior on the free terms |
pinned (or false) | nothing | — |
dw_da (default) | $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$ | 0.1 (solve.sigma_dw_da) |
dw_da_r | as dw_da, plus the free rotation (kalibr, rpng; same as dw_da under calyx, which has no separate rotation) | 0.1 (solve.sigma_imu_R) |
full (or true) | as dw_da_r, plus $\mathbf{T}_g$ | 0.05 (solve.sigma_tg) |

## The same model inside the reprojection factor

The reprojection factor integrates the same corrected readings from an anchor
state to each corner’s capture time
(Camera–IMU calibration math).
So $\mathbf{D}_w$, $\mathbf{D}_a$, the biases and t_ga are fitted by both
factors, with one consistent model.

## What this means for your recording

- Rotate about all three axes. Each column of $\mathbf{D}_w$ needs rotation
about its axis.

- Point every axis at gravity at some time. Gravity is the largest specific
force you have. Tilting the rig through many orientations separates
$\mathbf{D}_a$ from $\mathbf{b}_a$.

- Change the acceleration briskly. t_ga appears only through
$\dot{\mathbf{a}}_m$; smooth, steady motion leaves it loose.

- Leave $\mathbf{T}_g$ pinned unless the motion has strong linear acceleration
while it rotates. Hand-held motion rarely does.

More: Observability and Degeneracy.

# Cameras and IMUs | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/devices/components/

Every camera and IMU we have calibrated, by who made the chip. A label names a part only when the device maker, the dataset authors or a published teardown names it. Otherwise it says “not known”; we don’t guess. A measurement gives the frame rate, not the chip, so it never names a part.

- Maker: the device maker’s datasheet, product page, manual or written statement names the part. A private source has no link.

- Dataset: the dataset authors, or the device’s own calibration file in the dataset, name it.

- Teardown: a published teardown or trade article names it; the maker has not.

- Module: a packaged IMU module (Xsens, MicroStrain). We name the module; no source names the chip inside.

# Local gravity | OpenMVIS

URL: https://openmvis.com/reference/local-gravity/

A camera + IMU solve holds the gravity magnitude fixed. Gravity is most of what an
accelerometer measures, so the accelerometer scale (Da) takes up any error in it.
Set the gravity where the data was recorded:

cam_imu.yaml
gravity : 9.8013 # m/s², Newark, Delaware

Or give the place instead, with site:. MVIS takes the latitude and altitude and computes
WGS84 normal gravity from them, and the report then names the city:
site: {latitude_deg: 39.68, altitude_m: 40, name: "Newark, Delaware"} (name is only a
label). You may give both keys if they agree within 0.01 m/s². From MVIS 0.4.1 the report
names the place in the comment after the gravity: value; with site: it names the site.

- Without either key: MVIS uses 9.81 m/s² and the run log warns. The accelerometer scale
then reads high by 9.81 / g. In Shenzhen g is 0.23 % below 9.81, so the scale reads 0.23 % high;
at the equator 0.30 % high; in central Europe close to zero.

- A measured value from a gravity survey also goes in gravity:.

- site: takes coordinates, not a city name: names repeat (Córdoba, Spain and Córdoba, Argentina),
and a site outside any city still has coordinates. The calculator below finds them from a city name.

- Precision: anywhere in the right city is enough. One degree of latitude moves g by
at most 0.01 %, 100 m of altitude by 0.003 %. Altitude matters only for high places
(Kunming −0.06 %, Lhasa −0.11 %).

Requires MVIS 0.4.0 or later. The keys and their checks are in
Configuration.

## Calculator

Type your city and pick it from the list: about 34,000 places, every one with more than
15,000 people, with their latitude and altitude. You don’t need the longitude, and the altitude
only matters above about 300 m. Or press Use my location: your browser asks first, and the
location stays on this page. You can also type the latitude and altitude yourself.

The calculator uses the same formula as MVIS (WGS84 normal gravity with the free-air
correction) and runs in your browser: nothing you type is sent anywhere. It gives the
gravity: line to copy, and the site: line under it if you prefer to give the place.
With your own coordinates, put your label in place of “your place”.

The city list is from GeoNames (CC BY 4.0). The table under
the calculator lists common recording places.

City

Longitude is not needed. Altitude only matters above about 300 m.
